title: AIRoA-0: Long-Horizon, Precise, Cross-Embodiment Manipulation from Handheld Data
summary: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.
full_text: Introduction Data recorded with handheld grippers grows with the number of people who record it, not with the number of robots available: a person holds a gripper in each hand and does the task, and no robot is needed. UMI~ umi introduced the approach; with YUBI~ yubi , our open-source gripper of this kind, we have recorded 16,151 hours of bimanual demonstrations, 10.65 million subtask segments in all, each with a task instruction and a subtask instruction. ( ) uses handheld demonstrations for pre-training and post-training alike: no teleoperation, no reinforcement learning, no on-robot corrections and no simulation. The properties that let this data scale are the ones that make it hard to learn from. Every demonstration is made by a person, so nothing in the data shows a robot acting, failing or recovering. The policy sees only through the cameras on the grippers, the one view that is the same in a person's hand and on a robot: with no head or scene camera, it never sees the workspace as a whole and must follow a long task through two partial views that are often consistent with more than one of its steps. Data that anyone can record is the work of many operators, here across well over a hundred tasks, and a single model has to learn from all of it. And people record wherever they are, which is not where the robot will work. Deployment at an unseen site is therefore the ordinary condition of this approach and the one under which it must be judged: not one of the demonstrations learns from was recorded at the site where it is evaluated. works under all of these conditions at once. Given a single sentence of instruction, it sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells, deciding for each part which cell it belongs in, which hand should take it, and whether it must first pass from one hand to the other. It opens the zipper of a pencil case, which the two grippers must grasp almost side by side; it folds a towel; it replaces the mop pads and the brush of a robot vacuum. These are long tasks that demand precise contact, and the robot performs them with the grippers that people record with. On the ten tasks of our evaluation, averages a success rate of 78 , against 27 for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations: each of them with its best setting on every task, with one recipe for all ten. And although nothing in its data shows a robot meeting a disturbance, acts on what it sees: when a person pushes the bins aside as it brings a part to them, it moves over to the correct bin in one continuous motion (Figure~ fig:perturb ). Because those grippers mount on different arms, is embodiment-agnostic: the same weights run on robots such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR (Section~ sec:robots ). is built as one system that spans every layer between the gripper in a person's hand and the motion of the robot (Figure~ fig:pipeline ), and each of these difficulties is met at the layer where it arises. State and action are defined at the grippers themselves, so the same numbers describe a person holding them and a robot carrying them, on one arm as on another. Pre-training tells a single model, through language at two levels, both the task and the step in progress, and a visual evidence budget~ s2 teaches it, with no annotation of where to look, which regions of each wrist view matter for the task. Post-training adds a prediction of the stage a long task has reached and a memory of recent motion, and the inference harness smooths the predicted stage and decodes actions as a continuous stream on a non-uniform noise schedule that we propose. With this report we are releasing the full dataset of 16,151 hours of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights of and its post-training recipe. Together with the YUBI gripper's hardware design and collection software, which are already public, they open the path from a gripper in a person's hand to a policy on a robot: the gripper is built from the open design, the task is recorded by hand, and the pre-trained model is post-trained on it with the one recipe that serves every task in this report, in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs. Our contributions are: , a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld data, with no robot data collected at any stage. An open release of the path from a handheld gripper to a robot policy: the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions; the pre-trained weights; and the post-training recipe, alongside the public YUBI hardware design and collection software. Long, precise tasks carried out from a single instruction, through two wrist cameras, at a site where none of the training data was recorded. An embodiment-agnostic system: it runs on robots that take the recording gripper as their end effector, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. Results sec:results Ten tasks sec:bench On the ten bimanual tasks of Figure~ fig:tasks , evaluated on a Franka platform at a site where none of the training data was recorded, averages a success rate of 78 , against 14 to 27 for four other vision-language-action models (Table~ tab:benchmark ), and it has the highest success rate on every task, from sorting parts and stacking cups to folding a towel and servicing a robot vacuum. Each task is specified by a single instruction, given once at the start. Each is an average over 15 trials, with partial credit for a task that is partly completed. Post-training needs little data for each task: six of the ten tasks use between three and six hours of demonstrations, and only the cup pyramid and the earbuds use more than ten (Table~ tab:benchmark ). The four models are ~ pi05 , (XR-1)~ xiaomi , GR00T~N1.7~ groot17,groot and MolmoAct2~ molmoact2 , each starting from its public pre-trained checkpoint and post-trained on the same task demonstrations as . Each of them is post-trained on every task over a range of settings, with action horizons of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16, several action frequencies, and 60,000, 80,000 and 100,000 updates, and on every task we report its best result. is given no such search: every task is post-trained with the one recipe of Table~ tab:posttrain . Several of the tasks run for minutes: in the two minutes of Figure~ fig:longtask , takes the two used mop pads off a robot vacuum, attaches two new ones from the box and pulls out the brush, one step after another, from the single instruction it was given at the start. Videos of every task are on the project page. A changing scene sec:perturb Nothing in the training data shows a robot meeting a disturbance, and a policy that replayed its demonstrations would carry on with the plan it had made. acts on what its wrist cameras see. In Figure~ fig:perturb , a person pushes the row of bins aside as brings a green part to the green bin, so that the red bin comes to lie under the gripper. The arm, already on its way down, moves over to the green bin in one continuous motion and drops the part into it. Later in the same run the person swaps the green and yellow bins, and again puts the next green part into the green bin at its new place. Two parts of the system meet in this response: the policy places each part by what it sees, not by where a bin was, and non-uniform streaming decoding keeps the motion continuous as each new observation updates it (Section~ sec:stream ). Other robots sec:robots Nothing in refers to the arm that carries the grippers: state and action are defined at the grippers themselves (Section~ sec:anchored ), and the model sees only through the wrist cameras. A robot that takes the YUBI gripper and its cameras as its end effector can therefore run . Besides the bimanual Franka, three robots do: TX-G2, a humanoid; OpenArm, an open-source bimanual robot; and a pair of UR industrial arms. All four run the same weights for each task, with nothing retrained or adjusted for any robot. On TX-G2, performs four of the tasks of Section~ sec:bench : it stacks three cups and four oranges into pyramids, opens the pencil case and sorts the toy bolts and nuts into boxes by colour (Figure~ fig:robots , top). On OpenArm, it performs three: it sorts the toy bolts and nuts by colour, spells YUBI with the letter blocks and opens the pencil case; on the UR arms, it sorts by colour and stacks four oranges into a pyramid (Figure~ fig:robots , bottom). As on the Franka, none of the training data was recorded on any of these robots. Data sec:data The rest of this report describes how is built, in four parts designed with one another in view (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). This section describes the data, and the sections that follow take the other parts in turn. YUBI YUBI~ yubi is a handheld gripper built for collecting manipulation data at scale. It is driven by the fingers, so that closing the hand closes the jaws; it carries a camera at the wrist; and it is tracked in six degrees of freedom. A demonstrator holds one gripper in each hand and performs the task as they naturally would, and the recording holds the two wrist views, the trajectory of each gripper and how far each is open. The same gripper mounts on a robot arm as its end effector. What a demonstrator records is therefore what the robot will later see and do: the images come from the same camera in the same place on the tool, and the actions are motions of that tool. The corpus The corpus holds 16,151 hours of bimanual demonstrations (Table~ tab:corpus ). It covers well over a hundred tasks, spanning pick-and-place, sorting, assembly, insertion, cable routing, opening and closing, tool use and handovers between hands. Every demonstration is divided into subtasks, steps of a few seconds each, and it carries language at two levels: a , which names the whole job, and a , which names the step in progress. For one task, replacing the parts of a robot vacuum, the task instruction is ``Replace the parts of the robot vacuum cleaner'', and its subtasks run from ``Remove the first used mop pad and place it into the box'' through ``Remove the action brush and place it into the box'' to ``Attach the dustbin to the robot vacuum''. The corpus contains 10.65 million subtask segments. These two levels of language run through the whole system. The task instruction is what is given at run time. The subtask instruction is what it learns to predict in pre-training, and the unit from which the stages of post-training are built. Before any training, every demonstration passes through a data-processing pipeline that includes filtering, outlier detection and retiming. Pre-training sec:pretraining Pre-training teaches one model the corpus under the objective of See Less, Specify More (S2)~ s2 , which governs what the policy sees and how it is told what to do, with an auxiliary loss on the subtask (Figure~ fig:model ). Model takes its backbone from ~ pi05 : a SigLIP So400m/14 image encoder, a Gemma~2B vision-language backbone and a 300M action expert trained by flow matching, initialised from the public base checkpoint. On this backbone redefines the interface to the robot, adds a visual budget gate and changes the objective, and backbone and gate are trained together on the corpus for 300,000 steps at a batch size of 2,048. The model observes two wrist images at pixels, an instruction and a proprioceptive state, and in pre-training it outputs a chunk of 32 future actions on a 20\,Hz grid. Anchored actions sec:anchored State and action are both defined at the grippers. Actions are anchored: every action in a chunk is the pose a gripper should reach, expressed relative to the pose it has when the observation is taken. title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
comment: 29 pages, 9 figures. Project page: https://roboscope.pages.dev/ Code: https://github.com/MINT-SJTU/RoboScope-Kit
summary: Simulation benchmarks are the standard way to compare robot policies, but each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, and action convention, and evaluation is slow: 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU take 359.7 minutes. Profiling the official StarVLA evaluator shows that simulation occupies CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3% utilization. RoboScope Kit wraps each model once in a Python class called a Policy, and each benchmark once in an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator, so the benchmark's rules and scoring stay unchanged. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both from measured probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances; runtime optimization renders only the observations an action-chunk Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one 48 GiB RTX 4090, the concurrency search selects twelve simulator workers sharing three Policy replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45$\times$ faster than the official StarVLA evaluation with equivalent success rates, 2.78$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 1.52$\times$ faster than vla-eval at its tuned configuration. With CUDA MPS, which lets the replicas run their kernels concurrently, the search selects sixteen workers sharing four replicas, 6.16$\times$ faster than StarVLA, 3.85$\times$ faster than RLinf, and 2.10$\times$ faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation complete the 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04$\times$ faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps.
full_text: 6pt Introduction sec:v2-intro Simulation benchmarks evaluate complementary aspects of robot behavior: knowledge transfer in LIBERO libero2023 , bimanual manipulation in RoboTwin robotwin22025 , language-conditioned task sequences in CALVIN calvin2022 , and household manipulation in RoboCasa robocasa2024 . Each benchmark brings its own evaluator, observation layout, action convention, and episode bookkeeping, and each policy family brings its own preprocessing and inference loop. Connecting several policies to several benchmarks repeats this integration for every pair. Execution cost compounds the problem: with a StarVLA checkpoint, the official evaluation of 500 LIBERO-Long episodes takes about 50 minutes on one GPU, and running 500 RoboTwin Easy episodes with one simulator and one model on one GPU takes 359.7 minutes. Comparing checkpoints, seeds, or training stages multiplies these costs, and a shared evaluation layer can remove much of this repeated work. Profiling the official evaluators shows where this time goes (Section~ sec:v2-time-profile ). Simulation occupies CPU cores while one loaded model leaves the GPU mostly idle, so simulators and models are best scaled separately. On RoboTwin, an action-chunk Policy reads one of every 16 rendered observations, so the others need not be rendered. addresses the repeated integration with one interface and the execution cost with two acceleration mechanisms, scheduling and runtime optimization. wraps each model once as a Policy, a class that loads the checkpoint and keeps the model's own preprocessing, and each benchmark once as an adapter around the benchmark's own evaluator. The Policy also declares what may rely on: the observations it reads, the chunk length it returns, and how often it needs a new observation. It keeps each episode's state separate, so one loaded model can serve many simulators at once. Simulator workers, Policy replicas, scheduling, and result collection run as separate components, so the number of simulators and the number of loaded models vary independently. The concurrency search chooses and for each workload and host from short probes. Runtime optimization in the Simulation Runtime removes simulation work that the Policy never consumes, such as rendering observations between action-chunk boundaries. Beyond one host, partitions the work items deterministically across independent GPU instances, each running its own workers and replicas, and merges their results. This report makes three contributions: [itemsep=0.2em,topsep=0.3em] A measurement of where evaluation time goes. On one RTX 4090, the official StarVLA LIBERO-Long evaluator spends 55 of its time on simulation and per-step handling on CPU cores while the GPU averages 14.3 utilization. Adding simulators to one model saturates it at 45.7 utilization, and a second Policy replica raises utilization to 87.7 . On RoboTwin, the official evaluator renders three cameras at every control step, yet the StarVLA Policy reads one observation every 16 steps. A shared evaluation interface. A model is wrapped once as a Policy class and then runs on any benchmark that provides the inputs it needs, without changes to . Adapters cover six benchmark families. With a StarVLA checkpoint, a fixed configuration reproduces all 500 LIBERO-Long success outcomes of the official StarVLA evaluation. Fast evaluation through scheduling and runtime optimization. Scheduling runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, so simulators and loaded models scale independently and several simulators share each model; a time-bounded concurrency search sizes both pools for each workload and host, and deterministic sharding extends an evaluation across GPU instances. For runtime optimization, a Policy can declare that it needs a new observation only once per action chunk; then renders once per chunk, and each worker reuses one SAPIEN engine and renderer across its episodes. On one RTX 4090, the configuration chosen by the concurrency search evaluates 500 LIBERO-Long episodes in 485\,s, against 2,990\,s for the official StarVLA evaluation ( 6.16 ), with equivalent outcomes, and is 3.85 faster than RLinf and 2.10 faster than vla-eval. On RoboTwin Easy, scheduling and runtime optimization together cut the time for 500 episodes from 359.7 minutes, with one simulator and one model on one GPU, to 14.4 minutes on four GPUs ( 25.04 ). Background and Motivation sec:v2-motivation Simulation-Based Policy Evaluation Simulation benchmarks let researchers compare robot policies on fixed task distributions at a cost and scale that physical trials cannot reach. An evaluation runs a fixed set of episodes. Each episode starts from a benchmark-defined task and initial state, alternates between rendering an observation, querying the policy, and stepping the simulator with the returned action, and ends when the task succeeds or a step limit is reached. The benchmark then scores the episode records, usually as the fraction of successful episodes. Benchmarks differ at every stage of this path. LIBERO supplies two cameras, 16-D proprioception, and a language instruction, and expects a 7-D end-effector delta with a gripper command; RoboTwin supplies three cameras and dual-arm joint state and expects a 14-D absolute joint and gripper target; CALVIN and RoboCasa use further layouts (Appendix~ app:v2-contracts ). Termination rules, step limits, and scoring differ as well. Two policies, or two evaluation systems, are comparable when they run the same episodes under the same rules, so for every run in this report we record the episode list, checkpoint, software versions, and hardware. Where Evaluation Time Goes sec:v2-time-profile Simulation, rendering, and inference costs. An episode's wall time divides among simulator initialization and reset, physics stepping, rendering, observation transfer, Policy inference, and cleanup. These stages use different resources: physics, robot control, and environment logic use CPU cores, rendering uses the GPU's graphics pipeline, and inference uses GPU compute and memory. Figure~ fig:v2-native-timeline traces the official StarVLA evaluator and its policy server on 50 LIBERO-Long episodes on one RTX 4090. The evaluator runs one simulator and queries the server once per action chunk, so simulation and inference take turns. On CPU cores, simulation steps and the per-step handling of observations and actions take 55 of the evaluator's time. Most of it is robot control and MuJoCo forward kinematics, computed at each of the 25 physics substeps per control step; physics integration takes 11 . Rendering the two cameras on the GPU takes 3 . Episode setup, reset, and settling take 16 , and waiting for actions 26 . An inference takes 55\,ms, of which the GPU executes kernels for 26\,ms: the model issues about 3,100 kernel launches per inference, and the GPU waits between them. The server is busy 25 of the time, and the GPU averages 14.3 utilization (Appendix~ app:v2-time-profile ). Neither the CPU cores nor the GPU is kept busy. Since simulators consume CPU cores and Policy replicas consume GPU memory and compute, the two can be scaled separately. Unconsumed observations in action-chunk policies. Many current policies predict action chunks: one inference returns actions, which the evaluator executes over the next control steps before querying the Policy again. The StarVLA RoboTwin checkpoint has . The official RoboTwin evaluator still renders all three cameras at every control step, so 15 of every 16 rendered observations are never read. Rendering only at chunk boundaries keeps physics stepping, action execution, and success checks at the native control frequency, and the Policy receives exactly the observations it reads. Design Goals These observations lead to five design goals. (G1) Unified. Integrate each model and each benchmark once, and reuse it with every counterpart. (G2) Faithful. Reproduce the outcomes of each benchmark's official evaluation, under its own tasks, initial states, termination, and scoring. (G3) Efficient. Keep both CPU cores and GPUs busy, and skip simulation work that changes neither the Policy's inputs nor the score. (G4) Automatic. Configure each evaluation for its workload and host without manual tuning, and report what this costs. (G5) Scalable. Extend one evaluation from one GPU to several GPUs and instances. Design sec:v2-design Overview has four parts (Figure~ fig:v2-overview ). A Policy is a class, installed in its model's own environment, that loads a checkpoint and keeps the model's preprocessing. A benchmark adapter wraps the benchmark's native evaluator, which keeps task definitions, initial states, termination, and scoring (G2, faithful). Two runtimes connect the two. The Control Runtime schedules the evaluation. It expands a benchmark suite into a manifest, the ordered list of episode keys (task, episode, seed), and groups the keys into work items. It starts simulator workers, processes that each own one simulator, and Policy replicas, processes that each hold one loaded Policy, and collects one episode record per episode key. The Simulation Runtime runs inside each simulator worker: the native evaluator, instrumented by the adapter, steps the simulator, renders observations, and sends them to a Policy replica. Acceleration has two parts. Runtime optimization in the Simulation Runtime removes simulation work the Policy never consumes ( sec:v2-runtime ). Scheduling in the Control Runtime separates simulation from inference, chooses and , and shards work across instances ( sec:v2-architecture , sec:v2-selection , sec:v2-sharding ). An evaluation proceeds in four stages. The Control Runtime first validates that the Policy's declared capabilities match the benchmark's contract. It then runs the concurrency search, short probes that choose and , unless they are fixed. Next it runs the manifest as work items across workers that send observations to replicas. Finally it aggregates completed items into benchmark scores and execution metrics. Evaluation Interface sec:v2-policy Observation and action contracts. A model is integrated once as a Policy and a benchmark once as an adapter, and each is reused with every counterpart (G1, unified). Each benchmark specification names its observation features and its action. A feature has a canonical name such as , , or , a kind, a dtype, and an optional shape; the action has a name, a dimension, and a dtype. A Policy declares the features it requires, the suites it supports, the chunk lengths it returns, its action representation, and an observation stride per benchmark. Checkpoint-specific work, including image resizing and cropping, normalization, tokenization, and the transform from model outputs to benchmark actions, stays inside the Policy. Adapters apply returned actions in the benchmark's native convention and execute action chunks one step at a time at the native control frequency. Policy lifecycle and episode state. A Policy replica moves through five operations (Table~ tab:v2-lifecycle ). reads one checkpoint and returns the Policy's capabilities; allocates state for one episode; maps an observation to an action or action chunk, and its batched form , which defaults to calling per observation, serves several at once; releases that episode's state; and releases the model. Several simulator workers share a replica, so requests from different episodes interleave. Every request carries an episode identifier, and stateful Policies key their histories, caches, and action queues by it. Model weights and other replica-scope resources live from load to unload; episode-scope state lives from reset to end of episode (Figure~ fig:v2-lifecycle ). Interface validation. title: FlowBench: Counterfactual Imagination Training for Spatial Intelligence
summary: Humans imagine scene changes under hypothetical motions, an ability central to spatial reasoning and robotic planning. However, this capability remains underexplored in vision-language models and world models. We formalize this capability as Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) and introduce FlowBench, a resource for training and evaluating both, with 428K training examples spanning simulated and real-world scenes, household environments and tabletop manipulation, and diverse question types. A scalable, fully automatic pipeline pairs each hypothetical motion with spatial questions and, in simulation, exact outcome frames and optical flow. For VLMs, proprietary models exhibit an imagination gap, performing worse when motion outcomes must be inferred than when observed, and open-source models perform near chance; fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train raises its accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, a strong sim-to-real transfer. For world models, training on FlowBench-Sim improves text-to-flow prediction for all four model families we test, raising the accuracy of Psi-0.6 from 52.1% to 61.7%. FlowBench thus serves as a training and evaluation resource for both. Code and datasets are released at https://github.com/liuyifan22/FlowBench.
full_text: Humans imagine scene changes under hypothetical motions, an ability central to spatial reasoning and robotic planning. However, this capability remains underexplored in vision-language models and world models. We formalize this capability as Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) and introduce FlowBench, a resource for training and evaluating both, with 428K training examples spanning simulated and real-world scenes, household environments and tabletop manipulation, and diverse question types. A scalable, fully automatic pipeline pairs each hypothetical motion with spatial questions and, in simulation, exact outcome frames and optical flow. For VLMs, proprietary models exhibit an imagination gap, performing worse when motion outcomes must be inferred than when observed, and open-source models perform near chance; fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train raises its accuracy by 29.5 percentage points in simulation and 16.9 on real images, a strong sim-to-real transfer. For world models, training on FlowBench-Sim improves text-to-flow prediction for all four model families we test, raising the accuracy of -0.6 from 52.1 to 61.7 . FlowBench thus serves as a training and evaluation resource for both. Code and datasets are released at . Introduction Humans can mentally simulate scene changes under hypothetical interventions~ tolman1948cognitive,shepard1971mental,hassabis2007patients . For example, we can anticipate whether moving a sofa would block a corridor without physically moving it. This spatial foresight supports interaction with the physical world and could help robots anticipate how object motions affect free space, visibility, and proximity during navigation or manipulation. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong visual perception and reasoning abilities~ achiam2023gpt,comanici2025gemini,bai2025qwen3 , but understanding an observed scene does not necessarily imply anticipating its state after a hypothetical motion. Existing spatial benchmarks primarily evaluate observed visual information~ yin2025mindcube,zhang2026theory,hong2026esi , while work on mental simulation often considers camera motion in static scenes~ ray2024sat,yang2026mindjourney,liu2026abstract . Current counterfactual visual question answering benchmarks~ niu2021counterfactual,chen2025countervqa,cai2026if focus on semantic changes, leaving open whether VLMs can infer the spatial consequences of object motions in realistic scenes. These directions leave a gap in evaluating changes to the spatial configuration itself, beyond interpreting an observed scene or viewing it from another perspective. World models offer a complementary route: rather than reasoning in text, they simulate a described motion visually, predicting its optical flow or generating the frame after it~ psi,ran_fofpred_2026,brooks2023instructpix2pix , and their predictions are increasingly evaluated for physical consistency under interventions~ cai2026if . Training them for this requires text commands paired with the exact flow and outcome of the motion they describe, whereas video corpora offer only estimated flow and motion descriptions written after the fact. We therefore ask: How well can VLMs and world models reason about and simulate how a scene changes under hypothetical object motions, and can targeted training improve both? We formalize this capability as Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI). Given a scene image, a hypothetical object motion, and a spatial question, a model must answer with respect to the post-motion scene without observing it. CSI requires understanding the initial scene, interpreting the motion, and inferring its consequences for the relevant spatial relationships. We evaluate answers without requiring intermediate image generation, accommodating both implicit reasoning in VLMs and explicit visual simulation with world models; for world models, we additionally evaluate the simulation itself through its predicted optical flow and outcome frame. We introduce FlowBench, a training dataset and benchmark with approximately 428K training examples and held-out test splits spanning simulated household environments and real tabletop manipulation. FlowBench-Sim covers eight question categories probing changes in spatial relationships, visibility, and collision constraints relevant to navigation through changing layouts. FlowBench-Real focuses on object rearrangements across seven question categories. Their test splits assess generalization to unseen simulated scene styles and sim-to-real transfer. We develop a scalable, fully automatic pipeline for accurate CSI data generation that others can adapt to new settings. For FlowBench-Sim, deterministic programs compute ground-truth answers from AI2-THOR and ProcTHOR simulator metadata~ ai2thor,procthor . The pipeline scales across procedurally generated scenes and balances samples across question categories. Beyond question-answer pairs, each simulated motion comes with its text command, post-motion image, optical flow, depth, and semantic segmentation, all exact from simulator metadata, as well as textual reasoning annotations. The same data thus supervises VLMs, through questions and reasoning traces, and world models, through text-to-flow prediction and text-conditioned generation of the outcome frame. For FlowBench-Real, we extract motions from recorded robot videos, relabel them as hypothetical motion, and compute answers from estimated post-motion geometry and visibility. Evaluation examples undergo manual quality review, while simulated training data undergo VLM-assisted plausibility and correctness filtering. Our experiments reveal that proprietary VLMs retain an imagination gap: they perform worse when motion outcomes must be inferred than when those outcomes are directly observed. As illustrated in , Claude-Fable-5.1 and GPT-6 Astra exhibit gaps of 5.0 and 3.1 percentage points, respectively. Off-the-shelf open-source VLMs perform near chance and below the human baseline, further motivating the need for stronger counterfactual world-modeling capabilities in VLMs. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on FlowBench-Sim-Train improves performance by 29.5 percentage points on FlowBench-Sim-Test and 16.9 points on FlowBench-Real-Test, demonstrating strong sim-to-real transfer of the proposed data annotation pipeline with simulators, showing potential of its application to other tasks. Nevertheless, its imagination gap on real images persists after fine-tuning, while text-based chain-of-thought reasoning also offers inconsistent gains. On the world-model side, training on FlowBench-Sim-Train improves text-to-flow prediction on held-out scenes for all four model families we test, by up to 25.2 percentage points; the trained -0.6~ psi reaches 61.7 , above a modular perception pipeline given camera intrinsics ( ). Letting -0.6 imagine the outcome frame before answering does not yet help, as generated frames lose details the questions depend on, so world models must become more faithful before they can support VLM reasoning. Our contributions are fivefold: We formalize CSI as an important spatial reasoning capability for anticipating scene changes under hypothetical object motions. We introduce FlowBench, a diverse training dataset and benchmark spanning simulated household environments, real tabletop manipulation, and a broad range of spatial question categories. We develop a scalable, fully automatic pipeline for accurate dataset construction that pairs each motion with spatial questions, reasoning traces, and exact outcome supervision (post-motion image, optical flow, depth, and segmentation), supporting the training of both VLMs and world models. For VLMs, we show that proprietary VLMs can exceed human baseline on FlowBench-Real yet retain an imagination gap, while open-source models are near chance and benefit from targeted training with strong sim-to-real transfer. For world models, we show that training on FlowBench-Sim improves text-to-flow prediction for every model family we test, while world-model-assisted answering does not yet help CSI. Our code and datasets are publicly released to support research on CSI in both VLMs and world models, and on spatial foresight for robotic navigation and manipulation. Related Work and Spatial Intelligence. Spatial intelligence involves understanding and reasoning about the spatial structure of the physical world. VLM research examines spatial perception, memory, and recall~ yang2025thinking , alongside cognitive mapping~ yin2025mindcube . Further work studies the active construction and revision of spatial beliefs or abstractions~ zhang2026theory,yang2026mindjourney,liu2026abstract and 3D-based information aggregation~ hong20233d,lin2026qwen . Related benchmarks study motion perception as part of physical understanding~ riochet2018intphys,bakhtin2019phyre,bordes2025intphys2,patel2022cripp . Spatial instruction datasets and spatially grounded supervision also improve VLM spatial reasoning~ ray2024sat,chen2024spatialvlm,cheng2024spatialrgpt,cai2026sensenova . However, these studies primarily address perception, memory, and reasoning about observed environments. Humans can also imagine alternative spatial configurations and reason about them~ kosslyn1980image,epstein1998cortical,gardner2011frames ; developing this counterfactual spatial imagination in VLMs remains an open challenge. Reasoning. Counterfactual reasoning infers the consequences of hypothetical changes to observed reality. Humans naturally construct counterfactual mental models for learning, planning, and prediction~ kahneman1982simulation,byrne2002mental,van2015cognitive . From a causal perspective, this requires understanding how interventions alter outcomes rather than relying on observational correlations~ pearl2009causality . Multimodal studies examine language bias under hypothetical visual changes~ niu2021counterfactual , as well as visual causal reasoning and video understanding~ komanduri2025causalvlbench,chen2025countervqa . Beyond question answering, generative world models are evaluated on physically consistent future prediction under controlled interventions, advancing toward causal simulation of embodied environments~ cai2026if . However, existing benchmarks primarily address semantic changes, causal attribution, or future visual generation; predicting how spatial relationships evolve under hypothetical interventions remains underexplored in VLMs. Method Overview FlowBench evaluates Counterfactual Spatial Imagination (CSI) through multiple-choice visual question answering~ antol2015vqa . Each example consists of where is the initial scene image, describes a hypothetical object motion, is a spatial question with answer choices, and is the answer for the resulting scene. The model predicts from without observing the outcome. FlowBench combines simulated indoor environments and real robot manipulation scenes, targeting spatial reasoning relevant to navigation and manipulation. -Sim. As shown in~ , FlowBench-Sim-Train contains 420K questions from 10K ProcTHOR scenes~ procthor , covering eight question categories. FlowBench-Sim-Test contains 714 questions from 120 AI2-THOR scenes~ ai2thor held out from the training scene source, evaluating generalization to unseen scene styles. -Real. sec:real_overview FlowBench-Real-Train contains 8 , 575 questions, and FlowBench-Real-Test contains 1 , 083 questions on separate image pairs. Both are constructed from recorded robot manipulation videos: observed object displacements become hypothetical motions, while later frames provide the outcomes used for annotation. The eight FlowBench-Sim training categories are Occlusion, Feasibility, Left Right, Closest Three, Closer To, Count Near, Threshold, and Contact Wall. title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit-evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74-147 Hz, 5.9-17.5x faster than the JAX reference hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.7-16x faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.

Hamilton--Jacobi reachability, backward reachable tubes, level-set methods, real-time GPU computing, safety-critical control, deterministic safety layer, safety filter, ADAS and autonomous vehicles, humanoid robotics, vision--language--action policies, embedded GPU autonomy, multi-agent fleet dispatch, capture-basin Voronoi tessellation, in-kernel label propagation, wildfire response, time-varying wind fields, pursuit--evasion differential games. Introduction sec:intro The next generation of autonomous robotics --- advanced driver-assistance and self-driving vehicles (ADAS/AV), humanoid platforms, and vision--language--action (VLA) policies --- pushes decision-making into large, learned, fundamentally probabilistically determined models whose worst-case behavior is case-dependent and whose safety properties cannot be certified by inspection. A deterministic, model-based safety layer with formal guarantees is therefore not optional but a structural enabler of these stacks: it is the mechanism by which a black-box upstream policy can be trusted in safety-critical deployment, and the only available complement that gives the overall system the worst-case behavior the upstream model cannot. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability is the strongest available primitive for that role. The backward reachable tube (BRT) is the exact set of states from which a constraint violation cannot be avoided against the worst-case disturbance~ lygeros2004reach,mitchell2005tdhj,bansal2017survey . Three properties of the BRT make it the right object for safety, and keeping them distinct avoids a common confusion. First, depending on how it is computed, the BRT---or, more precisely, its boundary---delimits the set of states from which, regardless of the control, the worst-case disturbance can force the system into the target set (here, the unsafe set). Second, from any state outside the tube there always exists a control that keeps the system safe over the horizon. Third, on the boundary of the tube at least one control must be applied to stay safe: absent it, the disturbance can drive the system into the tube and ultimately into the unsafe set. A robot whose current state lies inside the BRT must either accept a failure outcome or apply the value-function-derived optimal control to escape, and so the BRT answers the most fundamental question a safety-critical autonomy stack can ask~ fisac2019safety,hsu2024safetyfilter . A BRT-based safety filter can sit downstream of a learned planner and either certify its proposed action or override it with a provably safe one~ hsu2024safetyfilter,fisac2019safety , giving the deployed ADAS/AV, humanoid, or VLA stack a deterministic floor of behaviour that the upstream learned policy is not by itself required to provide. The well-known drawback is that the level-set computation that delivers a guaranteed-fidelity BRT scales exponentially in the state dimension. The historical response has been to compute the BRT once offline and then use it as a fixed lookup in the control loop~ mitchell2008toolbox,helperoc,hjreachability . This is a critical limitation for next-generation autonomy: in any setting where the disturbance model, the obstacle set, or the dynamics are not known a priori --- the operating regime of every real ADAS stack, every legged platform on unmodeled terrain, and every VLA policy in an unfamiliar environment --- a stale offline BRT is a stale safety guarantee. With the implementation presented in this article, we demonstrate that the boundary between offline and online BRT computation has moved. On a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX~4000 Ada), the canonical Mitchell~Air3D 3D pursuit--evasion BRT~ mitchell2005tdhj solves in ms at 32-bit floating point (FP32) with the same numerical scheme used by the Stanford Autonomous Systems Laboratory (ASL) JAX reference ~ hjreachability , a 4D pursuit--evasion BRT at cells solves in ms, and the 2D drift-affected vehicle BRT solves at -- Hz at WENO5 fidelity. These rates place the level-set solver inside the inner control loop of a robot, and shift the design question from how to live with a single BRT precomputed for an entire mission to how to use a BRT that is recomputed at every control tick. Concretely, our solver implements the standard level-set HJI recipe on CUDA---fifth-order WENO (WENO5) reconstruction of the spatial gradient, total-variation-diminishing third-order Runge--Kutta (TVD-RK3) time integration, and a Lax--Friedrichs numerical Hamiltonian---with one fused kernel per RK3 stage (reconstruction, Hamiltonian, stage combine, and BRT clamp in-register), a division-lean WENO5 reconstruction, a host-static CFL step, and an FP32 precision mode that is the relevant regime for embedded robotic deployment. At matched 64-bit floating point (FP64) arithmetic (the academic-standard precision for verification studies) our solver agrees with on eight canonical benchmarking cases at -- the speed on matched hardware, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT~ mitchell2005tdhj to within of the reference cell count at , and is -- faster than a ~ ansel2024pytorch2 reimplementation of the identical scheme, a maximally-tuned tensor-compiler baseline. In FP32 mode the solver is -- faster than its own FP64 path with sub-grid BRT-set deviation, and -- faster than the JAX reference at matched FP32 on the same hardware. To verify that these rates are not specific to a desktop-class GPU, we re-run the solver on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor embedded developer kit and measure -- Hz on the 3D Air3D and 2D drifter cases ( -- faster than on the same device), with the closed-loop fleet solve drawing approximately W of total system input power. As a multi-agent application we extend the 2D solver with an in-kernel label-propagation kernel, in the spirit of competitive fast marching~ sethian1996fastmarching , that recovers the -agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve whose cost is independent of fleet size, with label agreement with a per-agent argmin reference. We demonstrate the latter on a closed-loop wildfire-response fleet of six quadcopters defending a km region under time-varying, non-uniform wind. The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section~ sec:background reviews the HJ reachability formulation and the level-set discretization recipe we use. Section~ sec:related positions our solver against the classical-fidelity offline tools and the learned-value online approximators at the two ends of the existing literature. Section~ sec:solver describes the CUDA implementation, the FP32 precision mode, and the boundary and obstacle postprocessors. Section~ sec:verification describes the verification protocol against , and Section~ sec:results reports cross-library agreement, the equi-accuracy comparison, and the FP32 real-time envelope. Section~ sec:applications presents the multi-agent wildfire-response Voronoi demonstration. Section~ sec:discussion discusses the dimensional ceiling, the FP32 fidelity floor, embedded-platform performance on Jetson AGX Thor, and future work. Section~ sec:conclusion concludes. Background sec:background For a dynamical system on with control values and disturbance values , admissible control and disturbance signals and (measurable maps from into and , respectively), and a failure set described by a signed-distance function , the time- backward reachable tube is the set of initial states from which the disturbance can force entry into within the horizon regardless of the control~ lygeros2004reach,mitchell2005tdhj . Mitchell, Bayen, and Tomlin~ mitchell2005tdhj showed that the BRT is the zero-sublevel set of the value function , which satisfies the Hamilton--Jacobi--Isaacs (HJI) partial differential equation integrated backward in time from the terminal condition ~ isaacs1965 , with the Isaacs-form Hamiltonian encoding the worst-case control--disturbance choice. The level-set formulation then handles all of: minimum-time arrival to a target, maximum-time avoidance of an obstacle, and reach-while-avoid~ mitchell2005tdhj,margellos2011reachavoid . Subsequent applications by Bayen, Mitchell, Oishi, and Tomlin~ bayen2007autolander (aircraft autolander reach-set analysis), by Weekly, Tinka, Anderson, and Bayen~ weekly2015hjriver (HJ-based optimal-control navigation of underactuated drifters under spatially-varying flow), and the FaSTrack framework of Herbert, Fisac, Tomlin, and colleagues~ herbert2017fastrack (real-time guaranteed-safe motion planning via a precomputed HJ tracking bound) demonstrated that the same level-set primitive transfers to operational robotic control once the fidelity-versus-runtime tradeoff is acceptable; historically, that tradeoff has restricted the primitive to offline mission planning. We solve on a uniform Cartesian grid by the standard recipe~ osher1991eno,jiang2000weno,shu1988tvd : WENO5 spatial reconstruction of , TVD-RK3 time integration, Lax--Friedrichs numerical Hamiltonian, and a CFL-limited time step. We apply Mitchell's BRT-clamp in-kernel so that is monotonically non-increasing under backward integration, the same role played by the postprocessor of ~ hjreachability . Related Work sec:related Classical level-set HJ tooling. Hamilton--Jacobi reachability was historically demonstrated at scale for control by Mitchell's level-set formulation~ mitchell2002thesis,mitchell2005tdhj,osher1988level , and the ToolboxLS MATLAB library~ mitchell2008toolbox together with its MATLAB wrapper helperOC and C++/CUDA port BEACLS~ helperoc are still in use today. OptimizedDP~ bui2022optimizeddp compiles the level-set HJ stencil to parallel multi-core CPU code via HeteroCL and reports order-of-magnitude speedups over ToolboxLS, making higher state dimensions tractable on the CPU. The Stanford ASL library~ hjreachability is a modern JAX/XLA rewrite that exposes the same numerical primitives and is the closest sibling of our solver; a PyTorch counterpart, of Choi et al.~ choi2025 , provides similar primitives in eager PyTorch at first-order accuracy. We treat the JAX library as the reference implementation in Section~ sec:results . title: DiMuRe: Diagnosis-Guided Multilevel Recovery for Robotic Task Execution
summary: Disturbances can invalidate the conditions required by a robot's next action even when much of its task program remains useful. A recovery system must therefore choose a response suited to the current state. We present DiMuRe (diagnosis-guided multilevel recovery), a framework for robot-use agents that uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA) grasping. After the original program exits, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can generate corrective code from images and execution feedback. Local verification checks the outcome of each recovery attempt. We also introduce LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for robustness and recovery under mid-execution disturbances, supporting program-based agents and VLA policies. On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local DiMuRe (program reuse and recovery skills) achieves 77.65% complete-task success, compared with 58.68% for the original program under the same physical-step allowance. Full DiMuRe achieves 81.90% with terminal replanning, an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program.
full_text: DiMuRe: Diagnosis-Guided Multilevel Recovery for Robotic Task Execution Renkai Yi , Yuwei Wu , Haoyu Zhang , Penghao Dai ,\\ Zhi Gao , Jin Chen , and Che Sun Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China\\ Shenzhen MSU-BIT University, Shenzhen, China\\ AInnovation Technology Group Co., Ltd.\\ \ renkaiyi, wuyuwei, zhanghaoyu, penghaodai, gaozhibit\ @bit.edu.cn \\ chen jin@bit.edu.cn; sunche@smbu.edu.cn Conceptual overview of diagnosis-guided recovery in DiMuRe. The center illustrates target shift, grasp slip, path obstruction, and receiver shift. On the left, diagnosis starts with state checks and adds relational checks or new scene observations when more evidence is needed. On the right, diagnostic evidence and method preconditions determine whether to reuse the program, invoke a recovery skill, or use MLLM-assisted replanning. The local recovery examples show a translated approach and a regrasp followed by a lift. The replanning loop generates corrective code from RGB observations, execution state, program context, and execution feedback. fig:dimure-overview Disturbances can invalidate the conditions required by a robot's next action even when much of its task program remains useful. A recovery system must therefore choose a response suited to the current state. We present DiMuRe (diagnosis-guided multilevel recovery), a framework for robot-use agents that uses phase-specific evidence and method preconditions to select program reuse or predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA) grasping. After the original program exits, a multimodal large language model (MLLM) can generate corrective code from images and execution feedback. Local verification checks the outcome of each recovery attempt. We also introduce LIBERO-Disturb, a benchmark for robustness and recovery under mid-execution disturbances, supporting program-based agents and VLA policies. On 801 scheduled disturbed Encore development cases, Local DiMuRe (program reuse and recovery skills) achieves 77.65 complete-task success, compared with 58.68 for the original program under the same physical-step allowance. Full DiMuRe achieves 81.90 with terminal replanning, an additional step allowance, and early handoff. Local DiMuRe also uses fewer physical steps per scheduled episode than the original program. Introduction When a target object moves during manipulation, a previously valid grasp command may fail even though much of the task program remains useful. Robot-use agents express perception, motion, and feedback through executable programs~ liang2023code,singh2023progprompt , which can already include checks and retries. Recovery therefore requires determining which parts of the existing behavior still apply. If the object has only shifted in position, translating a recorded grasp segment may suffice. If the grasp assumptions no longer hold, a different recovery procedure may be needed. Each recovery option has limits. Program reuse preserves task-specific motions but depends on the available segments and how they can be adapted. Predefined recovery skills, including bounded vision-language-action (VLA) grasping, handle particular failures when their preconditions are met. A multimodal large language model (MLLM) can compose new action sequences from visual observations and execution feedback, at the cost of additional inference and verification. Choosing among these options requires more than a failure alarm. The system needs evidence that a response is applicable and must then check whether it restores the state needed to continue the task. Obtaining this evidence also takes time, so the decision must account for the cost of further sensing and reasoning. To study these choices, an evaluation must introduce controlled disturbances during execution. Specifying a disturbance does not guarantee that it was applied, had its intended physical effect, or prevented task completion. Recording these outcomes separately makes it possible to assess both the original program's resilience and the benefit of added recovery. To address these challenges, we make two contributions: DiMuRe uses phase-specific diagnostic evidence to select among program reuse, predefined recovery skills, and MLLM-assisted replanning. It checks each method's preconditions and verifies the result of recovery before deciding how to continue. LIBERO-Disturb is a benchmark for mid-execution disturbance robustness and recovery in robotic manipulation. It separates disturbance injection and task evaluation from the tested system, supporting both program-based robot-use agents and VLA policies. The central hypothesis is that different recovery capabilities handle different failure conditions. The evaluation tests whether combining them improves task success while preserving the original program's successful outcomes. It also measures execution time and model use. Figure~ fig:dimure-overview illustrates the approach. Related Work Benchmarks as controlled evaluation settings. LIBERO~ liu2023libero organizes manipulation tasks to study knowledge transfer in robot learning. LIBERO-Disturb builds on these tasks and their goal predicates to evaluate responses to disturbances during manipulation. The disturbance protocol is separate from the tested controller, allowing evaluation of both program-based agents and VLA policies. DiMuRe is a recovery framework evaluated within this setting. Program structure as a source of recovery capability. Program-based control combines perception and action with feedback loops and precondition checks~ liang2023code,singh2023progprompt . These structures provide behaviors that can be reused when execution deviates from its nominal path. Encore constructs task programs before evaluation~ kang2026encore , while interactive coding interfaces allow observations and execution feedback to inform further actions~ chu2026openrua,si2026pyrua . DiMuRe retains existing routines and uses execution evidence to decide when to invoke additional recovery. From execution evidence to recovery decisions. Monitoring can assess explicit task constraints~ zhou2025monitor or use visual, temporal, and multisensor evidence to detect execution failures~ duan2025aha,agia2025sentinel,periasami2026frames . Such evidence supports both failure explanation and intervention: summarized execution histories can guide corrective planning~ liu2023reflect , while policy uncertainty or grasp-state checks can trigger recovery actions~ hung2021introspective,wang2026physicalagentic . The time and inference required for a decision also matter. AESOP~ sinha2024realtime connects fast anomaly detection to slower fallback selection while accounting for reasoning latency through model predictive control. DiMuRe uses diagnostic evidence to assess a candidate method's preconditions and verifies whether its execution restores the state required to continue the task. Restoring execution conditions and revising plans. Recovery methods can restore a required manipulation state or revise the actions used to complete a task. Geometric constraints and learned recovery skills support corrective actions~ huang2025rekep,vats2023efficient,zhao2026flare , while corrected strategies and recovery experience can be retained for later reuse~ luo2025roboreflect,liu2026recova . At the planning level, execution feedback can support new task plans, motion corrections, or code repair~ huang2023inner,chen2025promptrecovery,liu2025hycodepolicy . The timing of this reasoning also differs: DoReMi~ guo2024doremi monitors plan-execution constraints to trigger recovery, whereas AgentChord~ xu2026agentchord prepares recovery branches before execution for activation by compiled monitors. DiMuRe selects among recorded program segments, predefined skills including VLA grasping, and MLLM-assisted replanning using method preconditions and local verification. Its evaluation compares the individual recovery levels with their combined use, reporting task completion and execution costs under each configuration's stated budget. Problem Setting The agent executes an original task program . Its source remains fixed, including its original feedback and retry logic. Disturbances may displace a target, break a grasp, or move a receiving region. The task goal remains unchanged, but subsequent commands may fail unless the affected conditions are restored. Additional recovery is needed when the original program cannot handle these changes. Given the task instruction, program context, sensor observations, and action feedback, the problem is to determine when recovery is needed, which available method applies, and whether its outcome allows the task to continue. The objective is to complete the original task within a declared total physical-step budget , reusing existing behavior where possible and choosing additional recovery from the available evidence and resources. Online decisions do not use hidden simulator state, disturbance labels, or the native success predicate. The native evaluator assesses complete-task success independently. Layered Diagnosis and Multilevel Recovery Figure~ fig:dimure-method summarizes how phase-specific diagnosis connects original-program execution with local recovery and terminal MLLM-assisted replanning. Program Interface and Observations An execution monitor intercepts motion and gripper calls, records grasp and placement segments, and matches objects and receiving regions named in the program to sensor observations. In the Encore integration~ kang2026encore , the monitor uses RGB-D geometry, robot state, and gripper state to track object identity and motion and to assess grasping and release. It evaluates relations expressed in the task instruction using measured geometry. The index denotes an observation or decision event, which need not advance physical execution. Positions are expressed in the robot base frame, and all lengths are in meters. A hat denotes an estimate obtained from RGB-D geometry. Layered Diagnosis: When to Intervene The diagnoser checks execution conditions for the current manipulation phase using robot and gripper state, measured object geometry, and task relations. It requests additional observations when missing geometry or poor visibility prevents a decision. The diagnostic record is Here is the rule-based diagnoser, is the current phase, and contains robot state, measured object geometry, task relations, action feedback, prior verification results, and budget information. The output contains a diagnostic code, rule-based confidence, a suggested response, and supporting evidence. Missing measurements are treated as unknown. The confidence is not a calibrated probability of success. During original-program execution, the monitor first checks the gripper opening, then compares object and tool motion to assess whether the object is attached to the gripper. Their displacement residual is The vectors and are the current estimated object center and measured end-effector position. Subscript denotes the reference measurements stored for the current grasp check. The Euclidean norm measures the difference between the object and tool displacements. The test requires sufficient visible geometry and tool displacement , where is the minimum tool displacement required to evaluate attachment. These thresholds and measurements are lengths in meters. The monitor also requires evidence that the object is no longer supported. Insufficient motion or visibility leaves attachment unconfirmed. If the measurements suggest contact near the receiving region, the diagnoser requests release verification before classifying the object as held or slipped. title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
summary: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.
full_text: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training princeton-prism.github.io/RAFT github.com/princeton-prism/RAFT Introduction Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies, built on pretrained vision-language models and large robot datasets~ anil2023palm,open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023,khazatsky2024droid,kim2024openvla,pmlr-v305-black25a,bjorck2025gr00t , typically still require adaptation to reach the success rates needed to deploy the policy on a real-world target task~ black2024pi_0,kim2025fine . Because collecting task-specific demonstrations is expensive, this post-training often relies on a small dataset collected in a narrow set of environments. Fine-tuning can improve nominal success while reducing robustness to visual and semantic variations absent from those demonstrations~ gao2026taxonomy,zhang2025effective,wang2025generalization,xiang2025parallels,kaplanis2019policy,xing2025shortcut . Existing approaches address this problem through parameter merging, as in RETAIN~ yadav2025retain , or regularization during adaptation~ kachaev2025dontblind,huang2026breakinglockin . We study a complementary approach, aligning a pretrained policy with task-relevant reasoning supervision before adapting it to the target actions. Reasoning supervision can teach policies to identify task-relevant objects, spatial relations, and motion structure~ zawalski2024ecot,fang2026molmoact2,zha2026lap,li2025spatial . We study how reasoning capabilities in pretrained VLMs can support low-data adaptation of generalist VLAs to a target skill. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning ( ), a two-stage adaptation procedure. Stage~I learns low-rank adapters in the language and vision modules from task-relevant reasoning annotations while keeping pretrained parameters fixed. Stage~II freezes these adapters and fine-tunes the language model, action expert, and projection layers on action demonstrations. Action gradients therefore do not directly update the reasoning-adapter weights. We find that how reasoning supervision is incorporated matters: jointly co-training reasoning and actions underperforms plain fine-tuning ( vs.\ mean success on simulated pick and place), and updating the reasoning adapter during action learning falls below Plain FT ( vs.\ ) (Secs.~ sec:cotrain-control and~ sec:stage-ablation ). Staging the two, with the adapter frozen, yields these robustness gains. policies also place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity and episode-time position than plainly fine-tuned policies (Sec.~ sec:diagnostics ). We evaluate on two simulated tasks and two physical platforms: the single-arm DROID setup~ khazatsky2024droid and the bimanual YAM setup~ fang2026molmoact2 . title: ReflexArc: Bottom-Up Integration of Instantaneous Tactile Reflexes into Whole-Body Humanoid Control
summary: Humanoid robots operating in cluttered environments must react to unexpected contacts before the first impact peak, which arrives within tens of milliseconds. Learned whole-body policies running at 50 Hz introduce a policy-cycle delay and may suppress a protective withdrawal as a tracking error. To address these challenges, we propose ARC (Ascending Reflex Control), a bottom-up framework that integrates instantaneous tactile reflexes with learned whole-body control. ARC consists of two components: an instantaneous reflex pathway and bottom-up reflex integration. The reflex pathway detects hazardous contacts from full-body tactile sensing, solves a whole-body withdrawal pose, and delivers it directly to the motors within 10 ms. Bottom-up reflex integration combines reflex-in-the-loop policy learning, reflex-transparent policy alignment, and reflex-informed policy adaptation to sustain the withdrawal, maintain balance, and complete longer-horizon recovery. We deploy ARC on a Unitree G1 and evaluate three categories of hazardous contact. Compared with an otherwise identical reflex delayed by 20 ms, ARC reduces the first force peak by 34.1% and reduces the contact impulse from 0.2632 N s to 0.1225 N s (a 2.15x ratio). We further demonstrate protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal guided by foot tactile sensing. Project page: https://minusmodulo.github.io/reflexarc-website/
