Introduction sec:intro Humanoid robots increasingly operate in cluttered real-world environments, including teleoperated data collection~ he2024omnih2o,qi2026humanoidgpt,zeng2026scalebfm,ze2025twist2 , traversal over complex terrain~ wu2026php,xue2026cat,zhuang2024humanoidparkour , and operation alongside people~ haddadin2016phri,nguyen2018avoidance,roncone2016peripersonal . Unexpected contacts in these settings can damage the robot, its surroundings, or nearby people, and can cause falls. Reducing collision severity requires shortening contact before the first impact peak. Prior work~ koczi2026preload,haddadin2009requirements shows that a compliant layer can delay this peak to a few tens of milliseconds after contact, consistent with observations of human impacts~ robinovitch2009hip,lee2014age . This creates a brief window for protective withdrawal. Existing learned whole-body controllers face two challenges in using this window. First, their top-down control flow introduces latency: a tactile event routed through a policy can wait up to before the next policy update. Second, motion-tracking policies are trained to suppress deviations from a smooth reference, including those caused by a protective reflex. Distributed tactile sensing can trigger a reflex that bypasses policy inference and reaches the motors within milliseconds. However, bypassing inference alone does not resolve the interference between this bottom-up reflex and the top-down policy. Unlike a manipulator, whose low-level controller can take over during a reflex~ deluca2006collision,haddadin2017collisions , a humanoid depends on its whole-body policy to maintain balance throughout withdrawal. The ongoing task should also continue whenever possible. The two controllers cannot simply be assigned different joints: torso and knee reflexes directly affect balance, and even a hand withdrawal can require coordinated motion of the rest of the body. Both pathways must therefore act on the same joints at the same time. Domain randomization~ tobin2017domain,peng2018simtoreal further complicates this interaction by training the policy to reject abrupt disturbances, including the displacement produced by a reflex. To address these challenges, we propose \ (Ascending Reflex Control), which combines an instantaneous reflex pathway with bottom-up reflex integration (Fig.~ fig:overview ). The reflex pathway detects hazardous contacts on the first tactile frame and uses a model-based solver to compute a whole-body withdrawal pose, delivering the command directly to the motors within . Bottom-up reflex integration then coordinates the reflex and policy through three designs. Reflex-in-the-Loop Policy Learning exposes the policy to reflex-induced states during training. Reflex-Transparent Policy Alignment shifts observations and actions and uses counterfactual supervision to prevent the policy from cancelling the reflex. Reflex-Informed Policy Adaptation uses contact information and a human motion prior to complete longer-horizon recovery beyond the immediate withdrawal. We deploy \ on a Unitree G1 and evaluate protected motion tracking, teleoperation, and vision-free obstacle traversal. In a controlled impact experiment, adding to the same reflex increases the contact impulse by , highlighting the importance of direct motor access. Ablations assess the contribution of each integration design. Our contributions are threefold: Instantaneous tactile reflexes. A tactile startle detector and a model-based whole-body solver deliver protective commands to the motors within , before the first impact peak. Bottom-up reflex integration. Three complementary designs allow the reflex and a learned whole-body policy to act simultaneously, sustaining withdrawal while maintaining balance and enabling longer-horizon recovery. Real-world validation. Experiments on Unitree G1 cover three categories of hazardous contact, quantify the effect of reflex latency, and demonstrate protected tracking, teleoperation, and tactile-guided traversal without vision. Related Work sec:related Whole-Body Control under Contact Motion tracking has become the dominant paradigm for whole-body humanoid control, reformulating diverse tasks as the reproduction of reference human motion~ beyondmimic, zeng2026scalebfm . Scaling up training data and model capacity within this paradigm has produced general trackers that follow unseen motions zero-shot~ qi2026humanoidgpt, zeng2026scalebfm , and the same controllers underpin teleoperation and data collection systems that place humanoids in unstructured settings~ he2024omnih2o, ze2025twist2 . Robustness to physical disturbance is obtained almost universally through domain randomization~ tobin2017domain, peng2018simtoreal , which trains the policy to reject perturbations and return to the reference. This top-down paradigm, however, is not designed for contact. The reference motion is generated without knowledge of the surrounding scene, so a contact is never something the policy is asked to respond to---only something it is asked to overcome. Perceptive variants introduce exteroception to avoid obstacles before contact~ wu2026php, xue2026cat , but their reaction still passes through policy inference and therefore inherits its latency. \ retains such a policy as its task-level controller and asks a different question: what happens once a contact has already occurred, faster than the policy can act. Reflexive Control in Robotics Reflexive control separates time-critical reactions from slower deliberative processes: a dedicated pathway is triggered directly by sensing and acts before the deliberative layer can. Early layered architectures placed reactive behaviors beneath higher-level controllers~ brooks1986robust, payton1986architecture . Visual looming is the canonical instance: optical expansion conveys collision urgency without scene reconstruction~ lee1976theory, yilmaz1995visual , and has inspired real-time collision avoidance in robots~ rind2000collision . Learned systems retain this structure, placing safety mechanisms outside the main policy loop, such as reactive shielding~ alshiekh2018safe and tactile stabilizers~ veiga2020hierarchical . On humanoids, prior work has demonstrated protective whole-body reactions~ shimizu2012self , tactile withdrawal reflexes~ ma2016cross , and whole-body tactile compliance~ deanleon2019whole, armleder2025realtime ; SafeFall~ safefall follows the same logic on a learned humanoid, activating a protective policy that takes control from the nominal controller once a fall becomes unavoidable. Across these systems, the reflex either replaces the deliberative controller for its duration, or operates where no learned whole-body policy is present. Neither applies to a humanoid, which depends on its policy for balance precisely while withdrawing. \ therefore keeps both pathways active on the same degrees of freedom, and addresses the interference this creates. Instantaneous Reflex sec:method_reflex Tactile Startle Detection sec:startle We equip Unitree G1 with a full-body tactile suit that allows it to perceive potentially hazardous contacts. Tactile patches are conformally attached to the wrists, elbows, knees, chest, back, and the upper surface of both feet, covering the convex protrusions that most frequently collide with the surrounding environment during locomotion. Each patch is woven from flexible piezoresistive fabric and senses the pressure distribution over a area through taxels at , with each taxel reporting pressure as an -bit value in . Once the patches are mounted on the physical robot, we calibrate every taxel and register it into a digital twin that records its parent link, its position relative to that link, and its surface normal. Conventional tactile sensing emphasizes contact patterns accumulated over long horizons and sustained contact forces. Withdrawing before the first pressure peak leaves a far narrower window: a hazardous contact only becomes clearly distinguishable -- frames after onset, which is already too late. Detection must occur on the onset frame itself, while the contact is still faint and while the flexible patches are themselves deforming and vibrating under fast motion. We refer to this early recognition, as distinct from conventional tactile sensing, as tactile startle. Two properties separate an incipient contact from noise: an impact excites a compact, connected group of taxels whose neighboring taxels exhibit a coherent increase in readings, whereas substrate vibration is spatially diffuse; and taxels that stay quiet under nominal motion begin to respond. We exploit both directly. Each taxel is given an adaptive threshold derived from its own noise baseline during nominal locomotion, so that normally quiet taxels become correspondingly more sensitive, and the thresholded readings are grouped by connected-component labeling over the taxel grid. The location and direction of the reflex follow from the centroid of that component and the surface normals it spans, and are issued within of onset. We optimize a protective reflex pose using only onboard proprioception, including IMU measurements. This setting resembles inverse kinematics (IK) and whole-body retargeting, but neither meets the requirements of an instantaneous reflex. IK~ haddadin2017collisions, deluca2006collision , as used for manipulator reflexes, solves a local chain; on a humanoid such a chain is often blocked by the rest of the body, and impacts on high-inertia segments like the torso and legs admit no reasonable local solution. title: Controlling Action-Head Co-Adaptation to VLM Representation Anisotropy
summary: Modern learning systems increasingly combine pretrained models with downstream heads. Despite the growing importance of such modular designs, how the downstream model co-adapts to the geometry of pretrained representations remains relatively underexplored. We study this problem through vision-language-action models (VLAs), where a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) conditions an action model for control. We find that the action model progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of the VLM outputs. Through controlled experiments across different backbone-head models, we further show that counteracting this sensitivity concentration can be beneficial under representation--task mismatch settings. Motivated by these observations, we introduce \emph{Adaptive Interface Equalizer} (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights pretrained representations according to the evolving downstream sensitivity during training. AdaIE improves VLA success rates on simulation benchmarks, with gains of up to $+5.28$ percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1 and $+1.68$ pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and achieves an average gain of $+19$ pp across five real-world manipulation tasks. It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models.

It further generalizes to diffusion policies and world models, improving downstream performance in both settings. Our results highlight interface co-adaptation as an important optimization problem when coupling pretrained representations with downstream models. Introduction VLAs transfer pretrained VLM knowledge to robotic control~ ma2026survey,kim2024openvla . Recent approaches use diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads to map VLM representations of observations and instructions to continuous actions~ black2024pi_0,li2024cogact,chi2025diffusion,bjorck2025gr00t . Despite substantial progress in data pipelines, architectures, and training~ brohan2023rt,intelligence2025pi_,hou2025dita,li2026matters , the representation interface connecting VLMs and action heads remains comparatively underexplored. The VLM and action model are typically connected through a lightweight conditioning interface, such as cross-attention and concatenation. Through this interface, representations produced by the VLM are directly consumed by the action model for action learning. Despite its simplicity, this interface determines how the representation geometry learned from vision-language pretraining is exposed to the action head. In this work, begin by studying this interface in VLAs, we find that VLM outputs exhibit strong channel-wise anisotropy, and that the action model progressively becomes more sensitive to these dimensions during training (See Figure ~ fig:energy_sensitivity_alignment ). However, the two components are optimized for different objectives: the VLM is pretrained to organize information for vision-language understanding, whereas the action head is trained for control. We therefore ask: Why should an action head trained for control increasingly rely on the same feature dimensions shaped by a VLM pretrained for a different objective? To answer this question, we study the interface by tracking VLM channel variance and action-head sensitivity throughout training, and further compare sensitivity reweighting across interfaces with different degrees of representation--task alignment. We find that counteracting the evolving sensitivity imbalance consistently improves performance under representation--task mismatch. Motivated by these observations, we introduce Adaptive Interface Equalizer (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that reweights representations using evolving downstream sensitivity. We summarize our contributions as follows: We identify backbone--head co-adaptation: the head progressively concentrates its sensitivity on high-variance dimensions of pretrained backbone representations. We show that reducing sensitivity concentration can improve learning under representation--task mismatch. We propose Adaptive Interface Equalizer (AdaIE), a parameter-free mechanism that adaptively reweights backbone representations according to the evolving head sensitivity to regulate interface co-adaptation. We demonstrate AdaIE's effectiveness in VLAs, with success-rate gains of up to +5.28 percentage points (pp) on RoboCasa-GR1, +1.68 pp on RoboTwin 2.0, and an average of +19 pp across real-world manipulation tasks. We further show that its benefits extend to diffusion policies and world models. Action-Head Co-Adaptation to VLM Anisotropy We begin by examining the VLM--DiT interface, characterizing VLM channel-wise anisotropy and the evolution of action-head sensitivity throughout training in Section~ sec:vlm_anisotropic_coadaptation . We then investigate whether this emerging co-adaptation is beneficial for downstreaming learning in Section~ sec:probe . A highly uneven variance across channels indicates an anisotropic representation, where a small subset of dimensions varies more than the rest. Head sensitivity. To estimate efficiently, we use Hutchinson-style stochastic probing~ hutchinson1989stochastic (Algorithm~ alg:sensitivity ). To study those two metrics, we adopt a VLM--DiT architecture following GR00T-N1~ bjorck2025gr00t , where vision-language representations condition a flow-matching DiT action head through cross-attention. Following the RoboCasa-GR1 training setup in StarVLA~ community2026starvla , we use a pretrained Qwen3-VL~ bai2025qwen3 as the VLM backbone and train the action DiT from scratch. For clarity, Figure~ fig:energy_sensitivity_alignment visualizes the top-100 VLM channels with the highest variance. As shown in Figure~ fig:energy_sensitivity_alignment , the VLM exhibits a strongly anisotropic channel-wise variance, while the action-head sensitivity is relatively uniform early in training. As the training goes, the action head becomes increasingly sensitive to the same high-variance VLM dimensions. This growing alignment suggests that the action head progressively co-adapts to the anisotropic structure of the pretrained VLM representation. A similar phenomenon is also observed in other models (see Appendix~ app:co-adaption ). Is Co-Adaptation Beneficial for Action Learning? sec:probe The emerging co-adaptation has two opposing interpretations. One is that the action head becomes more sensitive to high-variance VLM dimensions because these dimensions are more useful for downstream control. An alternative view is that the action head is increasingly shaped by the anisotropic geometry inherited from vision-language pretraining, which may not be optimal for action learning because the VLM and action model are optimized for different domains and objectives. Under this view, reducing the emerging sensitivity imbalance may instead be beneficial. To distinguish between these two interpretations, we construct a controlled experiment on the sensitivity. We compare Exploit, which reinforces the emerging sensitivity pattern, with Equalize, which reduces it, using the original training as the Baseline. To examine when such co-adaptation is beneficial or harmful, we consider two types of backbone--head interfaces with different degrees of representation--task alignment: Aligned. The pretrained representation is expected to be well suited to the downstream task. We consider (1) DINOv2-S with a DPT head~ yang2024depth on NYUv2~ silberman2012indoor for depth estimation, and (2) DeiT~ touvron2021training on CIFAR-100~ Krizhevsky09learningmultiple for image classification. We consider (1) Diffusion Policy~ chi2025diffusion on Push-T for visuomotor action learning, and (2) GR00T~ bjorck2025gr00t on RoboCasa-GR1~ robocasa2024 for vision-language-action learning. To study how downstream heads co-adapt to pretrained representations, we initialize the backbone in each of the four tasks with pretrained weights and otherwise follow the official training recipe. Within each task, all compared variants use the same configuration, differing only in the value of . Detailed training setups are provided in Appendix~ app:prob_detals . The results are shown in Table~ tab:aligned_vs_mismatch . For the aligned tasks, sensitivity reweighting has only a marginal effect on performance, with all three variants performing similarly. title: Hybrid Particle-Voxel Dynamics for Multimodal 3D World Simulation
summary: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation.
full_text: Predicting how the world evolves in response to robot actions is central to policy learning, evaluation, and planning. However, many action-conditioned world models predict future observations in 2D image or video space without explicitly modeling the underlying 3D scene, making spatial consistency across viewpoints and over long-horizon interactions challenging. We introduce 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that jointly predicts appearance, geometry, and tactile observations from a unified 3D representation. Our approach combines a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder that compresses point clouds into compact 3D voxel latents with an action-conditioned latent dynamics model that predicts their evolution. The shared 3D representation supports geometrically consistent rendering from arbitrary viewpoints and flexible integration of spatially aligned tactile signals. Our experiments demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal prediction at 50 Hz. We then show how our model enables scalable data generation for policy training and evaluation using tactile and multi-view visual observations, including wrist-mounted and novel camera views. Furthermore, we scale our method to large datasets containing diverse objects and demonstrate model-based planning with unseen objects and robot configurations. Together, these results highlight the potential of hybrid particle-voxel dynamics as a foundation for multimodal 3D world simulation. Introduction Predicting how the 3D world evolves in response to interaction is a fundamental capability for intelligent robotic systems, with applications to data generation for policy training~ wang2026interactive , policy evaluation~ guo2026ctrl , model-based planning~ huang2026pointworld , and as backbones for world-action modeling~ nvidia2025cosmos . Existing action-conditioned world models are predominantly built using 2D video generation backbones. While able to produce photorealistic predictions, these models do not explicitly represent the underlying 3D scene, making it difficult to maintain spatial consistency across viewpoints and to model the precise spatial relationship between contact and geometry. Prior work has explored using 3D representations~ huang2026pointworld, zhang2024dynamic , but these methods typically rely on strong structural assumptions, such as object-specific state representations or explicit correspondences, that can be unreliable in complex interactions and limit broader applicability. In this work, we present 3D World Simulator, an action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework that predicts in a unified 3D representation space, providing a common interface capable of generating 3D particles, spatially aligned tactile signals, and multi-view consistent renderings from novel viewpoints. Our model supports interactive, long horizon, multimodal 3D video prediction at 50 Hz, and generalizes to diverse objects and environments when trained at scale. 3D World Simulator consists of two technical components. (1) Hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder. The encoder takes point clouds obtained directly from RGB-D video and compresses them into a compact 3D voxel latent. The decoder progressively upsamples this latent into higher-resolution voxels and then dense 3D particles in a coarse-to-fine manner. Each particle parameterizes a 3D Gaussian that can be rasterized from arbitrary viewpoints~ kerbl2023gaussian , while tactile signals are represented directly as 3D particles within the same output space~ huang20243d,huang2025vt . (2) 3D latent dynamics model. We learn an action-conditioned dynamics model that predicts the next 3D voxel latent directly. Because this latent encodes the scene as a whole, the dynamics model does not rely on object-specific state representations or explicit correspondences. A key advantage of our inherently 3D world model is that a single predicted scene state creates a common interface for multiple concurrent capabilities. Since appearance is grounded in a shared 3D Gaussian representation, our model can (1) produce geometrically and multi-view consistent renderings, including from novel and dynamic wrist-mounted camera viewpoints. The same spatial representation provides a (2) flexible and principled way of incorporating multimodal signals. Tactile predictions can be represented directly as 3D particles, remaining geometrically aligned with contacted surfaces. The shared 3D representation also makes our predictions (3) composable with existing 3D assets, including various static backgrounds, objects, and kinematic robot models, enabling additional controllability over the simulated observations from our model. The 3D World Simulator enables several important downstream applications. We demonstrate interactive, long-horizon, multimodal 3D video prediction across a diverse set of six tasks involving rigid, articulated, and deformable objects, outperforming state of the art 2D video and 3D baselines. Next, 3D World Simulator enables policy training and evaluation, generating synthetic data to train imitation learning policies that rely on visuo-tactile observations, as well as multi-view observations including novel and wrist-mounted camera views. Our model can further be used to evaluate policies, demonstrating strong correlation with real evaluations. Furthermore, 3D World Simulator is scalable to diverse objects. We train 3D World Simulator on the large-scale Deform360~ li2026deform360 dataset, a large-scale multi-view visuo-tactile dataset. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art 3D baselines and can be used for zero-shot model-based planning on unseen objects and robot arms. In summary, our main contributions are: (1) 3D World Simulator, a general action-conditioned multimodal world modeling framework for interactive, long horizon 3D video prediction, (2) hybrid particle-voxel dynamics in a unified 3D representation space, enabling view consistency and flexible integration of multimodal signals, and (3) a unified model that enables a range of applications, including policy training, policy evaluation, and planning. Related Works 2D Action-Conditioned Video Model. Existing 2D action-conditioned video models can predict photorealistic futures~ yang2023learning, nvidia2025cosmos, wu2024ivideogpt, jiang2025enerverse, agarwal2026cosmos, liao2026genie . They have shown promising results in robotic manipulation applications such as data generation~ wang2026interactive, gao2026dreamdojo , policy evaluation~ guo2026ctrl, quevedo2026worldgym, li2026dworldeval, huang2025vid2world, team2025evaluating , planning~ zhou2024dino, liang2024dreamitate, chen2025large, hafner2025mastering, hafner2025training, du2023learning, assran2025v , action prediction~ cheang2024gr, jang2025dreamgen, hu2025video, guo2024prediction, wu2024unleashing, bharadhwaj2025genact , policy steering~ wu2025foresight, jain2026weaver , and policy improvement~ yin2026playworld, guo2026vlaw . However, they do not explicitly represent the 3D world, making it difficult to enforce spatial consistency and model complicated object interactions. Among these works, Interactive World Simulator is the most closely related to ours~ wang2026interactive . The authors introduce a task-specific 2D action-conditioned video model that supports interactive, stable, and physically plausible long-horizon simulation. However, it predicts in purely pixel space, making prediction from arbitrary viewpoints and spatial consistency challenging. In contrast, our 3D World Simulator explicitly represents the underlying 3D scene, supporting spatially consistent predictions from novel viewpoint. We show that our model can also accurately model challenging object interactions, including cloth folding and part assembly. 3D Dynamics Models. Many prior works explore modeling object dynamics in the 3D world using various 3D representations, including point cloud~ huang2026pointworld, huang2026soma, bauer2024doughnet , sparse particles~ zhang2025particle, whitney2024learning, huang2025particleformer, zhang2024adaptigraph, jiang2025phystwin, li2018learning , neural radiance fields~ driess2023learning , 3D Gaussians ~ zhang2024dynamic, xie2024physgaussian, shao2025gaussim, abou2024physically, zhang2024physdreamer, lu2024manigaussian, lu2025gwm , and 3D mesh~ pfaff2020learning . Some of them focus on learning dynamics of specific types of objects, such as elastoplastic objects~ bauer2024doughnet, shi2023robocook, shi2024robocraft , cloth~ lin2022learning , fluid~ sanchez2020learning . Among these works, PointWorld and PGND are the closest to ours~ huang2026pointworld, zhang2025particle . Both train 3D world models in point or particle space and show spatially consistent and physically plausible results. However, both use point tracking to provide training supervision. In contrast, our model does not require point-tracking supervision and is transferable across diverse scenes. In addition, they do not focus on photorealistic 2D image rendering, which is essential for visuomotor policy training and evaluation. Instead, our model supports photorealistic 2D rendering from novel viewpoint, including fixed external cameras and moving wrist cameras, enabling scalable data generation and visuomotor policy evaluation. Multimodal World Models. Researchers have explored how to incorporate tactile sensing into world models by predicting 2D tactile images alongside 2D visual images~ higuera2026visuotactileworldmodels, zhang2026contactworld, huang2026vitacworld, ma2026feelworld, wu2026inference, tian2019manipulation, lou2026dream, ye2025learning, zang2026tacforesight, yuan2026vtam, wu2026tactile . In contrast, our model predicts in 3D space with spatial consistency. A closely related work, RoboPack, also models tactile sensing and object interaction dynamics in 3D space to accomplish challenging dense packing tasks~ ai2024robopack . However, its dynamics model mainly focuses on dense packing tasks and predicts over relatively short horizons. Method sec: method In this section, we first describe our problem formulation in Section~ sec:prob_form . Then we will describe how we train our hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder and 3D latent dynamics model respectively in Section~ sec:vae and Section~ sec:dyn . Lastly, we describe how we rollout autoregressively during the inference time in Section~ sec:inf Problem Formulation sec:prob_form We denote the input point clouds at time as , containing visual and, when available, tactile points. Each point contains its 3D world coordinates, RGB appearance, and an additional channel reserved for tactile information. Our experiments use the FlexiTac~ huang2026flexitac, huang20243d tactile sensor, but our method is compatible with various types of sensors. Our goal is to build a model that takes in history point clouds and action to predict next minimizing the difference with ground truth . Our model consists of two parts: a hybrid particle-voxel autoencoder and a 3D latent dynamics model. For the autoencoder, the encoder compresses the point cloud into a compact latent , from which a decoder then reconstructs the point cloud. To model the dynamics, our 3D latent dynamics model takes in latent , last history latents , as well as the robot action and then predicts . Hybrid voxel--particle autoencoder sec:vae Sparse voxel encoder. We first voxelize the input point cloud onto a sparse 3D voxel grid. We aggregate points by averaging the features of points that fall within each occupied voxel, producing features only at occupied voxel locations. The encoder then applies strided sparse 3D convolutions~ graham2018submanifold to progressively downsample the voxel input into a compact latent , avoiding unnecessary computation over empty space. title: Physical Diffusion Policy via MPM-Guided 3D Gaussian Simulation
summary: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments.
full_text: Learning robust manipulation policies for diverse everyday objects remains challenging because objects with different materials exhibit distinct deformation and contact dynamics. While diffusion policies provide a powerful framework for modeling multimodal manipulation behaviors, they typically lack explicit physical reasoning and may produce averaged actions when facing heterogeneous objects. We present a physics-aware diffusion policy that augments visual imitation learning with object physical understanding. Our framework recovers material properties from visual demonstrations by coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting with differentiable Material Point Method simulation, where video guidance and particle-level constraints enable accurate physical parameter estimation. The estimated physics conditions are further integrated into a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts diffusion policy, allowing adaptive behavior generation across different physical regimes. For practical deployment, we introduce a physics memory bank that provides efficient physical retrieval without requiring online simulation optimization. Experiments on a wide range of simulated and real-world objects demonstrate improved manipulation success and generalization over existing diffusion-based approaches. These results show that incorporating physical knowledge is critical for scalable robot manipulation in diverse environments. Introduction Robot manipulation in unstructured environments requires the ability to interact with objects that exhibit diverse physical properties. While humans can effortlessly adapt their behaviors by reasoning about material characteristics such as stiffness, deformability, and compliance, robots typically rely on visual observations and previously collected demonstrations to infer appropriate actions. This gap becomes particularly challenging when manipulating everyday objects, where even visually similar objects may require fundamentally different interaction strategies due to variations in their underlying physical dynamics. Diffusion policies~ chi2025diffusion have recently emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation by learning expressive action distributions from human demonstrations. Recent efforts have further improved diffusion policies by incorporating richer geometric representations, such as 3D point clouds and multi-view spatial features, to enhance scene understanding and manipulation precision~ liu2026twin,lv2026kinematics,wang2024gendp,ze2025generalizable,cao2025mamba,yang2024equibot,ke20243d,ze20243d . Nevertheless, existing diffusion policies primarily treat objects as visual entities and lack explicit awareness of their physical properties. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced in real-world manipulation, where objects with different materials can exhibit substantially different deformation and contact behaviors. Without physical understanding, a single policy may average incompatible interaction patterns, resulting in suboptimal behaviors when encountering heterogeneous objects. A natural solution is to provide manipulation policies with explicit physical knowledge of objects. However, obtaining accurate physical properties from visual observations remains challenging. Traditional system identification approaches typically require carefully designed interactions, force measurements, or object-specific simulators, which are difficult to scale to diverse real-world objects~ calandra2018more,zheng2025survey,chen2025learning . Recent advances in differentiable simulation~ hu2019chainqueen,chen2022diffsrl,si2024difftactile,xie2024physgaussian,zhao2025physsplat,lin2025omniphysgs provide an opportunity to infer physical parameters by optimizing simulation outcomes against observations. Nevertheless, existing methods are primarily designed for physical parameter estimation or sim-to-real transfer, rather than enabling robots to explicitly reason about object physics during policy learning. As a result, the challenge of incorporating physical understanding into general-purpose robot manipulation remains largely unresolved. In this work, we propose a physics-aware manipulation framework that bridges visual observations, differentiable physical simulation, and diffusion-based control. Given multi-view observations of an object, we construct a unified 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d and Material Point Method (MPM)~ sulsky1994particle,sulsky1995application,sulsky1996axisymmetric representation, enabling differentiable simulation and rendering. By optimizing the simulated dynamics against demonstration videos with particle-level physical constraints, our framework estimates object-specific physical parameters, including elasticity, plasticity, and viscosity-related properties. These physical properties are then used as conditions for a physics-aware diffusion policy. To better handle diverse material behaviors, we introduce a material-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, where a learned router dynamically selects material-specific experts to generate physics-consistent manipulation trajectories. Furthermore, we develop a physics memory bank that stores previously estimated physical properties, allowing efficient deployment without expensive online simulation optimization. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce a physics-aware manipulation framework that integrates differentiable physical simulation with diffusion policies, enabling robot manipulation conditioned on estimated object physical properties. We propose a differentiable 3DGS-MPM representation with video-guided optimization and particle-level constraints to recover material properties from visual observations. We design a material-aware MoE diffusion policy that adaptively selects specialized experts for different physical regimes, improving manipulation generalization across heterogeneous objects. We construct a physics memory bank for efficient deployment, avoiding costly online physical optimization while preserving physics-consistent manipulation performance. Related Work Diffusion Models in Robotics. Diffusion Policy~ chi2025diffusion establishes diffusion models as an effective framework for robot manipulation. Building upon this framework, subsequent works have explored different directions to improve policy representation and learning effectiveness. For example, DPPO~ ren2025diffusion further bridges diffusion policies with reinforcement learning, enabling effective policy improvement beyond imitation learning. More recently, latent-space reinforcement learning has also been introduced to steer pretrained diffusion policies toward downstream objectives while preserving their generative capabilities~ wagenmaker2025steering . Another active research direction focuses on incorporating richer 3D scene representations into diffusion policies. DP3~ ze20243d uses point-cloud representations to improve geometric perception during manipulation. 3D Diffuser Actor~ ke20243d directly conditions policy generation on 3D visual representations, while EquiBot~ yang2024equibot exploits SE(3)-equivariant representations to improve spatial generalization. More recent works further investigate efficient sequence modeling for 3D diffusion policies using hybrid state-space architectures~ cao2025mamba and extend DP3 to generalizable humanoid manipulation through egocentric 3D representations~ ze2025generalizable . Despite their strong geometric reasoning ability, existing diffusion policies largely ignore object physical properties. In contrast, our method explicitly conditions diffusion policies on estimated object physics, enabling material-aware manipulation. Simulation in Robot Learning. Simulation has long served as a fundamental tool for robot learning by enabling scalable data collection, policy optimization, and safe exploration before real-world deployment. Existing sim-to-real methods primarily focus on reducing the domain gap between simulated and real environments through techniques such as domain randomization, system identification, and adaptive policy learning~ peng2018sim,james2019sim,memmel2024asid,yu2019sim,zhang2025dynamics,scheikl2022sim,ju2022transferring . More recent simulation platforms further improve the realism of contact dynamics and large-scale parallel training, allowing manipulation policies to be trained efficiently in simulation and transferred to physical robots~ makoviychuk2021isaac,nvidia2021isaacsim . In contrast, our work leverages differentiable simulation from a different perspective. Rather than optimizing policies inside the simulation or improving simulator realism, we employ simulation as a physical reasoning module to estimate object-specific material parameters from visual demonstrations. The recovered physical properties are subsequently injected into a diffusion policy as physics conditions, enabling adaptive manipulation across diverse material categories without relying on online simulation during deployment. Physics-based 3D Gaussian Simulation. The emergence of 3DGS has enabled recent efforts to integrate explicit 3D scene representations with physics-based simulation for modeling dynamic object behaviors. Several works couple 3DGS with MPM to achieve physically plausible deformation, differentiable rendering, and editable dynamic scenes~ xie2024physgaussian,zhao2025physsplat,lin2025omniphysgs . By attaching Gaussian primitives to simulated particles, these methods preserve photorealistic rendering quality while enabling realistic physical animation under predefined material properties. Despite their impressive visual fidelity, existing 3DGS-based physics simulation methods primarily target computer graphics applications such as dynamic scene reconstruction, physical animation, and interactive editing. They generally assume that object material parameters are known a priori and focus on the forward simulation of object dynamics under prescribed constitutive models. Consequently, these approaches are not designed for robotic manipulation. In contrast, our method formulates the problem from an inverse perspective. Instead of using predefined physical parameters to animate a reconstructed scene, we leverage differentiable MPM-3DGS simulation to recover object-specific material parameters from visual demonstrations. The estimated physical properties are subsequently used to condition a diffusion policy, bridging differentiable physical simulation with physics-aware robot manipulation. Formally, given a set of multi-view images , FF-3DGS leverages a neural network to predict a collection of 3D Gaussian primitives via a single forward pass: where each Gaussian is parameterized by its center , opacity , rotation , scale , and color feature . By directly regressing geometric and radiometric attributes from visual observations, FF-3DGS offers superior computational efficiency and cross-scene generalization compared to its optimization-based counterparts. In this work, we adopt FF-3DGS to instantiate an object-centric Gaussian representation from multi-view inputs, yielding a high-fidelity rendering scaffold that is naturally amenable to downstream coupling with MPM-based differentiable physical simulation. \\ Material Point Method: The Material Point Method (MPM)~ sulsky1994particle,sulsky1995application,sulsky1996axisymmetric is a hybrid Eulerian–Lagrangian method for simulating continuum dynamics. title: Action Intent as a Bridge: Transferring Manipulation Knowledge from Human-Centric Videos to Robots
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines. Introduction The rapid progress of large-scale Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ bai2025qwen2 has established the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) paradigm as a promising route toward generalized robot control~ brohan2022rt . However, training VLA models typically relies on robotic demonstrations collected through teleoperation. This data collection process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and dependent on expert operators, which inevitably yields datasets of limited diversity and scale. To alleviate this data bottleneck, a growing body of research has turned to human-centric videos. Such videos are ubiquitous and abundant across the internet, and their diverse, real-world interaction scenarios make them a natural source of supervision for robotic learning. Existing human-to-robot learning approaches broadly fall into two categories: Motion Capture (MoCap) based~ kareer2025egomimic,wang2023mimicplay,li2025scalable and latent action learning~ chen2024igor,bjorck2025gr00t . As shown in Fig.~ figure:first (a), MoCap-based methods rely on MoCap-derived hand models to train robot manipulation policies. However, they still depend on specialized capture equipment, so data acquisition remains costly, and the embodiment gap between human and robot further limits their generalization. To exploit human videos more directly, latent action learning instead extracts transferable representations from raw videos to guide robot manipulation (Fig.~ figure:first (b)). Yet these representations are often contaminated by scene noise, which hampers effective knowledge transfer. Thus, the primary challenge of human-to-robot learning is to extract clean action representations from easy-to-acquire human-centric videos and transfer them to robot manipulation policies. Our key observation is that, before acting, humans first break a complex high-level task into an ordered sequence of simple atomic steps. For example, the instruction ``pick up an apple'' naturally decomposes into steps such as ``move forward, grasp''. We formalize this ordered sequence of atomic steps as the Action Intent. Building on this idea, we regard the Action Intent as a reliable bridge between humans and robots. As illustrated in Fig.~ figure:first (c), our method learns from the easy-to-acquire human-centric videos, yet transfers a clean action intent that is free of scene noise and shared across humans and robots, enabling effective knowledge transfer to the robot. To this end, we propose a two-stage framework built around the Action Intent: the Intent-Guided Latent Disentanglement stage extracts a clean Action Intent, and the Action Intent Policy Alignment stage employs it as a bridge to transfer knowledge and ground it into robot actions. In the first stage, we extract explicit action intents (e.g., ``move forward, grasp'') from both human and robot videos, and integrate them with the video inputs to further disentangle implicit action intent tokens, filtering out scene noise to keep the representation clean. In the second stage, a VLM backbone is jointly pre-trained on human and robot videos within this shared intent space, aligning the two domains, and an action decoder then maps the implicit intent tokens to precise robot actions. Through this design, the Action Intent bridges human videos and robotic VLA models, enabling manipulation knowledge to be transferred as a clean representation shared between humans and robots. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We design a method to extract a clean action representation, termed Action Intent, from human-centric videos in both explicit and implicit forms, and transfer it to robot manipulation policies. We propose a joint pre-training strategy that aligns human and robot data within a shared intent space, enabling effective human-to-robot policy learning. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world settings show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Related Work Vision-language-action Models Building upon the robust multimodal reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ alayrac2022flamingo,liu2023visual , Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged to generate robot actions conditioned on visual observations and language instructions. Pioneered by OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , some works discretize the action space, enabling VLMs to directly predict action tokens via end-to-end fine-tuning~ zitkovich2023rt . Conversely, other works explore more robust generation strategies by leveraging VLMs to produce intermediate representations, which are subsequently decoded into robot actions using diffusion models~ li2024cogact,wen2025diffusionvla,liu2025hybridvla or flow matching~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2504pi0 . More recently, several works~ zawalski2024robotic,zhang2025inspire,zhao2025cot utilize Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to enhance planning and reasoning capabilities for long-horizon tasks. Nevertheless, these methods remain inherently data-hungry. In contrast, our approach transfers knowledge from human-centric videos to VLAs, effectively alleviating the data scarcity bottleneck. Learning from human videos To address the data scarcity challenge in VLAs and unlock the rich information contained in readily available human videos, several studies have leveraged human data to facilitate robot policy learning~ luo2025being,bu2025agibot . Some works~ yang2025egovla,qiu2025humanoid employ Motion Capture (MoCap) devices or algorithms to acquire explicit human actions, conducting imitation learning to guide the robot policy. However, the significant embodiment mismatch between humans and robots severely limits the generalization capability of these methods. Other works~ bahl2023affordances,chen2025vidbot introduce affordance learning from human videos to acquire object-interaction knowledge. While offering new insights, these approaches often lack a concrete and explicit bridge for effective human-to-robot transfer. More recently, some works~ zheng2025flare,univla,lapa leverage latent actions extracted from videos as domain-invariant information to pre-train action models. Nevertheless, these latent actions often provide limited guidance due to task-irrelevant noise and insufficient information extraction. In contrast, our approach transfers a clean, embodiment-agnostic, and information-dense representation for human-to-robot learning. Proposed Method Preliminaries Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are designed to synthesize precise robotic actions conditioned on visual observations and language instructions . Standard methods follow a direct mapping paradigm , typically achieved by fine-tuning pre-trained Vision-Language Models. However, this supervised approach is inherently data-hungry and constrained by the scarcity of ground-truth robotic annotations. To address these data limitations, this paper introduces an Action-Intent-guided transfer learning strategy leveraging human-centric videos. Concretely, we assume access to a limited dataset of expert robot trajectories, denoted as . Each trajectory contains paired visual observations , language instructions , and ground-truth actions . This dataset supports supervised learning but is expensive to scale. We also utilize a dataset of human-centric videos, denoted as . Unlike robotic data, these videos consist solely of visual frames without associated action labels or language instructions. The challenge lies in extracting transferable knowledge from to improve the policy on the target robot domain. Motivation We observe that human manipulation follows a hierarchical process: a high-level decision of how to move is formed before the low-level motor command is executed. We formalize this intermediate decision as the action intent, and hypothesize that robots share the same hierarchical process. This shared structure allows us to use the action intent as a bridge for transferring knowledge from humans to robots. Building on this insight, we introduce an action intent variable and decompose the policy into a planning stage and an execution stage that reflect the above hierarchy. Here, is a representation shared between humans and robots, inferred from the current observation to link perception with motor control. Accordingly, the policy is reformulated as the transition: (o_t, l) a_t. Under this formulation, the shared planning stage becomes the channel through which human knowledge is transferred to the robot policy. Method Overview Concretely, our framework consists of two primary stages, as illustrated in Fig.~ figure:laten and Fig.~ figure:post . The Action-Intent-Guided Latent Disentanglement stage aims to obtain a clean action intent that serves as the bridge between the two domains, while the Action Intent Policy Alignment stage leverages this bridge to transfer human knowledge and ground it into executable robot actions. In the first stage, we extract the action intent from both the human dataset and the robot dataset . We first synthesize the explicit intent using a VLM-based strategy for human videos and a rule-based strategy for robot trajectories. By integrating the videos with these explicit intents, we then disentangle the clean implicit intent from scene noise, yielding a representation tailored for VLA comprehension: In the second stage, we align the human and robot representation spaces over the shared intents through joint pre-training, so that knowledge from human videos flows into the robot policy. An action decoder then maps to executable robot actions . Action-Intent-Guided Latent Disentanglement In this stage, we aim to acquire the action intent shared across human and robot videos. Our design follows a coarse-to-fine rationale: the explicit intent serves as a high-level semantic anchor that guides the disentanglement of the fine-grained implicit intent . To obtain , we tailor two generation protocols to the differing conditions of the two domains. Human videos lack both language instructions and action labels, so we leverage a VLM to jointly generate the instruction and the explicit intent . While robot trajectories already provide language instructions in their metadata, they still lack intent labels, so we derive directly from the precise proprioceptive states via a rule-based strategy. Guided by these explicit intents, we then introduce an Intent-Guided Disentanglement architecture, comprising an action tagger and a feature-wise generator, to distill the clean implicit intent from the videos. title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-Free World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.
full_text: 1.5 rll & Website & \\ & Code & \\ Introduction Pretrained video diffusion models offer a promising foundation for robot control~ zhu2025unified,kim2026cosmospolicy,gao2026dreamdojo . Through large-scale video pretraining, these models learn to predict how physical environments evolve over time, providing predictive knowledge that can guide robot actions. World Action Models (WAMs; ye2026dreamzero ) use this knowledge by adapting video models to predict visual futures and actions, demonstrating strong manipulation performance and generalization to new tasks and environments~ kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero . A common approach in WAMs is to use this predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models through future video prediction, either by jointly predicting visual futures and actions~ kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero or by decoding actions from predicted visual futures~ hu2025vpp,pai2025mimicvideo . These methods leverage the pretrained models' knowledge through their native video prediction process. However, iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference cost, and errors in the predicted visual futures can lead to inaccurate actions. Moreover, it remains unclear whether action prediction requires the same level of visual detail as video generation. A central question is how to make better use of the predictive knowledge in pretrained video models for action prediction. The success of video-generating WAMs demonstrates the value of this knowledge, while leaving open how it should be represented to support control. This motivates investigating whether predictive information can be made directly available in the visual features used for action prediction. We hypothesize that this predictive knowledge can be effectively captured in visual representations to support action prediction, without iterative video denoising. Our key idea is to distill the video model's predictive knowledge into the visual representations computed from the current observation. We train a visual encoder to anticipate visual futures from the observation by using the representations extracted from a pretrained video diffusion model. Our analysis shows that distillation enables the encoder to effectively capture future visual information from the current observation and make its features more useful for action prediction. The resulting predictive representations enable action prediction without generating future videos. Based on this finding, we introduce , a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion backbone as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. We train the model in two stages, separating predictive representation learning from action learning. In the first stage, a frozen video diffusion model extracts representations from both current and future frames of a video demonstration, and the visual encoder learns to predict these representations from the current observation. The encoder thus learns to anticipate scene evolution in feature space, making the video model's predictive knowledge available in a single forward pass without future video generation. This stage requires no action labels, allowing the visual encoder to learn from any in-the-wild video demonstrations. In the second stage, we train an action module on robot demonstrations to map these visual features to executable actions, with the visual encoder either frozen or jointly fine-tuned. We evaluate on diverse manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world environments~ khazatsky2024droid , demonstrating stronger performance compared to state-of-the-art VLA and WAM baselines~ intelligence2025pi_05,ye2026dreamzero . In real-world evaluations, succeeds on tasks involving object deformation or successive rearrangements where video-generating WAM fails (Figure~ fig:concept ). These successes suggest a benefit of using predictive visual representations for control without relying on potentially inaccurate video predictions. Experiments show that using a larger video backbone and additional pretraining video data improve success, demonstrating can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control without additional action annotation. We additionally show task transfer from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, showing that can learn new tasks from videos without collecting action annotations for those tasks. In addition to strong performance, offers a practical advantage for real-time control. During deployment, the policy obtains predictive visual representations in a single encoder pass and uses them to generate an action chunk without iterative video denoising. using a 14B video backbone achieves real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz, achieving a inference speedup over a video-generating WAM with the same video backbone size and latency comparable to that of a VLA (Figure~ fig:concept , middle). We outperform state-of-the-art VLA and WAM baselines in real-world manipulation without task-specific adaptation, while achieving real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz. We show that translates stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control. We demonstrate that can learn new tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotations for the new tasks. Related work Vision-language-action policies Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies adapt pretrained vision-language models to map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions~ intelligence2025pi_05, rss2025_pi0,zitkovich2023rt,bjorck2025gr00t,kim2024openvla . While their backbones provide semantic and linguistic priors, pretraining on static image-text pairs gives them limited knowledge of the spatiotemporal dynamics important for robot control. Video model-based robot policies Video model-based robot policies build on pretrained video diffusion models by coupling future visual prediction with action prediction. Some decode actions from video representations through inverse dynamics~ hu2025vpp,pai2025mimicvideo,rhoda2026dva , while others jointly denoise future video and action sequences~ kim2026cosmospolicy,li2026lingbotva,bi2026motus,ma2026dit4dit,ye2026dreamzero . These World Action Models (WAMs) transfer spatiotemporal video priors to control, achieving strong action-data efficiency and generalization. However, generating future video at deployment introduces substantial inference cost, and errors in the predicted video can lead to inaccurate action prediction. Recent works retain video prediction during training while enabling action prediction without future video generation at deployment~ yuan2026fastwam,ye2026gigaworld , yet how faithfully their representations preserve the video model's predictive knowledge remains unclear. title: Mass Scaling Laws for Energy-Optimal Horizontal Multirotor Flight
comment: Accepted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters, October 2026
summary: Multicopters are a type of aerial robot seeing extensive real-world applications but with range and endurance as critical bottlenecks. Optimization of its energy efficiency through energy-aware flight planning (e.g. cruise speed-scheduling) has hence been an important topic. The mass of the multicopter is an important factor to consider, as it has a significant impact on efficiency, and many common applications are subject to frequent mass variation due to payload change. This work derives closed-form scaling relationships between the energy-optimal steady horizontal flight behavior of a multicopter and its vehicle mass, and validates them experimentally on two multirotor platforms. Specifically, for mass-only variation, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show through a combination of numerical simulation, theoretical derivation, and experimental validation that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of vehicle mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle is constant with respect to mass; and (3) the optimal energy per meter is proportional to mass. The analysis shows that these three relationships arise from a common mass-similarity property of the steady-state flight and rotor-aerodynamic equations. Furthermore, the obtained scaling relationships enable simple yet effective cruise-speed planning to optimize energy efficiency and extend the range and endurance of the multicopter.

Aerial Systems: Mechanics and Control, Motion and Path Planning, Optimization and Optimal Control, multicopter, mass scaling. Introduction sec:Intro ulticopters have been emerging as a versatile aerial robot with wide applications, ranging from aerial photography and inspections, to intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions, to package delivery among many others. However, their widespread adoption faces a major challenge in range and endurance, as their flight time, typically around 30 minutes, poses significant constraints on their capability and performance scaramuzza2022 . Prediction and optimization of multicopter energy consumption and performance have been actively studied in aerial robotics. Extensive work has focused on modeling energy dynamics and estimating flight range and endurance scaramuzza2022, KIRSCHSTEIN2020102209, MURRAY2020368, POIKONEN2020104802, Stolaroff2018, FIGLIOZZI2017251, Li2024 . While many early models focus on hovering or quasi-hovering conditions, recent studies consider the coupled rotor aerodynamics, propulsion, and rigid-body dynamics during forward flight michel2022performance, scaramuzza2022 . These aerodynamic effects make energy consumption strongly dependent on horizontal cruising velocity, with competing effects such as rotor inflow and body drag giving rise to an energy-optimal velocity. In di2015energy , experimental measurements are performed to quantify the difference in energy consumption caused by horizontal velocity, while several model-based studies, including michel2022performance, scaramuzza2022, DUKKANCI2021102985 among others, investigate the relationship using simulation. These works reveal the trade-off of various factors affecting the energy consumption rate, such as inflow aerodynamic effects and body drags, and the existence of an optimal velocity that maximizes the efficiency. Therefore, cruise-speed selection has become an important topic in energy-optimal flight planning and control scaramuzza2022,Zeng2019,di2015energy, wu2020inflight, Michel2023asme . One remaining topic of significant theoretical and practical interest is how energy efficiency and energy-optimal flight behavior change with vehicle mass. In many multicopter applications, e.g. drone delivery and air mobility, vehicle mass is subject to frequent and substantial variations, making its impact on energy efficiency important. Several existing works DUKKANCI2021102985,Hwang11092221,TAMKE2023,Patnaik2025 have investigated how the energy consumption versus velocity curve changes with mass through simulations and experiments. Beyond the expected increase in energy consumption, these studies show that the energy-optimal velocity also increases with mass when other vehicle properties, including aerodynamics and geometry, remain unchanged. The form of this dependence, however, has not been established. In Hwang11092221 , it appears as a qualitative trend in a numerical endurance study as the payload-to-vehicle weight ratio is varied, with no explicit relationship stated. In DUKKANCI2021102985 , the optimal speed is obtained numerically from an energy model calibrated to a reference vehicle, in which vehicle weight enters only the induced-power term while rotor speed, and hence blade profile power, is held fixed. Neither work identifies the invariance of the energy-optimal pitch angle, from which the velocity scaling follows, or addresses the scaling of the minimum energy per meter. Existing analytical models have also characterized the relationship among energy consumption, velocity, and vehicle mass. A commonly used metric is Energy Per Meter (EPM), i.e., the energy consumed per unit distance. For example, Dorling201770 extends a hovering-based energy model to horizontal flight to study the metric, while Dandrea2014 derives velocity-dependent power consumption for forward flight and obtains energy per distance by dividing power by velocity. However, the former neglects forward-flight aerodynamic effects, while the latter simplifies them through a prescribed lift-to-drag relationship. In summary, the quantitative relationships between vehicle mass and energy-optimal flight conditions remain to be established. The contribution of this work is an in-depth theoretical, numerical, and experimental study of the relationships among energy efficiency, cruise velocity, and vehicle mass, as summarized in Fig.~ fig:Overall . Building on established multicopter energy dynamics michel2019multiphysical, michel2022performance,scaramuzza2022 , we combine a propeller model based on blade-element/momentum theory (BEMT) with steady-state force balance from the rigid-body dynamics to derive explicit mass-scaling relationships for the energy-optimal cruise condition. Specifically, for mass-only variation of a fixed vehicle configuration, i.e., when payload changes the vehicle mass while the airframe geometry, aerodynamic characteristics, and rotor configuration remain unchanged, we show that (1) the energy-optimal velocity is proportional to the square root of the mass; (2) the energy-optimal pitch angle remains unchanged with mass; and (3) the minimum energy consumption per unit distance, or EPM, is proportional to the vehicle mass. These relationships are derived theoretically and validated experimentally on two multirotor platforms under payload-induced mass variations. Multicopter Energy Dynamics Modeling The theoretical and simulation studies in this work are based on a physics-based multicopter model that captures key coupled dynamics governing energy consumption, with a particular focus on rotor aerodynamics and rigid-body dynamics. Strictly speaking, the analysis targets the mechanical and aerodynamic efficiency, which constitute the dominant contributors to energy consumption and are essential for characterizing energy-optimal cruise behavior. Other system components, including the motor, battery, and electronic speed controller (ESC), are not considered explicitly in the closed-form derivations, as their efficiencies are relatively constant over the operating regime of interest and have a comparatively smaller impact on the mass-scaling behavior. The influence of these components is discussed separately in Sec.~ OCE . Rigid Body Kinetics The motion of the multicopter is modeled using the rigid body dynamics according to the free body diagram in Fig. fig: OctoFBD . We consider 2D dynamics here, which are sufficient for forward flight, where and are the horizontal and vertical positions, and are the horizontal and vertical velocities of the vehicle (center of mass) in the global frame, and is the pitch angle. In addition, is the sum of thrusts of all rotors computed by the propeller model (with each rotor indexed by subscript and total number of rotors ), is the body drag force with being the body drag coefficient, is the total pitch-axis torque on the vehicle generated by the thrusts, is the moment of inertia about the pitch axis, and is the arm length of each rotor thrust to the pitch axis. Noted that we model the horizontal aerodynamic resistance as a quadratic body-drag term, and omit the linear drag component associated with rotor hub and in-plane forces, which are known from blade-element theory to grow roughly in proportion to the forward velocity~ Leishmann2000 . For the flight regime of interest, i.e., typical mid- to large-scale payload-carrying multirotors operating near energy-optimal velocity, the linear drag is comparatively small. Aerodynamically, these vehicles operate at low advance ratio because the rotor-tip speed is much higher than the forward velocity, and hence the rotor-generated in-plane forces scale approximately linearly with velocity. In contrast, the airframe and payload behave as bluff bodies whose drag grows with the square of velocity~ Anderson2017 . A drag law that increases faster than linearly is needed for a pronounced non-monotonic EPM-velocity curve typically observed in experiments. We have performed experimental studies to validate such treatment. Specifically, we compute the rotor thrust and linear drag for steady forward-flight conditions using a blade-element/momentum model calibrated on thrust-stand data reported in literature michel2022performance . Then, using real-world flight data, we determine the total drag directly from the measured velocity and pitch angle through steady force balance. The body drag term, which is the residual between the total and linear drag, grows approximately with the square of velocity in the neighborhood of the energy optima, and clearly dominates over the linear drag contribution in that regime. These physical considerations and experiment results together justify representing the dominant horizontal resistance near the optimal velocity as a quadratic drag term. title: Coordinating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Action-Conditioned Latent Foresight
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively.
