Introduction sec:introduction Everyday humanoid tasks require coordinated actions over time. To place a basket on a table, the robot must raise and position the basket while maintaining its grasp until the table supports it. To load a washer, it must open the door, carry a T-shirt to the drum without dropping it, and release it only once it is inside. These tasks connect whole-body motion with hand interaction: an execution decision concerns both the scene a command sequence will reach and the relationships among commands along the way. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate commands from images and language instructions~ openvla,pi0,pi05 , while humanoid models incorporate human motion and predictive representations~ psi0,wholebodyvla,motionwam,omega0 . When an action generator proposes several sequences, the robot must decide which one to execute. Latent world models provide predictions for goal-directed planning~ dinowm,vjepa2 . Most world--action models use future prediction to improve command generation~ dreamzero,dit4dit,fastwam rather than to compare sampled sequences before execution. Existing verifiers use VLM judgments~ robomonkey,forewarn , while DreamTrajectory combines predicted trajectory agreement with action smoothness~ dreamtrajectory . Two signals are relevant for evaluating proposed humanoid actions: predicted visual progress evaluates the endpoint relative to a task goal, while temporal consistency evaluates relationships among commands within the sequence. We introduce action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world--action model (WAM) that uses both signals for humanoid loco-manipulation (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). An action generator proposes joint motion--hand command sequences; an action-conditioned endpoint predictor scores their visual progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, and a joint temporal prior scores their temporal consistency. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. Our contributions are threefold: We propose action-conditioned latent foresight, which scores generated motion--hand sequences before execution using predicted visual progress and a learned joint temporal prior. We develop action consistency regularization for latent prediction. A training-only inverse action decoder reconstructs the first demonstrated command from both observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predicted features to retain information about the executed action. We evaluate ten SIMPLE~ simple simulation tasks and seven real-robot tasks, including unseen object configurations. Our method exceeds the evaluated baselines in average success; closed-loop ablations show gains from action consistency regularization and joint temporal scoring. Related Work sec:related Humanoid VLAs and World--Action Models VLA policies transfer vision--language representations to command generation~ openvla,pi0 . Heterogeneous co-training improves open-world generalization~ pi05 , and diffusion action heads generate continuous action chunks~ gr00tn1 . For humanoids, EgoVLA uses retargeted wrist and hand motion~ egovla , exploits egocentric pretraining~ psi0 , and WholeBodyVLA learns manipulation and locomotion latent actions from video before decoding upper-body and locomotion commands~ wholebodyvla . World--action models couple prediction with command generation. DreamZero jointly models video and actions~ dreamzero ; DiT4DiT and MotionWAM condition action or motion diffusion on intermediate video-model features~ dit4dit,motionwam . MotionWAM combines SONIC motion codes with hand-control channels~ motionwam , while -0 generates controller-compatible actions from future embeddings~ omega0 . WholeBodyWAM pretrains a motion expert to learn whole-body motion priors for robot action generation~ wholebodymotion . Fast-WAM and InternW0- use future supervision during training without generating video at test time~ fastwam,internw0 . In our method, the action generator supplies command sequences, and each sequence prefix is scored before execution using action-conditioned prediction and temporal consistency. Action Supervision for Latent Prediction Latent world models predict action-conditioned feature transitions for goal-directed planning~ dinowm,vjepa2 . V-JEPA 2.1 learns dense video features~ vjepa21 , and a study of JEPA world models examines how representation, predictor, and planner choices affect physical planning~ jepawms . VLA-JEPA learns VLM latent tokens through future-state prediction and uses them to condition flow-matching action generation~ vlajepa . Related models combine feature prediction with action modeling~ jepawam , or predict future latent states alongside actions~ lewam . Our predictor takes the proposed command prefix as input and estimates its endpoint features, allowing command sequences sampled from the same observation to receive different visual scores. Action supervision can also arise from discrete or constrained continuous latents~ lapa,lawm , inverse dynamics that turn generated video into executable actions~ unipi , or visual correspondences~ avdc . Our action consistency regularization uses an inverse action decoder to reconstruct the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, providing a training objective for the endpoint predictor rather than a test-time action decoder. Temporal Action Priors and Sequence Scoring Action-sequence models~ diffusionpolicy,act and cross-embodiment action priors~ actionpriors learn regularities that guide generation. PRISM combines state-conditioned priors with planning distributions~ prism , and DynaGuide uses learned dynamics to steer diffusion~ dynaguide . Action verification evaluates proposed actions before execution: RoboMonkey learns action preferences with a VLM verifier~ robomonkey , while FOREWARN aligns predicted latent rollouts with behavior descriptions for VLM-based action choice~ forewarn . DreamTrajectory combines agreement with intended end-effector trajectories and fixed smoothness penalties~ dreamtrajectory ; LeWAM's DemoDPO uses demonstration preferences for offline policy refinement~ lewam . Our temporal prior learns to predict the next complete command from the initial robot state and preceding motion--hand commands. Its prediction error is combined with visual progress when scoring proposed actions. title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations
summary: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro A world model that renders the consequences of a policy's actions can serve as a simulator: rollouts become parallel, repeatable, and free of the risk of damaging hardware. This sidesteps both the danger and the sample cost of online training on real hardware rlhf, ppo, rl_survey2024, sop , and avoids the sim-to-real gap soma, digital_cousin and the per-environment engineering that hand-built physics simulators demand. The idea runs from model-based reinforcement learning, where agents learn from imagined rollouts alone wm, dreamer, dreamerv3, daydreamer , through interactive video generation for games and open-ended worlds diamond, genie, matrix, gamengen, yume-15, hunyuan-gamegraft, echo-joy , to action-conditioned robot world models ctrl-world, dreamdojo, genie-envisioner, lingbot-world2 . What such a model must do is narrower than generating plausible video: it must adhere to the actions a policy issues, keep several camera views consistent, and stay coherent over rollouts far longer than the window it was trained on. We present PrimeSim, a world model built as a robot simulator that meets all three requirements. To enable faithful action following and consistent multiview generation, we adapt a pretrained video model to robot dynamics through midtraining on 30,110 hours of demonstrations spanning 22 robot platforms. For action following, we unify heterogeneous robot controls into a shared action representation and introduce frame-aligned dual-path action conditioning, combining temporally aligned attention with direct action injection to establish precise correspondence between robot controls and generated motion. For multiview consistency, we introduce view-aware interleaved attention, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving camera-specific representations through explicit camera identities. Through joint conditional flow-matching training, these designs allow a single model to learn action-conditioned, multiview robot dynamics across diverse embodiments, establishing the foundation for an interactive world model simulator. While midtraining establishes action-conditioned multiview generation within a fixed temporal window, turning the model into a practical robot simulator introduces a fundamental challenge: autoregressive simulation requires continuously conditioning on the model's own imperfect predictions, whereas conventional video generators are trained on fixed-length, ground-truth contexts. This mismatch leads to error accumulation over extended rollouts and is compounded by the computational cost of iterative video generation. To address these challenges, we develop a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that progressively transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient, long-horizon autoregressive simulator. First, we enable fast generation through chunk-causal adaptation and four-step consistency distillation, making sequential simulation and subsequent self-rollout training computationally tractable. Second, we improve self-conditioned stability through self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching against the frozen bidirectional teacher, allowing the model to learn from its own generated histories rather than relying solely on ground-truth context. Third, we introduce hierarchical temporal memory to support long-horizon coherence, preserving the initial scene, sparse long-term history, and dense recent motion within a bounded KV cache. Together, these components enable efficient autoregressive simulation that remains robust to self-generated context and scales beyond the original training window. Together, these designs enable PrimeSim to generate temporally coherent rollouts up to 105 seconds at 10.1 FPS, supporting diverse robotic manipulation tasks involving both rigid and deformable objects. Compared with five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim achieves state-of-the-art performance on WorldSimProbe worldsimprobe , leading four of its five suites: global trajectory coverage by 10.0 , action-source behavior preservation by 41.8 , and interaction dynamics by 48.4 , each measured against the strongest competing model on that axis, with interaction grounding also led at 85.7. On EWMBench, PrimeSim reaches the best overall score of 6.09, ahead of both GE-Sim variants (5.82 and 5.79) and every instruction-conditioned model, and is best on five of the eight dimensions, including perfect scores on high-level semantics, trajectory alignment and logical consistency, with action semantics (BLEU) 72.7 above the strongest GE-Sim variant. Beyond benchmark fidelity, we demonstrate the practical utility of PrimeSim as a learned simulator for GRPO-based policy optimization~ grpo , enabling policy improvement through model-generated interactions. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code to support further research. main contributions are summarized as follows: We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that transforms a pretrained video generator into an interactive robot world model through a progressive midtraining and posttraining framework. We develop a large-scale midtraining framework using 30,110 hours of demonstrations across 22 robot platforms. With unified cross-embodiment action representations, frame-aligned dual-path conditioning, and view-aware interleaved attention, PrimeSim learns action-faithful and multiview-consistent robot dynamics across diverse embodiments. We introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that combines efficient causal generation, self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching, and hierarchical temporal memory. This enables fast, self-conditioned autoregressive simulation while mitigating long-horizon error accumulation beyond the original training window. We demonstrate strong performance across diverse rigid and deformable object manipulation tasks: 10.1 FPS at four sampling steps, coherent rollouts of up to 105 seconds, 6.09 overall on EWMBench (first), and first on four of five WorldSimProbe suites against five open-source action-conditioned world models, retaining the lead on two of the three action-realisation axes and interaction dynamics. We further validate PrimeSim as a learned simulator for GRPO-based policy optimization. Data Engine sec:data_engine Our goal for training data was to learn from a massive and diverse pool of settings while keeping our representations simple. To this end, we assembled 30 , 110 hours of robot demonstration data from a mix of open-source and proprietary sources. Dataset statistics are shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , and an overview of the datasets used is provided in Table~ tab:datasets_frames . In general, we include any demonstration data that can be converted into our unified format with reasonable effort, whether humanoid, dual-arm, single-arm, UMI umi , or simulated. We describe the conversion pipeline, quality filtering, and dataset composition below and in the appendix. Robot Data Pooling. Motivated by the low cost of data collection, recent state-of-the-art methods pretrain on large egocentric human videos with a smaller ratio of robot data lingbot-va, dreamdojo, cwm . However, aligning robot actions to latent actions or predicted hand-to-end-effector poses adds additional complexity. Since pooled robot datasets, open- and closed-source together, now largely match the scale of the egocentric corpora those models relied on, we skip the alignment problem entirely: we train directly on robot demonstrations from both sources and simply unify their action and state spaces using the general action representation described in Sec.~ sec:action_repr . Dataset Staging. Each training stage serves a different purpose, so each should be trained on a different data distribution. For midtraining, we require vast and highly diverse data sources, so we use the entire dataset. For posttraining, the model has already seen the full corpus and the stage mainly aims to improve long-horizon and real-time responsiveness rather than to broaden coverage. We therefore train it on small datasets collected for specific downstream tasks, which are long enough to contain complete episodes and representative of what the deployed simulator is asked to continue, rather than on a subsample of the pretraining mixture. Data Pipeline Stage 1: Video Quality Filtering Spatiotemporal validity. We discard clips whose motion or temporal characteristics fall outside the corpus distribution. Motion is assessed via dense optical flow~ optical-flow : given the flow field between adjacent frames, we compute where is the image domain. The motion score is not used to retain only high-motion samples; instead, it supports distribution control. Near-static clips are downsampled so the corpus is not dominated by a small number of platforms that remain stationary. Motion scores are read within a platform rather than across the corpus, because the flow a camera records at rest varies markedly between fixed, handheld and wrist-mounted views. The retained data therefore spans subtle in-hand manipulation, camera movement, and larger end-effector displacement without collapsing toward either motion extreme. Artifact detection. We remove frames and clips containing JPEG encoding artifacts, and discard any whose state or action values are numerically corrupted. Episode length filtering. Clips shorter than 1 second are excluded, as they do not provide enough temporal context for autoregressive training. Stage 2: Action Quality Filtering Embodiment-type filtering. Datasets with dexterous hands or humanoid legs represent a small fraction of the pooled corpus. To keep the action representation simple, we filter these datasets out. This removes legged locomotion, not humanoids as a class: humanoid platforms on a wheeled chassis are kept, because their arm, torso and chassis commands all fit the slots the interface already provides, and they supply the largest single share of the corpus (Fig.~ fig:overview ). Anomaly detection. We discard sequences whose action signals contain discontinuities inconsistent with continuous robot motion. We detect these as outliers in the first difference of each action channel: an isolated step change far outside the distribution of adjacent steps indicates a sensor or logging fault rather than a commanded acceleration. Datasets containing corrupted video frames, or action values outside their admissible range, are discarded as well. Missing action detection. Some datasets leave certain action features blank, such as end-effector pose or chassis velocity. If these values cannot be recovered through forward kinematics, the affected data is dropped. Stage 3: Data Alignment Frequency alignment. We preserve each dataset's native sampling rate at collection time, but resample to a fixed 10\,Hz during training. If a dataset cannot be resampled to exactly 10\,Hz within a 0.03\,s timestamp tolerance, we use the closest achievable frequency. Camera alignment. The number of cameras varies across embodiments. To make batches collatable, we fix the model's camera count to three. Datasets with more than three cameras have their uncommon cameras dropped; datasets with fewer have the primary camera repeated until three slots are filled. Prompt alignment. Datasets differ in whether they provide natural-language task descriptions. For datasets that include prompts, we keep them as is. For datasets that do not, we generate a prompt from the task metadata with a template-based generator, so that every training sample is paired with a task description. Format conversion. All datasets are converted to LeRobot~ lerobot format. We chose this format for three reasons: (i) its storage is space-efficient, (ii) many open-source datasets already use it, and (iii) recent updates have made it reliable for large-scale training at the tens-of-thousands-of-hours scale use

title: Trusting Imagined Futures: Auditing Imagined Rewards for VLA Post-Training
summary: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.
full_text: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25 , improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33 to 70.00 across 60 candidate pools. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, providing pretrained policies that can be adapted to different tasks~ zitkovich2023rt2,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0 . When post-training relies on imitation learning, the quality of the supervision trajectories directly affects the behaviors the policy learns. Available trajectories vary in task progress and execution quality, and imitating them can cause the policy to reproduce undesirable behaviors. Selecting suitable supervision trajectories is therefore important for VLA post-training. Video world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions, providing imagined outcomes for behavior evaluation~ yang2023unisim,zhu2025wmpo . A reward model scores these outcomes to compare candidates and support policy learning~ zhu2025wmpo,zhang2026wise . When imagined outcomes are used to select supervision for VLA post-training, reward ranking identifies candidates with higher predicted utility. Accepting such a candidate as a replacement also requires assessing whether its predicted advantage over the existing trajectory is trustworthy. An apparently successful grasp or task completion in an imagined video may correspond to an unstable grasp, a collision, or an incorrect object interaction during real execution. Errors in world model predictions and reward estimates can give such candidates high scores~ gao2022overoptimization,jiang2026wovr . When they replace existing trajectories as behavior cloning targets, these evaluation errors can cause the policy to learn undesirable behaviors. We study whether auditing rewards predicted from imagined outcomes improves supervision selection and subsequent policy learning (Fig.~ fig:motivation ). We evaluate this question using fixed candidate pools with matched executions. We propose Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), which uses real execution feedback to train a risk auditor that complements reward scores when deciding whether to accept candidate trajectories as supervision. The reward model evaluates imagined videos along five dimensions: task progress, goal correctness, manipulation quality, safety, and execution stability. It jointly predicts a utility score for candidate ranking. The auditor learns from discrepancies between these predictions and the corresponding real execution outcomes to identify candidates with high predicted scores but poor execution quality. TIF first selects the candidate with the highest predicted utility. It accepts this candidate if its predicted advantage over the existing supervision trajectory (Source) exceeds a margin and its audit risk falls below a threshold; otherwise, it retains Source. We then update the VLA through behavior cloning using paired observations and actions from the retained real execution trajectories. We construct 32,000 pairs of real executions and imagined videos across four LIBERO suites~ liu2023libero , using real execution outcomes to supervise the reward model and auditor. Candidate pools are collected offline, with recorded executions providing labels, evaluation outcomes, and behavior cloning targets. Selection uses predicted scores and diagnostic information from imagined videos to accept a replacement or retain Source. At deployment, only the updated VLA is required. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25 , exceeding behavior cloning using only Source trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same number of training trajectories and behavior cloning budget. With the reward model and advantage margin held fixed, adding audit gating improves mean success by 1.47 percentage points. When the number of replacements is fixed, TIF still outperforms ranking by predicted advantage and selecting candidates by risk estimated through logistic regression. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose TIF, a supervision auditing method that learns from matched real executions when rewards predicted from imagined videos overestimate execution quality. TIF combines this risk with a candidate's predicted advantage to decide whether to accept a replacement or retain the existing supervision. We develop a multidimensional reward model for candidate ranking and risk auditing. The model jointly predicts five dimensions of execution quality and a utility score. Utility predictions rank candidates, while dimension predictions and their uncertainty provide information for auditing. We show that the auditor identifies discrepancies between high predicted rewards and poor execution outcomes. Comparisons with fixed replacement counts and downstream post-training experiments further show that using audit risk improves supervision selection and policy success. Related Work VLA Post-Training and World Models. OpenVLA-OFT improves supervised adaptation through changes to action decoding, representation, and learning objectives~ kim2025openvlaoft , while GRAPE aligns policies with preferences over successful and failed trajectories~ zhang2024grape . RIPT-VLA and VLA-RL use environment interaction for reinforcement learning, with sparse success rewards and process rewards, respectively~ tan2025riptvla,lu2025vlarl . WMPO reduces reliance on real environment interaction by optimizing policies through imagined rollouts from a video world model~ zhu2025wmpo . WoVR addresses accumulated prediction errors through keyframe initialization and joint updates of the policy and world model~ jiang2026wovr . WoVR+ extends this approach to multiple views, proprioceptive states, and training within individual stages of longer tasks~ zhou2026wovrplus . TIF uses imagined outcomes to evaluate fixed candidate actions and select real execution trajectories for behavior cloning. Robot Reward Models and Candidate Evaluation. Robometer learns rewards through progress supervision within trajectories and preference comparisons across trajectories~ liang2026robometer , while RoboReward augments supervision with negative and partial completion examples constructed through counterfactual relabeling and temporal clipping~ lee2026roboreward . RynnValue learns temporal distance to task completion and converts its predictions into dense rewards~ huang2026rynnvalue . During inference, V-GPS reranks actions using a value function learned through offline reinforcement learning~ nakamoto2024vgps , and RoVer uses process rewards to guide candidate expansion and selection~ dai2025rover . RARM gates progress rewards according to confidence in matching execution clips to a reference demonstration~ yang2026rarm . TIF uses matched simulator executions to supervise predictions of execution quality from imagined videos, providing a utility score for ranking and five dimension predictions for auditing. Reliability of Imagined Supervision. Recent methods use reliability estimates to control how imagined outcomes influence policy learning. WISE filters candidate groups using reward differences, ranking consistency, and reward variation across repeated imaginations, then updates the policy using relative advantages within each group~ zhang2026wise . HaWMPO learns video reliability from visual, geometric, and motion discrepancies against observed executions, together with image quality metrics, and adjusts reinforcement learning rewards through Reward-Soft~ chen2026hawmpo . MeRL uses visual prediction and reward proxy errors to regulate imagination length and data proportion, as well as sampling probabilities and training weights for individual chunks~ li2026merl . TIF learns the risk of reward overestimation from matched executions, targeting cases with high predicted utility, low executed utility, and a substantial gap between them. This risk and the predicted advantage over Source determine whether to accept the candidate with the highest predicted utility or retain the existing supervision. Method sec:method Overview. As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , TIF combines candidate utility prediction with reward risk auditing to select supervision trajectories for VLA post-training. We first train a multidimensional reward model using matched execution outcomes, then train an auditor on discrepancies between its predictions and those outcomes. During selection, the candidate with the highest predicted utility replaces Source only if its predicted advantage exceeds a margin and its audit risk falls below a threshold; otherwise, Source is retained. Observations and actions from all valid steps of the retained real execution trajectories are then used for behavior cloning. Candidate Actions and Paired Outcomes sec:paired_futures Given a visual observation , proprioceptive state , and task instruction at initial state , we construct a candidate action set . Each sequence contains at most eight control commands executed at 20 Hz. The component dataset contains four controlled candidates per initial state, providing varied execution quality for training and evaluation. The natural pool used for supervision selection contains five candidates: Source, one greedy branch, and three sampled branches. Source is a fixed action proposal associated with the initial state, taken from subsequent actions in a LIBERO demonstration or from saved policy action records. Sequences are extended when necessary according to the rules described in Appendix~ app:source . We execute Source in its associated scene and initial state. The remaining branches use the OpenVLA policy for the corresponding suite to generate actions step by step from the current execution observation, using greedy decoding or sampling. For every branch, we record observations, actions, and execution feedback until the sequence reaches its prescribed length or the environment terminates. We collect candidates offline and keep their actions and execution records fixed when comparing selection rules. The world model generates an imagined video from the initial observation and recorded action sequence, with an adapter converting initial proprioception into the required conditioning. For candidates that terminate early, we use only the valid executed action prefix. The matched execution trajectory provides training labels, outcomes for evaluating selection decisions, and paired observations and actions for behavior cloning. Selection uses predicted scores and diagnostic information from imagined videos. Reward Supervision from Execution

title: Caging Vision-Language Navigation for Legged Robots via Barrier-Certified Safety Architecture
summary: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.

Email: \ amkulk, saimouli, yuzedu, ghuang\ @udel.edu . Zijun Sha is with the Frontier Research Center, Toyota Motor Corporation, Tokyo, Japan. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bézier-parameterized MPPI planner with constraints. The proposed Legged- system is modular, making it compatible with various / models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities. Introduction Legged robots, including humanoids and quadrupeds, are being engineered to work hand-in-hand with humans and perform practical, real-world tasks with precision and purpose (e.g. unitree2025a2_video ). A fundamental prerequisite for accomplishing such tasks is the ability to navigate safely to locations where subsequent actions can be performed. Traditionally, navigation missions are specified as sequences of goal poses through a navigation interface, which typically requires either a trained operator or an expert-authored behavior tree Macenski2020IROS . Recent advances in / ~ Sapkota2025 have enabled , allowing users to specify navigation missions through intuitive natural-language instructions rather than manually defined waypoints. However, to deploy these robots alongside humans, it is imperative that systems are demonstrably safe—generating motion that are both semantically correct and collision free. This work directly addresses this critical challenge of ensuring physical safety in Legged- . The core issue is that while pretrained models offer powerful visual-semantic reasoning, their navigation outputs~ Cheng2025,Bu2025,Chen2025 typically ignore the robot's kinematics, local obstacle configurations, and formal safety constraints. Consequently, an end-to-end planner might propose an instruction-following navigation commands that are physically unexecutable or prone to collisions. Therefore, rather than executing these outputs directly, they must be treated as high-level navigation proposals that are physically grounded and verified. We refer to this verification process as caging: the interposition of a safety-assured physical-grounding layer between the / planner and the robot's locomotion controller, preserving the reasoning capabilities of pretrained models while providing provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions. To this end, we propose a dual-layer caging architecture for Legged- that integrates high-level semantic reasoning with low-level, safety-assured motion planning. We evaluate the complete framework in real-world indoor and outdoor environments using a Unitree G1 humanoid and a Ghost Robotics Vision 60 quadruped. Specifically, the main contributions of this work are: A dual-layer caging architecture that decouples semantic reasoning from physical execution by treating pretrained / outputs as high-level proposals and mapping them to locally feasible goal poses with open-vocabulary terminal alignment. A safety-assured motion planner utilizing an efficient, low-dimensional Bézier-parameterized formulation with -based constraints, providing provable collision-avoidance guarantees under stated assumptions. Extensive real-world validation on both humanoid and quadrupedal platforms, demonstrating cross-platform applicability and reliable, safe execution of natural-language navigation instructions. Related Work -language navigation for legged robots. VLN was formalized by the Room-to-Room benchmark~ Anderson2018 and later extended from discrete navigation graphs to continuous environments through R2R-CE~ Krantz2020 . Recent directly map visual and language observations to robot actions. Of particular relevance, QUAR-VLA targets quadruped control~ Ding2024 , while NaVILA performs language-conditioned navigation on legged robots~ Cheng2025 . These models provide strong semantic action proposals, but their learned outputs do not explicitly encode the robot footprint, the current local obstacle geometry, or a formal closed-loop safety condition. Recent safety-aware VLA methods address this gap either by aligning the policy through constrained learning, as in SafeVLA~ Zhang2025SafeVLA , or by correcting manipulation actions with a plug-and-play layer, as in VLSA/AEGIS~ Hu2025VLSA . Our work instead targets legged navigation: it leaves the semantic model unchanged and cages its proposals using online geometric perception and horizon-level motion certification. This separation allows the front end and robot platform to change without transferring responsibility for navigation safety to the learned model. and geometric grounding. Methods such as 3D-LLM~ Hong2023b and Chat-Scene~ Huang2024c enrich language models with 3D scene structure for spatial reasoning. Open-vocabulary detection and segmentation models, including Grounding-DINO~ Liu2023_arxiv and SAM2~ Ravi2024_arxiv , additionally enable language-specified objects to be localized without a fixed task vocabulary. Splat-Nav~ Chen2025TRO more tightly couples these domains by using a language-embedded Gaussian-splat map to specify goals, construct safe polytope corridors, and generate B\' e zier trajectories. Our architecture instead uses the learned front end and open-vocabulary perception to generate semantic goals and refine terminal alignment, while an incrementally updated environmental grounds every proposed motion in locally observed free space. Safety is therefore evaluated from geometric clearance rather than semantic confidence. in sampling-based predictive control. For legged robots, sequential MPC over convex safe corridors enables reactive bipedal planning in cluttered environments~ Narkhede2022RAL . supports derivative-free trajectory optimization with nonlinear and nonsmooth costs~ Williams2018_TRO ; low-dimensional trajectory parameterizations further improve sampling efficiency in cluttered environments~ Kulkarni2026ICRA . Discrete-time barrier conditions provide a route to forward-invariant safety~ Agrawal2017RSS,Zeng2021ACC , and recent sampling-based controllers incorporate barrier functions through shielded refinement~ Yin2023_arxiv , barrier-rate guidance with learned ~ Parwana2025_arxiv , or discrete barrier states~ Wang2025_arxiv . In contrast, our physical-grounding layer combines B\' e zier-parameterized MPPI, value-only queries to an incrementally updated environmental SDF, soft dEBF-guided sampling, and hard rollout certification with a safe backup. This construction cages interchangeable VLM/VLA proposals and is deployed unchanged at the planning level on both quadrupedal and humanoid platforms. System Overview sec:problem We address the problem of language-driven, safety-critical navigation for legged robots operating in cluttered, unknown environments. That is, given (i) a natural-language instruction describing a high-level task and optionally a target object, (ii) onboard sensing (e.g., vision, LiDAR, IMU, leg kinematics), and (iii) platform actuation limits, the objective is to synthesize a control sequence that steers the robot from an initial pose to a a goal region or an object-relative pose while being caged to safely execute the commands. Formally, the robot must: (i) ground the language into a sequence of high-level, spatially referenced subgoals; (ii) convert these into feasible, collision-free subgoals; and (iii) ensure safety at all times. The solution should be modular (compatible with different legged platforms and / models), and real-time capable. Success is achieved when the robot reaches the goal region or establishes a valid object-relative pose (for open-vocabulary targets), without violating safety constraints throughout the trajectory. Robot Dynamics and Environment Models We represent the robot pose in 2D as , where is the global position and the yaw. The control is the body-frame twist with sampling time , and we adopt a constant-velocity, discrete-time dynamic model: This planar body-twist model is suitable for motion planning for both the humanoid and quadrupedal robots. The local environment is encoded by a . For any point , returns the minimum Euclidean distance to the nearest obstacle surface; indicates free space, lies on an obstacle boundary, and is inside an obstacle. The Proposed Caging Framework Our framework employs a hierarchical control architecture that translates high-level semantic instructions into safety-assured motion (see Fig.~ fig:system_pipeline ). The upper layer converts visual and language inputs into spatial navigation goals. The lower layer converts these goals into feasible control commands while enforcing safety constraints. This separation allows the semantic planner and the robot platform to be changed independently, while preserving a common safety-assured execution layer. Semantic Grounding Layer This layer converts visual observations and natural-language instructions into a sequence of high-level navigation actions. A processes the user's command together with the current scene and predicts discrete actions, such as turning left or right in increments up to , or moving forward in \,cm increments up to \,cm. The Kinematic Goal Projector maps each action to a planar goal pose in the local map and verifies that the resulting waypoint is reachable and collision-free. title: HiLo-WAM: Decoupling Long-Horizon Task Evolution and Local Dynamics in World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) improve robotic manipulation by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Extending prediction horizons increases uncertainty and computation while entangling task-level evolution with fine-grained local dynamics, obscuring their dependencies and distinct roles in action generation. We propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples long-horizon task evolution from local visual dynamics while jointly modeling their interaction with robot actions. A sparse long-horizon visual stream captures historical task context and future evolution, while a dense local dynamics visual stream models short-horizon robot-object interactions. The two streams operate at different temporal scales within a unified dual-DiT architecture and guide actions through structured cross-stream attention. Progressive inference further reduces unnecessary computation through stream-wise partial denoising, joint denoising, and dynamic skipping. Experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance: HiLo-WAM achieves a 93.70% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 17.43 progress score on RoboDojo long-horizon tasks, with robust in-domain and OOD performance on the Fourier GR-3 robot. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a 2.93x speedup while improving performance.

However, most existing WAMs model dense short-horizon visual dynamics, capturing local interactions but providing limited long-range task context. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of long-horizon task evolution and local interaction dynamics, while temporal-scale analyses highlight the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a speedup while improving performance. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation through large-scale pretraining and diverse robot demonstrations ~ pmlr-v305-black25a,black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, kim2025fine,intelligence2026pi07steerablegeneralistrobotic . World Action Models (WAMs) further introduce predictive visual dynamics into action generation, either by conditioning actions on future visual states ~ li2026causal,hu2024video,du2023learning or by jointly modeling future visual representations and actions~ yuan2026fast, li2025unifiedvideoactionmodel,ma2026dit4dit,ye2026world . Most existing WAMs, however, focus on dense visual dynamics over relatively short temporal windows, which effectively capture fine-grained robot--object interactions but provide limited information about how a task evolves over a longer horizon. Long-horizon manipulation additionally requires understanding historical task progress and future evolution beyond the current interaction window~ cai2026aha,hu2026bagelvla,torne2026memmultiscaleembodiedmemory,yang2026memorywam . To incorporate such long-range task information, recent WAMs extend the temporal scope of visual modeling through longer observation histories~ li2026causal,ye2026world , persistent memory~ yang2026memorywam , extended future prediction~ xu2026forcingcausalworldmodeling , or long-horizon visual planning~ cai2026aha . These approaches provide richer temporal context by exposing the policy to task progress and future dynamics over a broader time span. Extending the temporal horizon of visual world modeling introduces a fundamental challenge: a single visual trajectory must capture both slowly evolving task-level progression and fine-grained local interaction dynamics. This not only increases prediction uncertainty and redundant computation~ agibotresearchteam2026geact20pretrainingscaling,cai2026aha,zhou2025act2goalworldmodelgeneral , but, more importantly, obscures the dependencies between different temporal dynamics and their distinct roles in action generation. This raises a key question: how can a World Action Model explicitly model different temporal dynamics and their dependencies on action generation? To address this problem, we propose HiLo-WAM, which decouples the two temporal roles of visual world modeling into complementary long-horizon and local dynamics streams while jointly learning their interaction with robot actions. As shown in Fig.~ fig:motivation , We adopt a multi-scale temporal modeling strategy to represent the two streams at different temporal resolutions. Specifically, the long-horizon visual stream sparsely models historical task context and coarse future task evolution, capturing how the task has progressed and where it is heading, while the local visual dynamics stream densely models short-horizon robot--object interactions required for precise control. Both streams are processed by a shared Video DiT and interact with an Action DiT through structured cross-stream attention, allowing long-horizon task information and local dynamics to jointly support action generation. This temporal decomposition further enables progressive stream-wise inference, where visual streams terminate and are cached at different stages to reduce unnecessary world-model computation. We evaluate HiLo-WAM in simulation and real-robot tasks. HiLo-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin and strong performance on challenging long-horizon manipulation tasks~ chen2026robodojounifiedsimandrealbenchmark . Controlled ablations and attention analyses show that long-horizon stream with historical context, future evolution, and dense local visual dynamics provide complementary information for action generation. Temporal-scale analyses further demonstrate that long-horizon world modeling benefits from an appropriate temporal scale that balances temporal coverage and resolution. Progressive inference further achieves a speedup while improving performance. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We propose HiLo-WAM, a World Action Model that decouples visual world modeling into complementary long-horizon and local dynamics processes, and jointly exploits both for robot action generation. We introduce a multi-scale temporal modeling strategy with structured cross-stream interaction and progressive stream-wise inference, enabling effective coordination across temporal scales while reducing unnecessary world-model computation. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate strong long-horizon manipulation performance, with ablations and further analyses validate the benefit of complementary temporal information, the importance of balancing temporal coverage and resolution, and the efficiency of progressive inference. Related Works sec:related Video Models and World Action Models. Recent advances in video generation have enabled visual prediction to serve as a powerful dynamics prior for robot learning~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,Wang_2026_CVPR,hu2024video . Prior works use video models to generate future observations for planning and control~ hu2024video,du2023learning,li2026causal , or jointly model future visual states and robot actions within a unified World Action Model (WAM)~ yuan2026fast,li2025unifiedvideoactionmodel, ma2026dit4dit,ye2026world . While early WAMs mainly focus on short-horizon interaction dynamics, recent approaches incorporate longer context, persistent memory, or long-range future prediction and visual planning~ ye2026world,yang2026memorywam,cai2026aha,zhou2025act2goalworldmodelgeneral,agibotresearchteam2026geact20pretrainingscaling to support more complex long-horizon manipulation. HiLo-WAM instead decouples long-horizon manipulation into two complementary visual streams: a long-horizon stream for long-horizon task evolution and a local stream for fine-grained interaction dynamics. Hierarchical Policies for Long-Horizon Manipulation. A parallel line of work addresses long-horizon manipulation through hierarchical or temporally abstract policies. These methods typically use high-level language plans, subgoals, visual goals, or intermediate states to capture task-level structure, and condition a downstream policy on these representations to generate fine-grained actions~ shi2025hi,li2025hamster,long2026scaling,pmlr-v305-black25a, yang2026hivla,intelligence2026pi07steerablegeneralistrobotic, 11093669,hu2026bagelvla . HiLo-WAM shares the motivation of combining long-range reasoning with precise local control, but approaches it through visual world modeling rather than a separate planner--policy hierarchy. It decouples the visual dynamics of a unified WAM into long-horizon and local streams and jointly learns their interaction with robot actions. Method sec:method Overview. We introduce HiLo-WAM, a World Action Model that decouples visual world modeling into two complementary visual streams: a long-horizon visual stream which sparsely models historical task context and coarse future evolution for task-level evolution and a dense local visual dynamics stream for fine-grained interaction dynamics. HiLo-WAM adopts a multi-scale temporal modeling strategy, representing the two visual streams at different temporal scales. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:framework , the model follows a dual-DiT architecture consisting of a Video DiT for visual world modeling and an Action DiT for action stream generation. Both visual streams are jointly modeled by the shared Video DiT and interact with action stream through structured cross-stream attention, allowing long-horizon task evolution and local dynamics to jointly guide action prediction. During inference, all streams are progressively denoised: the long-horizon visual stream terminates and is cached first, followed by the local visual stream, while the action stream is refined to completion. title: Nested Field-of-View Barriers for Teleoperated Multi-Robot Relay Chains
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Submitted to the American Control Conference (ACC)
summary: Teleoperation of mobile robots in communication-denied environments requires maintaining a communication link while allowing the operator to maneuver freely. We propose a shared-autonomy framework in which a teleoperated leader is followed by a chain of autonomous robots that relays a line of sight to a fixed base station, a geometric proxy for the link. Connectivity is enforced geometrically through visibility-based Control Barrier Functions (CBFs), with each agent computing its control input locally through a quadratic program. A strict visibility constraint guarantees connectivity, but a follower with no independent motion objective remains stationary, stalling the leader at the boundary of the safe set. Relaxing it preserves mobility at the cost of the guarantee. Our framework resolves this conflict through nested hard-soft visibility constraints: a full field-of-view (FoV) constraint enforced strictly to guarantee connectivity and a contracted FoV constraint imposed on each follower as a relaxed behavioral objective that drives it inward before the connectivity boundary is reached. We prove feasibility of the local quadratic programs and forward invariance of the connected, collision-free set under the resulting distributed controller. The contraction parameter shapes follower behavior without affecting the guarantee, which follows from the strict constraint alone. The framework is evaluated in confined and cluttered environments on two simulated systems: a kinematic integrator and software-in-the-loop Crazyflie quadrotors. Compared with a baseline tuned to reach the goal in comparable time, the framework keeps the links far closer to the connected set and moves the followers less.

Compared with a baseline tuned to reach the goal in comparable time, the framework keeps the links far closer to the connected set and moves the followers less. Introduction sec:introduction Shared-autonomy teleoperation blends the intent of a human operator with the reactive safety of onboard autonomy li2023the , but it works only for as long as the communication link holds. In cluttered or subterranean workspaces, non-line-of-sight propagation and severe attenuation rappaport1996wireless, cid2024wireless separate the operator from the robot through delay and dropout khasawneh2019human, gulecyuz2025enhancing long before its endurance is spent. We propose a framework in which the robots themselves become the infrastructure. A leader is teleoperated, while a chain of autonomous followers positions itself so that line-of-sight (LoS) is relayed from the leader back to a fixed base station (Fig.~ fig:chain ). Connectivity is treated geometrically, and LoS is seen as a proxy for the link rather than a model of it. Each follower keeps its predecessor inside a field of view (FoV) that is bounded in range, limited in aperture, and cut by the obstacles within it; the shaded wedge of Fig.~ fig:chain is the part of a FoV that an obstacle denies. In the DARPA Subterranean Challenge, leading teams extended their range by dropping static radio relays as they advanced ohradzansky2022multi, tranzatto2022team, kottege2025heterogeneous . Such nodes are simple and effective, but committed irrevocably at drop time and left behind; we evolve from that solution by keeping the relays mobile. Other works deploy mobile robots as relays using signal-strength heuristics Laclau2021 or alternate between exploration and chain modes Tian2025 , while network-aware teleoperation adapts to link quality but presumes that an infrastructure is already in place chen2024network . We instead make connectivity a deterministic geometric constraint, imposed by Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) ames2019control, ames2017control , which have been applied to connectivity maintenance lee2025maintaining, ong2023nonsmooth, bhatia2024decentralized, capelli2020connectivity and LoS preservation pan2025robusttrajectorygenerationcontrol, BaiICRA2025 . Our visibility constraint is adapted from the FoV barriers developed for pursuit-evasion under occlusion koga2023hide, zhou2025control , whose scope differs decisively from ours. There, keeping the target in view is the pursuer's own objective, and the barrier certifies a motion that the nominal controller already produces. Here, visibility is a supporting requirement, not an objective. Followers carry no reference of their own and move only when a constraint compels them. That absence of a reference is what makes the constraint hard to use. The hard barrier is minimally invasive by construction, reacting only once the FoV boundary is met. The team therefore rides that boundary. The leader is braked at the limit, each follower advances no further than it is forced to, and the chain stalls at the border of the safe set. Slack variables restore mobility but surrender the guarantees. Inspired by the approach in roncero2025multi , we combine two nested CBFs on each neighboring pair. The full FoV is enforced strictly on both agents so that the connected set stays forward invariant. A contracted copy of it, set in from the range limit and from the aperture edges by a margin and drawn dashed in Fig.~ fig:chain , is imposed on the follower alone as a relaxed constraint. It supplies the drive the follower lacks and pulls it inward before the strict boundary is reached, yielding whenever the environment makes that unattainable. We nonetheless keep that minimal invasiveness. Giving the followers a reference of their own would resolve the stall by turning the framework into a formation controller, committing each relay to a shape fixed in advance; here a relay with no objective is moved by the relaxed constraint alone, while one carrying a task of its own has that task filtered rather than replaced. We contribute (i) a nested hard-soft formulation that separates the connectivity guarantee from the behavior that sustains the chain, (ii) a distributed synthesis with proofs of feasibility and forward invariance of the connected, collision-free set, and (iii) an evaluation on two simulated systems and two workspaces that traces the residual violations to tracking error and to field-of-view resolution. title: CRONOS: Benchmarking Non-Episodic Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce CRONOS, a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. CRONOS leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using CRONOS, we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. full_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) is promising for adapting robot policies to unstructured real-world environments. However, standard RL pipelines rely on episodic training with frequent scene resets, which is impractical for real-world deployment due to the need for substantial human intervention. While prior work has studied non-episodic RL in relatively small policies trained from scratch, its behavior when fine-tuning modern large-scale pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce , a simulation benchmark for RL fine-tuning of VLAs under non-episodic scene resets. leverages high-fidelity physics simulators and adopts shared-scene multi-task settings. Using , we show that naively fine-tuning pre-trained policies fails in non-episodic settings due to shifts in object configurations and end-effector poses; however, these challenges can be mitigated through targeted reset allocation and by addressing biases in pre-trained models. Moreover, we find that non-episodic training enhances long-horizon manipulation and improves generalization to previously unseen object configurations and task sequences. Introduction introduction Learning to adapt is key to deploying robots in continually changing worlds. Recently, behavior cloning has emerged as a dominant learning approach in robotic manipulation. It trains state-of-the-art visuomotor policies, often termed vision-language-action models (VLAs; ), on large-scale expert demonstrations~ o2024open,bu2025agibot , enabling robots to perform complex manipulation tasks~ black2024pi0,zheng2026x . However, VLAs are not robust to unseen conditions during training: even a slight change in lighting, object appearance or scene layout can cause a VLA's failure~ barreiros2025behavior . Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a compelling solution. RL adapts policies by trial and error, eliminating the persistent need for collecting demonstrations to cover new failures. Recent studies show that RL fine-tuning substantially improves a VLA's generalization and robustness to novel scenarios~ intelligence2025pi,zhang2026hy . Despite its generality, standard RL pipelines rely on an unrealistic assumption of episodic training---scenes are frequently reset at each episode to prevent robots from being trapped in low-reward states during training, to enhance RL's training efficiency. Because scene reset is free in simulation, this has been widely overlooked in prior work that studies RL fine-tuning in simulation~ liu2025can,yu2026rlinf . In contrast, in real-world settings, scene reset requires human intervention and incurs substantial overhead. This has prevented RL from being deployed at scale in real robotic systems. To address the limitation, a wide range of non-episodic RL algorithms have been proposed, including manually scripting the reset robot policy~ levine2016end,sharma2020emergent , instrumenting the reset mechanism~ zeng2020tossingbot,kalashnikov2018scalable,mtopt2021arxiv , or tackling scene resets through a multi-task learning framework that either treats scene resets as additional tasks~ eysenbach2018leave,zhu2020ingredients , or decomposes a task into a set of subtasks, allowing the execution of each to reset the others~ gupta2021reset . However, these approaches are proposed prior to the surge of VLAs, and confined to simpler settings of training policies from scratch. We present an initial study to highlight challenges in RL fine-tuning VLAs under non-episodic scene reset, despite the prior success of episodic training. We answer three questions: (1) how does RL fine-tuning VLAs perform out of the box, under non-episodic, multi-task settings? (2) what are the key factors impacting the performance? (3) what are the advantages of non-episodic training, aside from reducing the labor cost? Experiments are primarily conducted in simulation benchmarks, as they are less time-consuming and offer better reproducibility than real-world benchmarks. We introduce ( ), a simulation benchmark carefully designed to facilitate systematic study on non-episodic scene reset RL. consists of a suite of 16 pick-and-place tasks, evenly distributed across 4 scenes. It addresses multiple limitations of existing benchmarks. First, targets recent advances in VLAs. It evaluates non-episodic RL fine-tuning of these pre-trained policies, rather than policies trained from scratch~ gupta2021reset . Second, adopts a realistic multi-task learning setup by sharing scenes across tasks, in contrast to prior benchmarks that isolate each task into a separate scene~ yang2024robot . This compounds manipulation errors not only over the horizon, but also across tasks, as in real-world deployment where a robot keeps working in the same environment. Third, builds upon a high-fidelity physics simulator, Maniskill~ tao2025maniskill3 , and its extension of manipulation tasks suites~ li2024evaluating,liu2025can . In contrast, existing benchmarks rely on outdated simulators~ balsells2023autonomous with simplified physics and limited visual realism. Both our multi-task learning setup and usage of modern simulators make non-episodic scene reset RL more challenging. We present an overview comparison between common multi-task episodic RL and our shared-scene multi-task non-episodic scene reset RL in Figure~ fig:teaser . We test two off-the-shelf VLAs: OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla and SpatialVLA~ qu2025spatialvla , on . We arrive at following findings: (1) Non-episodic RL fine-tuning for pre-trained VLAs is ineffective. We show that distribution drifts in initial scene layout and initial robot configurations make non-episodic training inefficient, (2) Targeted resets improves non-episodic training. We found that resetting strategies, that handle the distribution drifts, can improve non-episodic RL's efficiency, while others show no benefit. (3) Non-episodic training brings stronger out-of-domain generalization. While difficult to train, we found that policies fine-tuned with non-episodic RL are more robust to novel object configurations and long-horizon robotic manipulation, than their episodically fine-tuned counterparts. Preliminaries sec:preliminary In this section, we present a general formulation of multi-task RL problems, and extend it to non-episodic scene reset multi-task RL (NSR-MTRL) problems without loss of generality. Multi-task RL. Multi-task RL problems consider learning optimal policies for a set of tasks sampled from a task distribution . A task defines a Markov decision process (MDP) , where is the state space, is the action space, denotes the transition dynamics of the environment, is the reward function of the task, is the initial state distribution, and denotes the discount factor. Given policy conditioning on task , the RL objective is to maximize the expected return for every task: Non-episodic Scene Reset Multi-Task RL (NSR-MTRL). We extend this formulation to non-episodic scene reset settings. Evaluation remains episodic, with trajectories rolled out from the initial state for each task; whereas, training trajectories are rolled out continually across tasks with no or only occasional scene resets~ sharma2022autonomous . title: EndoS3:Endoscopic Semantic Splatting SLAM
summary: Purpose: Despite advances in 3D surgical scene understanding, semantic simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM) remains under-explored for two key reasons. First, it requires solving three challenging tasks in parallel: camera pose tracking, high-fidelity deformable reconstruction, and semantic mapping, making progress particularly demanding. Second, the scarcity of datasets providing the necessary ground truth to evaluate all three tasks comprehensively under conditions that closely reflect real surgical procedures environments. Method: We propose EndoS3, a Gaussian Splatting-based semantic SLAM framework that uses instance masks to guide all three tasks. An instance-level motion decomposition module separates static and dynamic instances by evaluating residual flow after compensating for camera motion, accounting for flow noise and comparing motion across neighbouring instances. The camera is tracked against the static Gaussians, while an instance-aware warp field gives each dynamic instance its own control nodes and deformation network. A semantic node allocation module redistributes a fixed node budget across instances according to their size and non-rigidity. We also introduce CRCD++, an ex-vivo Cholecystectomy dataset with RGB-D frames, camera pose and instance annotations for full semantic SLAM evaluation. Results: EndoS3 surpasses all state-of-the-art general-purpose and surgical semantic SLAM methods in tracking, reconstruction and semantic mapping on the CRCD++ and SemSup datasets. Conclusion: Semantic-aware motion and deformation modelling is vital to surgical semantic SLAM. EndoS3 and CRCD++ offer a method and benchmark for improved geometric and semantic understanding in endoscopy.
full_text: , , , , Introduction Spatial understanding of the endoscopic field supports surgical navigation and context-aware decision-making~ lin2023semantic,acar2026perseus . Reaching it requires complementary geometric and semantic information: geometry describes the spatial relationships between the camera, anatomy, and instruments, while semantics identifies them and analyses their interactions. Surgical semantic simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM) achieves this understanding through jointly performing camera pose tracking, scene reconstruction, and semantic mapping, though it suffers from several key challenges. First, image motion is inherently ambiguous: pixel displacements may arise from camera motion, tissue deformation, or independently moving instruments~ hayoz2023robust . Misattributing scene motion to the camera corrupts pose estimates, while the opposite degrades the reconstruction. Previous approaches use geometric cues to decompose the sources of motion and limit the influence of tissue deformation on camera pose estimation~ hayoz2023robust , yet the role of instance-level semantics in motion decomposition remains under-explored, even though it can provide valuable information by associating pixels with entities that exhibit distinct motion characteristics. Second, surgical scenes exhibit heterogeneous, time-varying deformations: Rigid instruments move quickly and independently of the tissue they manipulate, while organs deform slowly and largely coherently. Deformation models must capture these differences and adapt to the content currently in view. Current approaches, however, model the motion of the entire scene with a single warp field, driven by a shared set of control nodes~ huang2024sc,hayoz2024online,li20254d , which can blend instrument and tissue motion near their contact points. Third, a fixed set of control nodes~ li20254d also limit adaptation to instruments entering or leaving the view and regions of greater tissue deformation. Existing methods primarily use semantics for map labelling and data association~ shan2024dds,zhu2024sni,li2024sgs,zhu2025semgauss , while their use in motion decomposition and deformation modelling remains unexplored. Moreover, progress is further limited by the scarcity of evaluation data. Existing datasets lack joint ground truth for camera poses, depth, and segmentation~ lin2023semantic,hayoz2023robust . These annotations are needed to evaluate tracking, reconstruction, and semantic mapping jointly and determine how improvements in one task affect the others. We propose EndoS , a semantic SLAM framework that uses instance semantics to guide motion decomposition for camera tracking and deformable semantic mapping. We also present CRCD++, a cholecystectomy dataset with camera poses, depth, and instance annotations for a complete evaluation of semantic SLAM methods. Our code and data are at: . Our main contributions are: Instance-level motion decomposition, which separates static and dynamic instances by investigating camera-compensated flow residuals, their signal-to-noise ratios, and motion differences across instance boundaries. Instance-aware warp field, which assigns every instance its own control nodes and deformation network and restricts motion propagation to within that instance. Semantic node allocation, which redistributes a fixed node budget across instances at every frame according to their size and non-rigidity. CRCD++, an ex-vivo Cholecystectomy dataset with all of the necessary ground truth needed to perform an in-depth evaluation of surgical semantic SLAM methods. Related Work General-purpose semantic SLAM: Dense semantic SLAM builds the map using implicit fields or explicit primitives. SNI-SLAM~ zhu2024sni fuses appearance, geometry and semantic features in a neural implicit map through cross-attention; SGS-SLAM~ li2024sgs jointly optimises the appearance, geometric and semantic features of a Gaussian map and uses semantics to select keyframes; and SemGauss-SLAM~ zhu2025semgauss embeds semantic features in the Gaussians and enforces consistency through semantic-informed bundle adjustment. All three regularise a static map and are evaluated on indoor scenes~ straub2019replica . None model deformation or dynamics, so in scenes that feature either, they cannot disentangle scene from camera motion, typically using the latter to explain the former. Surgical semantic SLAM: Among sparse methods, Semantic-SuPer~ lin2023semantic builds a surfel map with a sparse embedded deformation graph and uses semantic masks within tissue tracking to pull surfels into their semantic region, but assumes a stationary camera. PERSEUS~ acar2026perseus combines learned segmentation and monocular depth with a learning-based SLAM backend to label a point cloud. It neither produces high-fidelity renderings nor models deformation, and is evaluated only on static sequences. Among dense methods, DDS-SLAM~ shan2024dds models deformation as a hash-grid canonical scene with a time-dependent neural field and uses a semantic distance loss. Deformation is supervised only through rendering, and tracking does not separate static from moving regions, leaving camera and tissue motion entangled. It is evaluated on deforming scenes~ hayoz2023robust,lin2023semantic and outputs no semantic map; as they are used in its optimisation solely. None of these methods use semantics to disentangle scene motion from camera motion. EndoS uses a Gaussian Splatting framework where instance semantics guides motion decomposition: the camera is tracked against the static instances only, separating camera from scene motion, while an instance-aware warp field models moving organs and instruments individually and allows each to deform independently. Surgical benchmarks: Semantic SLAM evaluation requires RGB images, depth, camera poses, and segmentation annotations. Existing datasets~ hong2020cholecseg8k,allan2020endovis18,mascagni2025endoscapes offer sparse segmentations or lack poses. StereoMIS~ hayoz2023robust and D4D~ docea2026dresden provide poses but segment only tools; D4D also provides measured depth. eCRCD~ oh2025expanded annotates two tissue classes but lacks tool masks and propagates labels from one frame per clip. CRCD++ alone meets all four requirements. Unlike the general abdominal scenes in StereoMIS and D4D, CRCD++ provides clinically meaningful organ annotations specific to Cholecystectomy (Table~ tab:surgical_datasets ). Methods As shown in Fig.~ fig:main , given an RGB-D sequence and per-frame instance segmentation masks , EndoS adopts a 3D semantic Gaussian Splatting scene representation~ zhu2025semgauss . Our Instance-level motion decomposition module, separates the Gaussians into (semi-) static and dynamic. Tracking is then performed on the static part of the scene, while mapping utilises our Instance-aware warp field module to model deformations in the scene. This module operates on a fixed set of control nodes, distributed between instance regions using our Semantic node allocation module, and propagates the estimated deformation to all dynamic Gaussians in an instance region. To obtain robust region-level evidence, the residuals are aggregated in SLIC superpixels split along the instance boundaries, so that each superpixel lies within a single instance. Each is summarised by its median residual and its median forward--backward flow error , which estimates the local flow uncertainty. An instance , covered by the superpixels , is then tested with two complementary statistics: measures residual motion relative to flow noise, while measures motion differences across the boundary with neighbouring instance . For boundary superpixels , we define the median residual, robust scale estimate, and superpixel count: The same quantities are computed on the neighbouring side.
