title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
summary: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

Introduction sec:introduction Learning vision-language-action (VLA) models requires demonstrations that connect language goals, visual observations, and executable actions~ pi06,li2026groundingvln,Mao_2026_CVPR,li2026hsgm . Collecting such data at scale in the physical world is costly, requiring robotic hardware, human supervision, and repeated environment setup~ khazatsky2024droid . Video games offer a practical setting for collecting large-scale interaction data: human players can perform diverse tasks in rich virtual environments, while visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions can be recorded together~ sima2024scaling . Paired with language annotations, these trajectories support learning to translate task instructions into actions grounded in visual observations. In particular, 3D games demand close coordination between high-level decision-making and low-level control, requiring agents to navigate, scout, engage opponents, and interact with the environment through rapid and precise keyboard-and-mouse actions. Under partial observability and continuously changing conditions, agents must continually adapt their decisions and actions to environmental feedback. Tasks in 3D games often require agents to combine multiple skills across successive stages. For example, an agent asked to approach the building, scout the entrance, engage the enemy, and fall back to cover to recover may fight effectively yet continue chasing an opponent when it should retreat. Successful task completion therefore requires agents to understand how each skill serves the current subgoal and to select, compose, and switch skills as the task progresses. This motivates two complementary data requirements. First, hierarchical annotations linking tasks, subgoals, and skill-level instructions: demonstrations should connect overall objectives to local goals and concrete instructions, making explicit what to achieve and how to act, with temporal boundaries indicating subgoal transitions. Second, large-scale action data covering diverse goals and tasks: extensive keyboard-and-mouse trajectories should span varied scenarios and skill combinations, capturing how navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery are executed and composed for different objectives. Together, these properties support learning both task structure and the behaviors needed to realize it. Existing game-interaction datasets exhibit limitations in both behavioral coverage and supervision for task structure. EgoCS-400K~ guo2026egocs provides detailed replay-grounded actions and multi-granularity captions, but remains confined to Counter-Strike and primarily describes local clips and action chains. Open-P2P~ yue2026scaling broadens game coverage, yet its sparse, goal-oriented instructions provide limited supervision for connecting fine-grained skill execution with intermediate and overall objectives. GameHorizon~ wang2026gamehorizon introduces multi-horizon instructions aligned with action recordings, but constructs its instruction hierarchy under predefined duration ranges for operations, goals, and strategies. These constraints may split a sustained subgoal or combine several brief subgoals, making temporal hierarchy an imperfect proxy for task-stage structure. These limitations motivate demonstrations with broader behavioral coverage and explicit, objective-driven stage annotations, linking each task to its constituent skills and marking when execution transitions between subgoals. To bridge this gap, we introduce AceAction-5M, a dataset that unifies multi-game tasks, fine-grained hierarchical instructions, and temporally aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories. Each episode pairs a global task description with temporally bounded stage-level subgoals, and aligns local action instructions frame by frame with the keyboard-and-mouse actions that realize them. The resulting trajectories capture how navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery are composed and switched, providing a data foundation for learning to map complex task instructions to continuous, fine-grained control. Our contributions are as follows: A hierarchically annotated, multi-game action dataset. AceAction covers 42 games and 5,027.87 hours of play, with 5,476,222 episodes in which task descriptions, stage-level subgoals, and local action instructions are jointly aligned with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse trajectories. An annotation scheme that makes stage structure explicit. We define 43 skill categories spanning navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, and mark the start and end of every stage, turning when to switch from an implicit property of the data into an explicit, learnable signal. Related Work Game Data and Benchmarks for World Modeling Gameplay data supports action-conditioned world modeling by aligning visual observations, actions, and environment states. GameNGen~ valevski2024diffusionmodelsrealtimegame learns video prediction from DOOM trajectories collected by a reinforcement learning agent, while DIAMOND~ alonso2024diffusionworldmodelingvisual demonstrates interactive world modeling using recorded CS:GO gameplay. WildWorld~ li2026wildworld provides frame-level annotations of skeletons, camera poses, and depth for evaluating action following and state consistency. EgoCS-400K~ guo2026egocs synchronizes player states, actions, and events extracted from CS:GO/CS2 replays with over 10,000 hours of first-person video. Its multi-granularity captions and video generation prompts link visual changes to replay information, providing language supervision for world modeling. GameVerse~ he2026gameverse provides minute-scale gameplay videos with temporally coherent camera trajectories and event-aligned structured captions, supporting long-horizon interactive world modeling. GameHorizon~ wang2026gamehorizon combines 5,000 hours of gameplay from 21 games with synchronized keyboard-and-mouse actions and three levels of instructions: operations, goals, and strategies. Its offline benchmark evaluates action understanding, goal decomposition, and cross-horizon consistency through multiple-choice questions, with predicted action sequences matched to answer options for scoring. Our work links subtask instructions to waypoints and temporally aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories within multi-stage tasks, providing supervision for subgoal transitions and continuous control. Game Action Data for Instruction Following sec:related_action_data Large-scale gameplay demonstrations support action policy learning~ zhang2026social,zhou2026main . MineRL~ guss2019minerl provides human demonstrations in Minecraft with automatically annotated states and actions. VPT~ baker2022video uses inverse dynamics to infer keyboard-and-mouse actions from Minecraft videos, while NitroGen~ Magne_2026_CVPR extracts gamepad actions from online videos for cross-game behavior cloning. Language-based supervision further connects gameplay behaviors to task goals. MineDojo~ fan2022minedojo combines an open-ended task suite specified in natural language with an internet-scale multimodal knowledge base of videos, tutorials, wiki pages, and forum discussions. Open-P2P~ yue2026scaling provides cross-game keyboard-and-mouse trajectories with sparse goal-oriented instructions. SIMA~ raad2024scaling learns to follow language instructions across 3D environments, focusing primarily on short-horizon tasks, while SIMA 2~ bolton2025sima extends this setting to complex instructions and instruction chaining. STEVE-1~ lifshitz2023steve supports text- and visual-goal control in Minecraft and composes multi-step behaviors through sequential subgoal prompts. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete multi-stage tasks, with annotations spanning overall goals, stage-level subgoals, and local skill instructions. Each subtask is associated with a waypoint, explicit temporal boundaries, and aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories. This structure connects individual skill execution to task progression, providing supervision for action execution and the timing of subgoal transitions. Dataset sec:dataset Data Source Our dataset comprises two complementary components: directly collected gameplay and publicly sourced gameplay. The directly collected gameplay was recorded from full-time in-house staff who held a Gold rank and consented to participate. These recordings were transcribed in anonymized form during data collection. Together, these components provide approximately 5,180 hours of gameplay recordings paired with keyboard-and-mouse actions. collected gameplay. We collected gameplay recordings and corresponding keyboard-and-mouse actions from human players. This component includes approximately 1,891 hours of Game for Peace, including combat scenarios, and 261.17 hours of Valorant. These recordings pair gameplay observations with the actions performed by human players. sourced gameplay. To broaden coverage across games and tasks, we incorporate 2,103.05 hours of CS:GO and CS2 gameplay from match recordings collected online, 811.50 hours of annotated 3D gameplay from Open-P2P, and 113.25 hours of Minecraft gameplay from VPT. These durations refer to the portions included in our dataset rather than the complete upstream datasets. representation and sampling rates. Across both components, we use a common action representation that encodes keyboard and mouse-button states, together with horizontal and vertical mouse displacement. Our directly collected gameplay is recorded at 16 Hz, corresponding to one action step every 62.5 ms. For publicly sourced gameplay, we CS:GO and CS2 action sequences are 16 Hz, while retaining the original 20 Hz sampling rate for Open-P2P and VPT. title: LoopQ: Fair, Closed-Loop Evaluation of Quantized Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) for vision-language-action (VLA) models promises smaller and faster VLA deployments. However, when analyzing existing VLA quantization works, we realised that it is hard to reason about the performance of the suggested quantization method compared to existing, similar, or in many cases, simpler PTQ methods. We present LoopQ, a closed-loop benchmark that compares multiple quantization policies on the same checkpoint, layers and engine, varying only the method and the kernels. We evaluate RTN, AWQ, GPTQ, ActQuant and QuantVLA on four VLAs with more than 180,000 episodes of LIBERO and LIBERO-plus, compare against QVLA's reported results on the same layers, and benchmark whether the four public VLA-quantization releases can be reproduced. We benchmark the methods on an NVIDIA H100, an L4, and a Jetson AGX Thor. Our results show that while quantization reliably saves memory, 2-3x for real low-bit models, VLA-specific PTQ methods underperform compared to simpler generic baselines. At 4 bits, RTN, AWQ and GPTQ match or exceed ActQuant and QuantVLA, plain RTN matches the calibrated methods, and plain AWQ matches the success QVLA reports for itself. Standard LIBERO hides the losses that do exist: configurations with no significant LIBERO loss lose 1.5-4.3 points under paired LIBERO-plus perturbations. Speed is a weaker story. At batch 1 on the H100, no quantized pi0.5 or OpenVLA-OFT configuration is faster than its 16-bit model (1.06-1.58x slower on library kernels); only the L4 with int8 kernels gains (4-14%), the Thor is slower on every 4-bit configuration, and the engine alone changes latency by 2.1x. Profiling explains why: pi0.5's quantized backbone is compute-bound, while its memory-bound action expert, 63% of GPU time and 13% of the parameters, stays in 16 bits.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera images and a language instruction to robot actions by coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with an action decoder~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00t,bu2025univla . Their millions to billions of parameter backbones are hard to fit within the memory, latency and power budgets of robots, so post-training quantization (PTQ)~ frantar2023gptq,lin2024awq,zhao2024atom,lin2025qserve , is increasingly treated as a prerequisite for deployment. Recenlty, a large number of VLA-specific PTQ methods have claimed that action-aware sensitivity, mixed precision or activation smoothing yields smaller and faster policies without loss of task success~ akbari2026actquant,zhang2026quantvla,xu2026qvla,wang2026holoq .However, we find that these works rarely answer three basic questions about these claims. Is the gain over a fair baseline? VLA-specific methods are compared with generic methods such as AWQ~ lin2024awq and GPTQ~ frantar2023gptq , but under their authors' own setups and rarely with plain round-to-nearest (RTN). For example, at the layer scope chosen by QVLA~ xu2026qvla , our plain AWQ reaches 96.6 on OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft , against the 92.5 QVLA reports for AWQ and the 96.7 it reports for itself. RTN, which needs no calibration, matches AWQ and GPTQ on all four models we test: ~ black2025pi05 , GR00T~N1.5~ nvidia2025gr00t , UniVLA~ bu2025univla and OpenVLA-OFT ( ). Is task success really preserved? VLA quantization papers report their main results on standard LIBERO~ liu2023libero , with 50 (QuantVLA~ zhang2026quantvla ), 250 (QVLA~ xu2026qvla ) or 500 (ActQuant~ akbari2026actquant ) episodes per suite and no perturbations. LIBERO is near saturation (93--98 for the full-precision policies we test), and small samples hide small losses: at 50 episodes per suite, the 95 interval of the four-suite average is 4.7 points. On the more recent paired LIBERO-plus tasks~ fei2025liberoplus , configurations with no significant LIBERO loss lose 1.5--4.3 points ( ). Is the deployed policy faster, and what actually runs? Three of the four releases we audit only simulate quantization in floating point, so their speed cannot be measured ( ). The bit width alone also says little about speed: on , the same 4-bit AWQ weights run , or slower than F16, depending on which kernel executes them. Even ActQuant's real 3--4-bit models, which is faster than eager PyTorch, are -- slower than the same model in 16 bits on its own engine ( ). Speed-ups must be measured against the same model on the same engine. In this paper, we built to answer these questions under one controlled protocol ( ); concurrent work~ xu2026vlaquantbench studies layer scope and numerical format with RTN only. In every comparison only the quantizer changes: the checkpoint, the quantized layers and the engine stay the same, the kernel path and real or simulated execution are reported separately, and each quantized policy runs on exactly the same tasks as its unquantized baseline. We evaluate RTN, AWQ~ lin2024awq , GPTQ~ frantar2023gptq , ActQuant~ akbari2026actquant and QuantVLA~ zhang2026quantvla on ~ black2025pi05 , GR00T~N1.5~ nvidia2025gr00t , UniVLA~ bu2025univla and OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft , using 1 , 000--2 , 000 LIBERO~ liu2023libero episodes per configuration plus paired LIBERO-plus~ fei2025liberoplus tasks ( ). and OpenVLA-OFT run real low-bit; GR00T and UniVLA use simulated quantization, as in QuantVLA and QVLA~ xu2026qvla ( ). We time every policy in the closed loop, in isolation and per operator on an H100 NVL, repeat the efficiency study and a paired task-success subset on an NVIDIA L4 and a Jetson AGX Thor ( ), and audit four public VLA-quantization releases ( ). shows the two headline results. To summarize, we make the following five contributions. [leftmargin=1.2em] . We build the first VLA quantization benchmark that puts VLA-specific and generic methods at the same scope, times real low-bit models per kernel path on three GPUs, and tests robustness with paired distribution shift. will be open-sourced upon acceptance. Fewer bits, no speed-up. We show why real low-bit quantized models need -- less memory, but can be significantly slower than 16 bit configurations ( -- on library kernels) explaining why this occurs using Profiling. For example, the quantized backbones run one compute-bound pass, and 's memory-bound action expert, which takes 63 of GPU time, stays in 16 bits. Even if the quantized layers took no time at all, a call would be at most faster ( ). LIBERO hides the losses. PTQ configurations that look lossless on LIBERO lose up to 4.3 points under paired LIBERO-plus perturbations. Most of these losses come from the PTQ VLA-specific methods, ActQuant and QuantVLA, and from 4-bit UniVLA; plain RTN does as well as AWQ and GPTQ on all four models ( ). The GPU decides the speed, the method decides the success. The same 4-bit files run up to 14 faster on an L4 with int8 kernels but up to slower on a Jetson AGX Thor, while task-success outcomes agree on 90--99 of episodes across the three GPUs ( ). What a release lets you check. Of four VLA quantization releases, only ActQuant can be timed, and it runs slower than its own 16-bit model. QVLA's reported margin over AWQ disappears once AWQ runs under our protocol ( ). Background and Related Work sec:related VLA architectures. We study four VLAs that differ in how they generate actions. ~ black2025pi05 (3.36\,B parameters) encodes two camera images with SigLIP-So400m~ zhai2023siglip , runs a PaliGemma/Gemma-2B prefix~ beyer2024paligemma once per call to fill the KV cache, and generates a 10-step action chunk with a Gemma-300M-based action expert (0.43\,B parameters) over 10 flow-matching steps. GR00T~N1.5~ nvidia2025gr00t pairs an Eagle-2.5 VLM with a diffusion-transformer action head (8 denoising steps). UniVLA~ bu2025univla is a 7\,B autoregressive VLA that predicts discrete latent-action tokens, while OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft uses a similar Llama-2 backbone but predicts continuous action chunks with an MLP head. PTQ and low-bit kernels for LLMs. Weight-only methods such as RTN, GPTQ~ frantar2023gptq and AWQ~ lin2024awq target memory-bound LLM decoding, where less weight traffic means lower latency. LLM.int8()~ dettmers2022llmint8 brought 8-bit inference to scale mainly for memory, and weight-activation methods such as SmoothQuant~ xiao2023smoothquant , QuaRot~ ashkboos2024quarot and DuQuant~ lin2024duquant quantize both operands to use integer arithmetic. Actual speed-ups depend heavily on the kernel and batch size~ zhao2024atom,lin2025qserve,frantar2025marlin . VLAs differ from LLM decoding as the mostly process a prompt of several hundred tokens in one pass and then run a short action loop, so it is unclear which phase dominates and whether low-bit kernels help. VLA-specific PTQ. ActQuant~ akbari2026actquant assigns mixed sub-4-bit llama.cpp formats using an action-guided sensitivity measure; its reported speed-up is measured on OpenVLA, comparing a 4-bit build in its C++ engine with PyTorch ( ). QuantVLA~ zhang2026quantvla builds on DuQuant-style W4A8 quantization with attention-temperature and head-balancing corrections, QVLA~ xu2026qvla assigns per-channel bit widths by action sensitivity, and HoloQ-VLA~ wang2026holoq targets uniform W4A4 with block-wise rotations. All four report their main results on standard LIBERO, but they quantize different layers, use different numbers of episodes, and run real or simulated kernels, so their results are hard to compare; none tests robustness under perturbation. Concurrent work~ xu2026vlaquantbench benchmarks layer scope and numerical format with RTN, but not VLA-specific methods, real low-bit speed, or robustness. Robustness evaluation. LIBERO-plus~ fei2025liberoplus perturbs LIBERO tasks along seven axes (camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language, lighting, background, sensor noise and object layout), each at five difficulty levels, and shows that even full-precision VLAs struggle under these shifts. We ask a narrower question: does quantization add failures beyond the base policy's? We run both policies on the same perturbed tasks and use paired tests, so that the base policy's own failures are not blamed on quantization. Benchmark Design sec:design follows five design principles: (1) Change only the quantizer. Every variant of a model uses the same checkpoint, the same quantized layers, taken from the VLA-specific methods themselves, and the same calibration data ( ); (2) Report how the model runs, not just its bit width ( ). The same ``W4A16'' file can run in very different ways; in llama.cpp~ llamacpp , for example, it runs on int8 kernels that also quantize activations. We therefore report each kernel path separately; (3) Use enough episodes, and pair them ( ). Each configuration runs 1 , 000--2 , 000 LIBERO episodes and is compared with its baseline task by task on thousands of LIBERO-plus tasks, so losses of one to two points become visible; (4) Time the full policy on the same engine ( ). The engine alone changes the latency of the same 16-bit by , so every speed-up is measured against the unquantized model on the same engine; and (5) Check what each release can actually reproduce ( ): does it run, does it match its paper, and can its memory and speed be measured? Models, scopes and engines sec:models lists the four VLAs, how each runs and how many episodes each configuration gets. title: IGSW: Multi-Weather Urban Scene Reconstruction with Intrinsic-Decoupled Gaussian Splatting
summary: High-fidelity weather editing of 4D scenes can support end-to-end training and closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving. Combining generative image editing with dynamic Gaussian representations enables multi-weather scene reconstruction, but weather-edited images often contain structural distortions. Directly fitting their appearance may propagate errors from teacher images into the reconstructed 4D scene, compromising the original scene structure and temporal continuity. To address these challenges, we propose IGSW, a two-stage framework that combines intrinsic-decoupled 4D Gaussian scene modeling with structure-preserving weather refinement. In Stage I, background Gaussian appearance is decomposed into weather-shared albedo and normals and weather-specific irradiance and residuals. Weather teacher images generated by a diffusion-based image editing model and intrinsic maps estimated by a diffusion-based inverse renderer provide feature-level soft supervision for stable structure and illumination changes. In Stage II, a structure-preservation gate combines semantic conflicts with cross-weather intrinsic discrepancies to suppress unreliable teacher regions. Per-Gaussian weather transport variables and target-weather branches then strengthen the desired weather appearance over the intrinsic-decoupled scene. Experiments on nuScenes and Waymo show that IGSW achieves the highest content similarity and semantic consistency and the lowest temporal error among the compared methods, while retaining pronounced weather-dependent illumination and atmosphere. The project page is available at https://akaxi6.github.io/IGSW/ .
full_text: IGSW: Multi-Weather Urban Scene Reconstruction\ Intrinsic-Decoupled Gaussian Splatting Zhongquan~Wang, Long~Cao, Peijia~Xie, Senlei~Ma, Jie~Li, and~Guofa~Li High-fidelity weather editing of 4D scenes can support end-to-end training and closed-loop simulation for autonomous driving. Combining generative image editing with dynamic Gaussian representations enables multi-weather scene reconstruction, but weather-edited images often contain structural distortions. Directly fitting their appearance may propagate errors from teacher images into the reconstructed 4D scene, compromising the original scene structure and temporal continuity. To address these challenges, we propose IGSW, a two-stage framework that combines intrinsic-decoupled 4D Gaussian scene modeling with structure-preserving weather refinement. In Stage~I, background Gaussian appearance is decomposed into weather-shared albedo and normals and weather-specific irradiance and residuals. Weather teacher images generated by a diffusion-based image editing model and intrinsic maps estimated by a diffusion-based inverse renderer provide feature-level soft supervision for stable structure and illumination changes. In Stage~II, a structure-preservation gate combines semantic conflicts with cross-weather intrinsic discrepancies to suppress unreliable teacher regions. Per-Gaussian weather transport variables and target-weather branches then strengthen the desired weather appearance over the intrinsic-decoupled scene. Experiments on nuScenes and Waymo show that IGSW achieves the highest content similarity and semantic consistency and the lowest temporal error among the compared methods, while retaining pronounced weather-dependent illumination and atmosphere. The project page is available at . Gaussian splatting, intrinsic decomposition, weather editing, dynamic scene reconstruction, autonomous-driving simulation. Introduction sec:intro eather editing can extend captured driving scenes to conditions that are difficult to record with matched viewpoints and traffic states. Rain changes illumination and road reflections, whereas snow changes surface appearance and contrast. These effects should not alter the spatial layout or motion of roads, buildings, and traffic participants. Weather editing therefore requires more than realistic individual frames: it must construct a unified scene representation whose weather appearance remains consistent across views and time. 3D Gaussian Splatting~ r1 and dynamic urban scene representations~ r3,r4 provide a foundation for efficient reconstruction and rendering. Text-guided image editors such as Qwen-Image~ r18 can further synthesize target-weather observations beyond the captured condition. WeatherEdit~ r6 and WeatherCity~ r5 combine such appearance priors with scene-level modeling, extending weather synthesis from independent image editing to three-dimensional scenes. Nevertheless, a unified representation alone does not distinguish valid weather changes from erroneous structural changes in edited images. Strengthening weather appearance can also amplify implausible modifications to scene content. Generated clouds may establish a rainy atmosphere while occluding a building that should remain visible; convincing reflections may be accompanied by inconsistent vehicle details. Strongly anchoring optimization to the original RGB observations can suppress these errors, but may also weaken the intended weather effects. Effective weather editing must therefore answer two coupled questions: which scene factors should change with weather, and which teacher regions provide reliable supervision. Intrinsic decomposition provides a basis for the first distinction. Albedo and surface normals offer material and structural cues, whereas irradiance describes illumination variation. Generative inverse rendering, as used by IntrinsicWeather~ r19 , estimates these factors from original and weather-edited images. Independently estimated intrinsic maps, however, can contain local errors and cross-view inconsistencies. We introduce IGSW (Intrinsic Gaussian Splatting Weather), a two-stage framework for intrinsic-decoupled 4D Gaussian modeling and structure-preserving weather refinement. Stage~I decomposes background Gaussian appearance into weather-shared albedo and normals and weather-specific irradiance and residuals. Intrinsic feature supervision anchors shared content to the original scene and guides the weather branches toward the target illumination change. Stable content and weather variation thus assume distinct modeling roles within one renderable Gaussian scene. Intrinsic decoupling does not imply that every teacher change is valid, because weather-specific branches may still reproduce structural errors. Stage~II addresses this issue through reliability-aware refinement. A structure-preservation gate combines semantic conflicts with differences between the original and edited albedo/normal estimates to identify unreliable teacher regions. Reliable regions retain teacher appearance supervision, whereas conflicting regions use weather-styled targets that preserve original spatial content. With geometry and the shared intrinsic representation fixed, per-Gaussian weather transport variables and target-weather branches refine illumination and residual appearance. Experiments on nuScenes and Waymo show that, among the compared scene-editing baselines, IGSW improves content preservation, semantic consistency, and temporal stability while retaining pronounced weather-dependent illumination and atmosphere. These properties support multi-weather urban reconstruction and subsequent data generation for autonomous-driving simulation. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose an intrinsic-decoupled 4D Gaussian weather representation. Gaussian appearance is separated into weather-shared albedo/normals and weather-specific irradiance/residuals, explicitly assigning stable scene content and weather variation different representational roles. Then we incorporate intrinsic information to guide the iterative optimization of the decoupled Gaussian representation, promoting material and structural consistency while modeling weather-induced illumination changes. We introduce an intrinsic-preserving Gaussian weather refinement method. A structure-preservation gate combines semantic conflicts with cross-weather albedo and normal discrepancies to mitigate the propagation of structural errors from weather-edited teacher images into the 3D scene. With geometry and shared intrinsic representations fixed, per-Gaussian weather transport variables and weather-specific branch optimization refine irradiance and residual responses, strengthening target-weather appearance while preserving the original scene structure. We validate IGSW on nuScenes and Waymo. Full-sequence rain and snow evaluations, visual comparisons, and ablation studies demonstrate that IGSW balances target-weather expression, preservation of original scene content and semantic structure, and temporal continuity, supporting multi-weather scene simulation and data generation for autonomous driving. Related Work Image and Video Weather Editing Weather generation and restoration have long supported robustness research for autonomous driving. Early directions include GAN-based weather transfer~ r11 , extreme-weather synthesis with ClimateNeRF~ r10 , and multi-weather restoration~ r12 . Diffusion and text-guided editors, including InstructPix2Pix~ r13 , ControlNet~ r14 , Prompt-to-Prompt~ r15 , and Qwen-Image~ r18 , provide more flexible control over image-level appearance. Video editors such as TokenFlow~ r16 and FRESCO~ r17 propagate correspondence to reduce frame-wise inconsistency. FluencyVE~ cai2026fluencyve uses temporal-aware Mamba and bypass attention for efficient video editing. Qian et al.~ qian2026semantic combine semantic appearance guidance, physical particle simulation, and geometric conditioning for weather video synthesis. IGSW distills weather edits into a dynamic 4D Gaussian scene while filtering teacher-induced content errors. Intrinsic Decomposition and Generative Inverse Rendering Intrinsic decomposition separates material, geometry, and illumination factors to provide a structured representation of scene appearance. Albedo describes the underlying material color, normals characterize surface orientation, and irradiance captures lighting variation, providing complementary cues for appearance editing and relighting. Yang et al.~ yang2025relighting incorporate intrinsic decomposition into a two-stage single-image relighting network. Intrinsic Image Diffusion~ r20 , IntrinsicEdit~ r21 , RGB X~ r22 , Uni-Renderer~ r23 , and DiffusionRenderer~ r24 use generative priors to estimate or manipulate intrinsic properties. IntrinsicReal~ wei2026intrinsicreal adapts a diffusion-based albedo estimator to real objects using confidence- and ranking-based pseudo-label selection. IntrinsicWeather~ r19 extends this reasoning to weather editing through albedo, normals, and irradiance, but remains an image-space method. IGSW instead models shared and weather-specific intrinsic factors within a dynamic Gaussian scene, supporting weather-dependent appearance changes while preserving stable scene content. Three-Dimensional Weather Scene Modeling NeRF~ r2 and 3D Gaussian Splatting~ r1 reconstruct and render multi-view scenes through implicit radiance fields and explicit Gaussian primitives, respectively. Street Gaussians~ r3 and DrivingGaussian~ r4 extend reconstruction to dynamic traffic participants. TrAME~ luo2025trame couples progressive view editing with Gaussian updates to improve multi-view consistency. Cao et al.~ cao2026supportaware improve cross-view consistency through support-aware appearance residual distillation. These representations provide the basis for scene-level weather editing, but observations from one condition do not determine how the same scene should appear under another. WeatherGS~ qian2025weathergs removes weather artifacts and masks lens occlusions for Gaussian reconstruction, whereas WeatherDrive~ hua2025weatherdrive studies multi-view street-scene generation under multiple weather conditions. ClimateNeRF~ r10 , WeatherEdit~ r6 , Weather-Magician~ r7 , and WeatherCity~ r5 incorporate weather variation into three-dimensional or dynamic scenes, whereas RainyGS~ r8 and Let It Snow~ r9 model specific rain or snow effects. Even with fixed Gaussian positions, fitting edited images may reproduce false occlusions and content changes. IGSW addresses these errors through intrinsic factorization and reliability-aware refinement. Method sec:method Given calibrated multi-view driving images with temporal correspondence, IGSW learns a dynamic Gaussian scene that renders a target weather condition while preserving the scene structure. Figure~ fig:pipeline summarizes the pipeline. Text-Guided Weather Teacher Images sec:teachers We use Qwen-Image with weather-specific prompts that describe illumination, reflections, and environmental appearance for rain or snow while requesting preservation of the scene layout and visible content. Although the resulting teachers include weather-dependent changes to roads, buildings, and other surfaces, Qwen-Image edits frames independently and imposes no explicit cross-frame or cross-view constraint. Its sequences may therefore contain illumination drift, texture changes, or content errors such as clouds covering buildings. title: WayTrace: A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy for Embodied Urban Navigation
summary: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
full_text: : A Map-to-Language-to-Trace Hierarchy\ Embodied Urban Navigation Manthan Patel , Jonas Frey , Pascal Roth , Marco Hutter , and Cesar Cadena Real-world deployment of through a city centre, given the request ``Go to the nearest Starbucks'' (426\,m away). (A)~One step of the hierarchy at the entry to a crossing. A web map (e.g., Google Maps) provides turn-by-turn language directions once at the start of the mission ( , shortened here). The orchestrator VLM ( , Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a remote server) receives these directions, a robot-centric top-down satellite crop, the current camera image and a history of past images, and it issues the next atomic language command, shown with its condensed reasoning. The trace predictor VLM ( , onboard) predicts an image-space trace conditioned on that command. The trace is lifted to 3D using depth and tracked by an RL-based navigation policy ( ). (B)~The planned route, the driven path and each new orchestrator command (orange dots) on the satellite map, together with six moments along the mission. Each moment shows a third-person view of the robot, the robot camera with the predicted trace (inset) and the current orchestrator command. fig:teaser Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present , a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as ``cross the road to the left''. An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, completes real-world missions of up to 1.37\,km at about 1.1\,m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: Navigation, Vision-Language-Action Models, Foundation Models, Embodied AI Introduction sec:intro umans navigate unfamiliar cities with little effort. Given a destination, a person consults a web map and follows its turn-by-turn directions, such as continuing along a sidewalk, turning onto a crosswalk or taking the stairs. Neither a metric goal nor precise position is required. The map indicates the next manoeuvre and its approximate location, while vision resolves where the crosswalk begins and when a turn has been completed. Since web maps provide such directions for nearly every place where people walk, a robot that follows them in the same manner could be deployed in any city given only a destination and without a prior mapping run, enabling applications such as last-mile delivery, urban inspection and guidance of visually impaired people. Existing learned navigation methods fall short of this goal over long routes. Point-goal methods~ roth2024viplanner,liu2025citywalker,castro2025vamos,hirose2025omnivla,yang2025sru receive the route as a sequence of GNSS waypoints, and their performance is therefore bounded by the accuracy of the position estimate. In cities, GNSS errors of several metres are common~ merry2019smartphone , enough to place a waypoint on the road or on the opposite side of the street, and over routes of several hundred metres such errors inevitably lead to failures. Waypoints also carry no notion of the social norms, such as staying on the sidewalk and crossing at crosswalks, so a policy that reaches every waypoint may still violate them and pose a safety risk in urban traffic. Vision-language navigation (VLN) replaces coordinates with natural-language instructions, but it has been studied predominantly in simulated indoor environments~ anderson2018r2r,ku2020rxr and on street-view panoramas~ chen2019touchdown . Recent models bring vision-language navigation to real robots~ huang2026ticvla,zhang2026foresight,cheng2025navila,zhang2025ventura , but they are typically demonstrated on single instructions over short distances. We find that these models are brittle even at the level of a single atomic instruction ( ), which makes it infeasible to follow a kilometre-long route by chaining such instructions. In this work, we simplify the problem. Web-map directions already decompose a route into a sequence of atomic instructions, each describing a single manoeuvre such as ``cross the road'' that can be grounded in the camera image. Long-range navigation thus separates into deciding which atomic instruction applies at the current moment and executing that instruction reliably. The first problem requires the map and contextual reasoning but only a coarse position, since GNSS is needed only to identify the current step of the route rather than the exact position of the robot. The second problem requires only the camera and a short observation history. Language is a suitable interface between the two levels, since it is what web maps produce and what vision-language models (VLMs) reason in. Based on this observation, we propose , a map-to-language-to-trace hierarchy ( ). An off-the-shelf orchestrator VLM reads the web-map directions, a satellite map of the surroundings and the recent camera images, and issues the next atomic command. An onboard trace predictor draws the path for this command in image space, and a reinforcement learning (RL) policy tracks the path lifted to 3D. We evaluate on ten long-range missions in a simulated old town and in real-world deployments. With perfect GNSS, completes 83\, of the missions. It achieves the highest success rate at every level of GNSS error, and its success rate decreases gradually to 63\, with a drifting GNSS error of 7\,m RMS, whereas that of point-goal baselines drops below 25\, and they leave the crosswalk or the sidewalk about ten times as often. Vision-language baselines complete at most 7\, of the missions, even with language commands from a tuned oracle. In the real world, completed three missions of up to 426\,m through a busy city centre fully autonomously, and a 1.37\,km mission along rural trails and through a university campus with two short operator interventions. The main contributions of this work are as follows. , a hierarchical navigation framework that translates web-map directions into atomic language commands and executes them as image-space traces. A language-conditioned trace predictor together with an automatic labelling pipeline that produces most of its training data from unlabelled street-level image sequences. An extensive evaluation against point-goal and vision-language navigation baselines in simulation, an analysis of each component and real-world deployments on a wheeled-legged robot. We will release the simulation environment, the long-range navigation benchmark, the trace prediction benchmarks, the dataset, the models and the code. Related Work sec:related Long-Range and Map-Guided Outdoor Navigation Navigation foundation models learn goal-conditioned policies from data pooled across robots and environments~ shah2023gnm,shah2023vint,sridhar2024nomad , and recent work scales point-goal navigation with crowd-sourced robot data~ suomela2026datascaling,hirose2026mbra or with walking videos from the web~ liu2025citywalker,xia2026longtail . Vision-language-action models for navigation additionally accept GNSS poses, images or language as goals~ hirose2025omnivla . VAMOS~ castro2025vamos plans candidate paths in the image with a VLM and re-ranks them with an embodiment-specific affordance model. Over long distances, these policies are guided by GNSS goals or waypoints, so the route they follow is only as accurate as the position estimate. Several systems follow routes from map services. ViKiNG~ shah2022viking reached kilometre-scale goals by using overhead images as heuristics for a learned local policy, and Sorokin et al.~ sorokin2022sidewalks followed public map routes with a legged robot while staying on sidewalks. UrbanVLA~ li2026urbanvla aligns noisy route waypoints from a map service with the camera observations in an end-to-end policy. Walk With Me~ zhang2026walkwithme lets a VLM ground instructions in map data and GNSS as waypoints for a low-level policy and defers difficult situations, such as crossings, to the VLM. DA-Nav~ yuan2026danav reduces web-map directions to four discrete commands that a VLM grounds as cells in the image, and NaViRrator~ lee2026navirrator verbalises a map route once into an instruction for a VLN policy. In , the route is converted into atomic language commands in closed loop. Each command is grounded in the current observation rather than in metric coordinates, and hence GNSS errors do not displace the path that the robot follows. Vision-Language Navigation Vision-language navigation was established on simulated indoor benchmarks~ anderson2018r2r,ku2020rxr,krantz2020vlnce and on street-view graphs of real cities~ chen2019touchdown,schumann2021map2seq,vasudevan2021talk2nav,schumann2024velma , where an agent follows a paragraph of instructions written for the whole route. Video-based VLMs transfer such models to real robots~ zhang2024navid,zhang2025uninavid,wei2026streamvln , and recent navigation foundation models scale this approach to millions of samples across tasks and embodiments, unifying instruction following, object search and point goals in a single model~ zhang2025navfom,chu2026abotn0,gong2026abotn1,zhang2026qwenrobotnav,wang2026lightnav0,bounhar2026robostral . NaVILA~ cheng2025navila lets a VLM issue metric language actions that an RL locomotion policy executes on a legged robot, and UrbanNav~ mei2026urbannav learns language-guided urban navigation from city-walking videos. TIC-VLA~ huang2026ticvla couples language reasoning with control and accounts for the delay of its reasoning in dynamic environments. Foresight~ zhang2026foresight lets a VLM propose motion plans in the image and iteratively critique and refine them. VENTURA~ zhang2025ventura adapts an image diffusion model to generate path masks that a lightweight policy executes. These models execute one instruction or goal at a time, which a user or a higher-level agent has to provide~ zhang2026qwenrobotnav . keeps each instruction atomic and lets an orchestrator decide which instruction applies along the route. Hierarchical Systems with Language as the Interface Decomposing long-horizon tasks into language subtasks for a low-level policy is well established in manipulation. In SayCan~ ahn2022saycan , a language model proposes skills that are scored by affordance functions, and RT-H~ belkhale2024rth predicts language motions as an intermediate step between the task and the actions. title: Asynchronous Robot Policies

summary: Scaling vision-language foundation models has significantly advanced generalist robot manipulation, but the increased model scale introduces computational latency that degrades real-time physical reactivity. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action ex- ecution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. To address this, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policy (ARP), an architectural framework that decouples semantic reasoning from low-level action generation using asynchronous processes operating at independent frequencies. In ARP, a high-capacity Vision-Language Model (VLM) asynchronously updates a semantic memory at low fre- quency, while a lightweight Vision-Action Expert, conditioned on this semantic memory, generates robot actions at a much higher control frequency. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18% higher success rate and 20% less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 times baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at 10 times lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models.

Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures execute high-level semantic reasoning and action execution sequentially within the primary control loop, creating a fundamental tension between semantic-reasoning capability and robot agility. Such a formulation, enables having a fast perception-action loop without compromising on the semantic capability. To overcome asynchronous memory staleness, ARP trains the vision-action expert on the semantic staleness and execution delay, with temporally mismatched observation across processes. On Franka manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an higher success rate and less time need for execution in quasi-static setups, while 3-5 baseline performance in dynamic simulation environments. Furthermore, ARP enables operating the VLM at lower than its nominal frequency with no significant performance loss making it much more efficient than the baseline. These results highlight the architectural advantages of modeling robot policies as asynchronous processes, enabling real-world reactive deployment without sacrificing the scale of foundation models. For code, checkpoints and more results, check out ARP Project . Introduction Scaling has become the dominant paradigm of modern artificial intelligence~ kaplan2020scaling . However, scaling model size incurs a fundamental trade-off: increased capability at the cost of higher computational latency and degrading real-time responsiveness. While higher latency may be tolerable in static or text-based applications, it presents a critical failure mode in robotics. Physical robotics requires tight perception-action loops to handle real-time contact dynamics and sudden environmental shifts, such as grasping falling objects or absorbing unexpected bumps. Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA)~ brohan2022rt,zitkovich2023rt2 models fall victim to this bottleneck, creating a persistent tension between model capability, computational overhead, and closed-loop reactivity. Consequently, scaling the vision-language backbone improves high-level reasoning at the expense of motor agility, yielding a system that is semantically rich but physically lag-bound and depends on open-loop deployment. To resolve this friction, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policies (ARP). As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser_b , ARP breaks the reactivity-capability trade-off, enabling the seamless integration of significantly larger foundational models into robot pipelines without significantly compromising dynamic reactivity or real-time performance. Existing generalist VLA policies execute the vision-language foundation model and the action expert sequentially within the primary control loop. Their latencies therefore add up, giving a total perception-to-action latency of , as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (a). In contrast, ARP decouples VLM and action expert into asynchronous processes running at different frequencies. The VLM operates at a lower frequency for high-level semantic reasoning, while a compact vision-action expert operates at a higher frequency . Under ARP, the effective perception-action loop latency is strictly reduced to the expert execution time ( ), so that control reactivity no longer grows linearly with the VLM scale. Importantly, this decoupling allows ARP to benefit from larger, more capable VLMs while maintaining reactivity, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (b). Making robot policies asynchronous, however, introduces several new challenges. The fast action expert must continuously act on a compact semantic memory produced by a slower VLM, while the robot state evolves during both VLM and action expert inference. This creates two sources of mismatch: the semantic memory may be stale relative to the current observation, and newly predicted actions may arrive after execution has already progressed. Performing the two loops asynchronously can therefore lead to outdated conditioning, delayed actions, and discontinuities across replanning cycles. ARP addresses these challenges by compressing rich VLM activations into fixed-width asynchronous memory, explicitly conditioning the action expert on semantic staleness and execution delay, and training with temporally mismatched memories and action-prefix conditioning to support smooth continuous replanning. Asynchronous paradigms have been explored in prior work, mainly for cloud-to-edge VLA deployment, extending the action expert's contextual history, or smoothing execution through asynchronous action chunking~ hirose2026asyncvla,hu2026ar,tang2025vlash,black2025training . However, these approaches still retain dependencies on the main model pipeline. To our knowledge, ARP is the first truly asynchronous robotic control framework, where one can vary the rate of two processes, featuring an autonomous Vision-Action Expert. This expert is capable of executing high-frequency reactive motor commands independently while continuously synthesizing semantic updates from the asynchronous VLM. Evaluated on quasi-static Franka robot manipulation tasks, ARP achieves an 18 higher success rate while taking 20 less time than conventional VLA baselines. In dynamic environments, ARP achieves 3-5 the performance of the baseline, successfully handling target perturbations where synchronous policies fail. Furthermore, ARP reduces computational demand by running the VLM at 10 lower frequency with no significant loss in performance owing to the asynchronous nature of ARP. These results indicate that ARP offers a viable blueprint for bridging the gap between large-scale semantic reasoning and agile physical control. Related Works Generalist Robot Policies Inspired by the scaling laws and multi-modal pretraining paradigms established in Large Language Models (LLMs)~ touvron2023llama, team2024gemma, alexandrov2024mitigating and Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ liu2023visualinstructiontuning, wang2024qwen2 , VLA paradigm extend these generalist representations to robot control. Typically, VLAs adapt pretrained VLM backbones to map visual and natural language instructions directly to continuous or chunked robotic motor actions~ brohan2022rt, kim2024openvla, black2024pi_0, team2025gemini, nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation, nikolov2025spear1scalingrobotdemonstrations . Although VLA architectures represent the current state of the art in policy generalization, their real-world deployment is frequently bottlenecked by catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning~ dey2024revla as well as limitations in heterogeneous training data scale and diversity~ open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023, walke2023bridgedata, khazatsky2024droid . Another line of work relies on LLM and VLM driven program to ground the semantic reasoning in robotic primitives via code generation~ 10610784 , TAMP-based approach~ shen2026tiptop or agentic-harness-style approaches~ chen2026volo . A complementary research frontier leverages world-models ~ nvidia2026cosmos3 and video-generation models~ wan2025,nvidia2025cosmospredict2 as alternative backbones in World-Action-Model(WAM). These paradigms learn predictive environmental representations by forecasting future states in pixel space~ hu2023gaia , latent feature space~ chen2026lawam,zhou2024dino , or directly in action space to carry out planning~ assran2025v . While this work primarily benchmarks against standard VLM-based VLA architectures, ARP can be extended to make WAMs asynchronous, by incorporating world-models as the backbone for the semantic expert. Asynchronous Systems AR-VLA~ hu2026ar proposes an autoregressive action expert to decouple the VLM cache from action generation. Similarly, AsyncVLA~ hirose2026asyncvla shares architectural similarities with ARP by pairing a local action expert with a high-latency remote VLA. However, while AsyncVLA is deployed to handle latency from cloud server to edge devices, ARP investigates unconstrained, process-level asynchronous execution and training approach in an end-to-end manner. Meanwhile, VLASH~ tang2025vlash and Training-Time RTC~ black2025training introduce training-time augmentations to compensate for VLM latency, optimizing specifically for sequential action-chunk alignment. In contrast, ARP addresses latency at the inter-process boundary, conditioning a high-frequency vision-action expert on temporally mismatched semantic memory representations. More broadly, streaming VLMs~ xu2026streamingvlm,wang2026streambridge and duplex-audio architectures~ zhao2026realtime have demonstrated the benefits of asynchronous processing for video understanding and conversational assistants. In robotics, the Robot Operating System (ROS)~ doi:10.1126/scirobotics.abm6074 established non-blocking publisher-subscriber abstractions as a standard paradigm. Drawing direct inspiration from ROS, ARP adopts this publisher-subscriber model to decouple high-level VLM reasoning from real-time policy execution. Method sec:method Generalist robotic manipulation requires rapid sensory-motor feedback, yet real-time execution often conflicts with the heavy computational footprint of high-capacity generalist Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Coupling action generation directly to the VLM forward pass tightly ties the robot's control frequency to the scale and latency of the underlying language backbone. To resolve this bottleneck, we propose Asynchronous Robot Policies (ARP), an architecture that factors policy execution into two asynchronous computational loops operating at distinct rates: Slow Semantic Loop (Semantic Expert): Periodically processes observations through a VLM to produce a compact, fixed-dimensional semantic memory representation. Fast Action Loop (Vision-Action Expert): Predicts low-level motor control actions at a high control frequency by conditioning a lightweight policy on real-time sensory inputs and the most recently available semantic memory. title: RoboTryOn: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
summary: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.

Introduction sec:intro Robot foundation models trained on large-scale demonstrations have made substantial progress toward general-purpose robot control oneill2024oxe,octo2024,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,liu2024rdt,nvidia2025gr00t,intelligence2025pi05 , while extending them to new tasks and environments still requires additional robot demonstrations oneill2024oxe,khazatsky2024droid,bu2025agibot . Collecting such demonstrations through teleoperation requires robot hardware, a teleoperation system, and substantial operator effort zhao2023aloha,wu2024gello,chi2024umi,khazatsky2024droid . The burden is heaviest for dexterous hands, where operators must coordinate many degrees of freedom and fine-grained contacts through retargeting interfaces that are challenging to develop and operate handa2020dexpilot,qin2023anyteleop,cheng2024television,wang2024dexcap,xu2025dexumi . Alternatively, human videos offer another way to demonstrate a new task. In particular, egocentric recordings of human object manipulation already exist at internet scale and far outnumber the demonstrations teleoperation can produce, ranging from in-the-wild collections to manually annotated corpora recorded for robot learning~ goyal2017something,shan2020100doh,damen2022epickitchens,grauman2022ego4d,grauman2024egoexo4d,liu2022hoi4d,hoque2025egodex,li2025vitra,punamiya2026egoverse . They capture how people grasp and manipulate objects, including coordinated bimanual interaction, without a robot during collection. Recent works use these videos to learn transferable visual and behavioral knowledge~ nair2022r3m,yang2025egovla,luo2025beingh0,dyna2026dyna2 , or convert them into robot data through retargeting kareer2025egomimic , rendering lepert2025phantom,lepert2025masquerade,wang2026ego2robot,liu2026egoengine , or generative translation song2025mitty,ci2025h2rgrounder . However, a human video is separated from a robot demonstration by a visual gap and an action gap, and both are severe for dexterous hands liu2025immimic,punamiya2025egobridge,liu2026egoengine . In terms of appearance, human videos show a human arm and hand, whereas the policy observes a robot at deployment. Prior work narrows this gap by masking the human arm or overlaying a rendered robot, and must apply the same edit to the robot's camera stream during both training and deployment kareer2025egomimic,lepert2025phantom,lepert2025masquerade . In terms of action, the reconstructed hand pose is itself imprecise, and no exact retargeting map takes it to robot joint commands, since human and robot hands differ in morphology and kinematics handa2020dexpilot,qin2023anyteleop,kong2026retargeting . Even a perfect mapping would reproduce only the shape of the hand, not how firmly the robot must grip the object chen2025dexforce,liu2026egoengine . Our approach. We address these gaps by treating human-to-robot transfer as virtual try-on, which keeps the motion and changes the embodiment. converts a human manipulation video into a paired robot demonstration with action labels. To this end, we first generate a target robot video performing the same task in the source scene and then predict the corresponding joint-space actions with an inverse dynamics model (IDM), rather than deriving robot actions directly from reconstructed hand motion. As in keyframe-based video virtual try-on~ zuo2025dreamvvt , we autoregressively translate selected human frames into robot keyframes, and synthesize the motion between consecutive keyframes under the guidance of the human hand skeleton flow. Our generative models learn this translation from robot videos through a shared arm mask and hand skeleton interface, allowing the same conditions to be extracted from human videos at inference without paired human and robot demonstrations. We then train a policy on the synthesized robot demonstrations, enabling the robot to learn new tasks with few or no teleoperated demonstrations. Our experiments show that consistently improves policy performance when task-specific robot demonstrations are limited or unavailable. In particular, averaged over two robot embodiments, increases the success rate from 2.1 to 60.0 on out-of-domain tasks with goals, skills, and objects unseen in real robot demonstrations. It also achieves 45.9 on challenging bimanual tasks despite all teleoperated demonstrations containing only single-arm manipulation. Finally, training with demonstrations derived from human video matches the performance of training on teleoperated demonstrations alone while requiring approximately a third of the collection cost (see ). We summarize our main contributions below: [leftmargin=*,topsep=0.0em, itemsep=0.0em] We introduce , which turns an egocentric human video into a robot demonstration the way virtual try-on swaps a garment, with generative models trained on robot data alone. We show that our synthetic data bridge the visual and action gaps in human videos, removing the need for test-time visual editing and generating better action labels than retargeted actions. Through experiments on two real robots with dexterous hands over diverse out-of-domain tasks, we demonstrate that our synthesized demonstrations enable learning tasks without teleoperated demonstrations and reduce data collection costs relative to teleoperation. Related Work sec:related Learning from human videos. Human videos provide a scalable source of visual and behavioral knowledge for robot learning. Early work learns visual representations from human videos for downstream robot control nair2022r3m,majumdar2023vc1 , while recent approaches incorporate human videos into robot foundation model training to learn transferable visual and behavioral knowledge yang2025egovla,luo2025beingh0,dyna2026dyna2,nvidia2025gr00t . Another line converts human demonstrations into robot training data through motion retargeting kareer2025egomimic , often combined with rendered robot observations lepert2025phantom,lepert2025masquerade,wang2026ego2robot . Approaches based on simulation further construct digital twins to generate robot observations and refine action trajectories liu2026egoengine . Generative human-to-robot translation. Recent advances in video diffusion models have enabled direct translation of human demonstrations into robot videos. Mitty song2025mitty conditions generation on human videos and learns from paired human and robot data, including synthetically rendered pairs. H2R-Grounder ci2025h2rgrounder removes the need for paired supervision by reconstructing robot videos from inpainted backgrounds and gripper pose cues. Our approach supports multiple dexterous embodiments through shared generative models and produces demonstrations with action labels for real-world policy learning. Video synthesis and action labeling. Constructing robot demonstrations through video generation requires both temporally consistent synthesis and corresponding action labels. Video virtual try-on studies consistency when modifying a subject's appearance fang2024vivid,zuo2025dreamvvt . In particular, DreamVVT generates keyframes and uses them to guide video synthesis. We adopt this decomposition for embodiment translation and, following prior work~ baker2022vpt, du2023unipi,jang2025dreamgen , use IDMs to infer actions from the resulting videos. Method sec:method Problem Setup and Overview sec:overview Policy learning from demonstrations. We consider a teleoperated robot demonstration dataset , where each demonstration contains a visual observation , a proprioceptive state , and a robot action at each timestep , together with a task instruction . We mainly use vision-language-action models (VLAs) as our base policy , which predicts an action chunk of horizon conditioned on . Demonstrations from human video. aims to augment with demonstrations synthesized from human video to address the expensive cost of collecting real robot data. A human demonstration For simplicity, we omit the demonstration index. contains egocentric observations and the instruction . Given and a reference image of the target robot , uses a three-stage pipeline to generate a robot demonstration that follows the human motion (see ). First, an image generation model translates selected human keyframes into robot keyframes ( ). Next, a video generation model synthesizes the robot video between keyframes under the guidance of the hand skeleton ( ). Finally, an inverse dynamics model predicts the action labels from the synthesized video, and the states are then derived from the predicted actions ( ). The resulting demonstrations form synthetic data , on which we train the policy alone or together with ( ). We train the three models and the policy in the same way, as conditional flow-matching models~ lipman2023flow,liu2023rectified . We provide the details of the flow matching process in . Keyframe Translation sec:keyframe In this section, we describe how \ selects keyframes from the human demonstration and translates them into target robot keyframes. We first train the image generation model on robot demonstrations and apply it to the selected human keyframes at inference. Keyframes. We select keyframes from the wrist trajectories of the reconstructed human hands~ zhang2025hawor . A frame is selected when the speed of both wrists reaches a local minimum, where the hands are unblurred, and a wrist has moved more than a threshold from its position in the previous keyframe. We also always include the first and last frames. The resulting keyframe indices form the set . Conditioning. We condition on an arm and hand mask and a hand skeleton . As in virtual try-on methods~ choi2021vitonhd,choi2024idmvton,jiang2024fitdit,lee2025voost , we enlarge and smooth , so its outline does not reveal the embodiment it covers. The skeleton is a 2D projection of hand keypoints obtained by forward kinematics for a robot or by retargeting the reconstructed hand for a human. We define a conditioning function , which masks out the region of a frame and draws the skeleton over it. The same function gives the conditioned robot frame for training and the conditioned human frame for inference. To make the model robust to imperfect hand retargeting, we perturb and randomly drop the skeleton during training. The skeleton then provides only coarse guidance on hand position and motion, while detailed hand configuration comes from the learned prior over robot hands. Mode

title: Should the Action Expert Train the VLM? Action-Token Supervision and Gradient Routing in Mixture-of-Transformer VLAs
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly pair a pre-trained vision-language model (VLM) with a flow-matching expert that conditions its action predictions on the VLM's key-value representations. Those representations must carry information useful for control, yet the VLM was never trained for the action expert's flow-matching objective. Two signals can address this: gradients backpropagated from the expert's loss (coupling), or VLM supervision to predict discrete tokens encoding the same target actions. Prominent training recipes forgo the first, blocking expert-to-VLM gradients (insulation) to protect the VLM's existing capabilities, while also supervising it on vision-language data and action tokens. Because vision-language co-training also aims to preserve those capabilities, the additional protection provided by insulation is unclear. At the same time, insulation removes a direct signal about which features continuous action prediction requires. On the other hand, action-token supervision offers an alternative way to learn action-relevant representations, which may explain why insulation succeeds in practice. We disentangle these factors in autonomous driving and manipulation by independently varying action-token supervision and whether the expert's loss updates the VLM. In open-loop driving, insulation is competitive with coupling when action tokens are supervised; without them, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25%. When both components are trained jointly from the outset, coupling increases closed-loop driving route progress by approximately 17% with action-token supervision and 40% without it, and similarly improves robot manipulation performance under both settings. These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe.

These findings show that the value of gradient insulation depends on the VLM's action supervision and the evaluation setting, challenging insulation as a default VLA training recipe. Introduction sec:introduction Pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) bring broad perceptual, semantic, and reasoning capabilities to embodied control. Robotic control, however, requires precise continuous outputs at frequencies poorly suited to autoregressive decoding with large VLMs. Many recent vision--language--action (VLA) models therefore use Mixture-of-Transformers-style architectures liang2024mixture , pairing an autoregressive VLM with a smaller diffusion or flow-matching action expert black2024pi_0 . The VLM processes visual observations and language instructions, while the expert efficiently generates continuous action chunks conditioned on the VLM's per-layer key--value (K/V) representations intelligence2025pi_05 . This architecture leaves open a consequential training decision: should the continuous-action loss train only the expert, or also the VLM that produces its conditioning K/V cache? Allowing expert gradients to update the VLM (coupling) enables co-adaptation and can teach the backbone which information its representations must preserve for precise control. Yet it also exposes pretrained visual and linguistic features to gradients from a newly introduced, often randomly initialized expert, which may degrade the VLM's semantic and world understanding. Popular approaches therefore block the action expert's gradients from entering the VLM (insulation), either through stop-gradient or frozen-backbone training intelligence2025pi_05,driess2026knowledge . However, full-parameter fine-tuning on a narrow robot training distribution can degrade pretrained capabilities regardless of gradient routing hancock2025actionslanguagefinetuningvlms . When vision--language co-training is also used to mitigate forgetting, it is unclear whether insulation provides additional protection. Insulation is also rarely evaluated in isolation. Blocking expert gradients removes one source of action-relevant learning signal, but such systems typically supply another: they train the VLM to predict discrete action tokens pertsch2025fast , which directly supervise the behavior the expert models. Co-training on general vision--question-answering (VQA) and chain-of-thought examples may preserve the VLM's semantic capabilities, but it does not explicitly encourage representations relevant to control. In the absence of action-token supervision, insulation may therefore eliminate the only objective that directly adapts the VLM for trajectory prediction. Crucially, defining an analogous discrete proxy for continuous prediction targets is a domain-dependent design choice whose effectiveness must be established empirically. It is therefore unclear whether the reported benefits of insulation arise from gradient blocking itself or depend on this auxiliary supervision. Prior work has not isolated this interaction. Knowledge Insulation reports benefits from insulated training while supervising the VLM with FAST action tokens and vision--language objectives, but does not evaluate insulation without FAST supervision driess2026knowledge,pertsch2025fast . In contrast, Wall-OSS-0.5 reports stronger action performance from coupled training even when discrete-action and multimodal objectives are retained yu2026walloss05technicalreport . Because these systems also differ in training recipes, initialization, data, and optimization, their seemingly opposing results cannot isolate the contributions of action-token supervision and expert-to-VLM gradient flow in downstream control or determine how the two mechanisms interact. Contributions. In this work, we study how a VLA's representations are made action-relevant, and whether the two available signals---the expert's gradient and discrete action-token supervision---substitute for one another. We cross action-token supervision with expert-to-VLM gradient flow in autonomous driving and robot manipulation, under both joint training and training schedules in which one component is adapted first. Within each training schedule and action-token setting, routing comparisons hold data, architecture, optimization, and semantic co-training fixed. In open-loop driving evaluations, the two routing choices are nearly indistinguishable with action-token supervision; without it, coupling reduces trajectory-prediction error by roughly 25 . This pattern holds across training schedules and in both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations. Under joint training, coupling improves closed-loop performance regardless of supervision: driving route progress increases by approximately 17 with action tokens and 40 without them, while manipulation task progress improves under both settings. Together, these results identify action-token supervision as a factor previously entangled with gradient routing and show that VLM insulation is a conditional choice, not a default training recipe for training VLAs.
