title: PolicyIK: High-Precision Inverse Kinematics for Robot Arms with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Inverse kinematics (IK) converts end-effector pose commands into joint motion, and many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on it to act on a given arm and to transfer across embodiments. Precise IK remains laborious: redundancy and singularities complicate the inverse mapping, execution depends on hand-tuned controllers, and training data on physical robots are costly to collect. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning policy for high-precision IK. It updates joint-position references from pose feedback and observes its accumulated reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Two-scale pose errors with an error-dependent action gain resolve millimeter residuals while preserving large motions. Progress and dwell rewards teach it to both reach the tolerance and stay within it. In simulation, a single attempt by the trained PPO policy keeps the mean errors over the final second within 1 mm and 0.2° on 93.5% of held-out tasks, and a deployment protocol raises success to 98.9%. When trained directly on a physical arm with an off-policy RL learner, PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, PolicyIK executes the end-effector commands of the $π_{0.5}$ VLA policy with 95.7% success. These results show that reinforcement learning can provide high-precision inverse kinematics for robot arms. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/PolicyIK.

Code is available at . .toc mainbody Introduction sec:intro Many learned manipulation policies act on a robot arm through inverse kinematics (IK), which turns end-effector pose commands into joint motion. Vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist policies often predict end-effector poses or pose increments and leave the conversion to joint commands to an IK or operational-space controller oxe2024,octo2024,openvla2024 . Because this interface is shared across arms, the same policy can run on different robots chi2024umi,mirage2024,shadow2024,umi2024 . Such transfer delegates the feasibility and accuracy of every command to the target robot's IK. Transfer methods assume controllers that reach commanded poses within a few millimeters mirage2024 , yet transfer fails at joint limits and on motions the arm cannot follow chi2024umi,polybot2023 . IK accuracy thus carries over to every policy that acts through it. Developing and deploying a precise pose controller raises three challenges. First, the inverse mapping itself is difficult. A redundant arm can reach a pose with many joint configurations burdick1989 , and near singularities small pose corrections demand large joint motions, so numerical solvers trade accuracy for robustness and can fail even on reachable poses buss2004,deo1995,beeson2015 . Second, the realized pose depends on robot-specific execution. Finite gains, gravity, and joint limits shift where a position-controlled arm comes to rest. Controller dynamics also affect how action errors propagate during policy execution~ bronars2026tune . The controllers that compensate for these effects rely on damping factors, task weights, and gains that experts tune for each robot lynch2017,charbonneau2018,buss2005,lee2026space . Third, collecting training data on physical robots is costly, as each trial requires robot execution and a reset. We investigate reinforcement learning (RL) for this setting. An RL policy learns the mapping from pose error to joint commands through interaction with the robot's dynamics. Sampling goals from reachable configurations yields feasible goals across the workspace, and the designed reward targets the required tolerance. Prior RL controllers have reached position goals with fixed-base arms and tracked full poses with legged manipulators, with errors from several millimeters to a few centimeters jailer2021,aljalbout2024,portela2025,pake2026 , and a hybrid reaches sub-millimeter accuracy in kinematic simulation by pairing the policy with damped least squares, which supplies the final correction mpdik2025 . Reaching millimeter-level full-pose accuracy with the policy alone calls for a formulation designed around terminal precision. We present PolicyIK, a goal-conditioned RL formulation that learns high-precision IK for robot arms through a joint-position interface (Figure~ fig:control-loop ). Like closed-loop IK siciliano1990 , the policy updates a joint reference from pose feedback, but learns this update from interaction. The formulation addresses three properties of precise regulation. First, the policy accumulates its actions in the reference and observes the reference relative to the measured joints, so it can retain the offset that the position controller needs at rest. Second, pose errors enter the observation at coarse and fine scales, and an error-dependent gain shrinks actions near the goal, which resolves small residuals while preserving large motions. Third, the reward credits progress beyond the best error so far and time within tolerance, so it trains both reaching and holding. We train with PPO schulman2017ppo in parallel simulation orbit2023 and with FlashSAC kim2026flashsac on physical arms. Since every hardware transition costs robot time, a reverse curriculum and near-goal sampling focus training on the terminal phase, while a latent-alignment critic handles large-rotation detours. We evaluate PolicyIK in simulation and on a physical arm (Figure~ fig:task-overview ). On a simulated 7-DoF arm, PolicyIK reaches median errors of 0.25\,mm and and meets the 1\,mm and tolerance on 93.5 of held-out tasks in one attempt and on 98.9 with a deployment protocol. Removing any design component lowers single-attempt success by 1.8--9.2 points. Direct hardware training demonstrates the value of learning to maintain a pose after reaching it. PolicyIK achieves higher reaching and holding success than all four classical IK controllers under the same time budgets. In simulated pick-and-place, it executes the end-effector commands of ~ pi05_2025 with 95.7 success across ten adapted LIBERO-Object tasks~ libero2023 , without pick-and-place data in its training. These capabilities come with a low inference cost: an actor forward pass takes 0.035\,ms on CPU, well below the 33\,ms control period. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=3pt] We show that goal-conditioned RL formulates inverse kinematics for robot arms and can train a policy to reach and hold millimeter-level full-pose precision through a joint-position interface. We identify three design choices behind this precision: observing the joint reference relative to the measured joints, sensing pose errors at centimeter and sub-millimeter scales with smaller steps near the goal, and rewarding each new best error and every step within tolerance. Ablations show they affect reaching and holding separately. We train PolicyIK directly on two physical arms (OpenArm and xArm7) with FlashSAC kim2026flashsac , hindsight goal relabeling andrychowicz2017hindsight , and a curriculum from near-goal starts pmlr-v78-florensa17reverse to large rotations. It holds reached poses within 1 mm and more reliably than classical IK controllers, and executes a VLA policy's commands in simulated pick-and-place with 95.7 success. Related Work sec:related Inverse kinematics and task-space control. Classical approaches map pose commands to joint motion analytically, numerically, or through feedback. Closed-form solutions exist mainly for arms with special geometry diankov2010 , so general and redundant arms rely on damped least squares or constrained optimization wampler1986,deo1995,beeson2015 , and closed-loop controllers convert task-space error into joint references under joint limits and secondary objectives siciliano1990,haviland2023,rmpflow2021,fabrics2021 . These methods require tuning for each robot charbonneau2018,buss2005 and leave execution of joint motion to the robot's controller. Learned IK models fit the inverse map from sampled configurations or demonstrations ikflow2022,habekost2024,mimicik2026 and rely on numerical refinement for high accuracy cppflow2024 . In contrast, PolicyIK learns closed-loop IK from interaction with the robot's dynamics and regulates the realized pose. Reinforcement learning for reaching and pose tracking. Reinforcement learning controllers for end-effector reaching range from benchmark tasks to fixed-base arms and legged manipulators. Common multi-goal benchmarks count a reach as successful within 5\,cm of a position goal plappert2018,metaworld2019 . Policies for fixed-base arms map task-space errors to joint commands and reach position goals with errors of millimeters to centimeters jailer2021,aljalbout2024 , while whole-body controllers track full end-effector poses on legged manipulators to within a few centimeters umi2024,portela2025,pake2026 . When tighter tolerances are needed, learning is paired with a classical solver, such as damped least squares, that performs the final correction mpdik2025 . PolicyIK learns joint-reference updates for millimeter-level full-pose reaching and sustained holding, without a numerical IK solver. Learning for execution-error compensation. Residual methods add learned corrections to a conventional controller or its reference trajectory residual2019,pavlichenko2022 and build on its tuning. Integrating methods accumulate policy outputs in the commanded state to reduce steady-state error industreal2023,aljalbout2024 . Integral state augmentation exposes accumulated information for reference tracking iasa2022 . Once commands are integrated, the accumulated reference becomes part of the system state. PolicyIK observes this reference relative to the measured joints and pairs it with two-scale pose errors and error-dependent action scaling, so one policy handles both large motions and millimeter corrections. Problem Formulation sec:problem Classical IK computes a joint configuration from a goal end-effector pose, but commanding that joint target on a position-controlled arm does not guarantee that the end effector reaches the target pose: gravity, finite gains, and joint limits shift where the arm comes to rest. The controller must therefore close the loop on the pose error, drive it below the tolerance, and hold it there. We formulate this closed-loop regulation as a goal-conditioned RL problem. title: Human-to-Robot Transfer via Bridging Representation and Action Space in VLAs
comment: Accepted for Oral Presentation at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Scaling H2R. Project page: https://junhyeong-park.me/h2rb/
summary: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies provide a strong starting point for deployment, but adapting them to a target robot and environment still requires costly embodiment-specific demonstrations. Human demonstrations are far easier to collect, yet directly leveraging them is challenging due to the substantial human-robot embodiment gap, particularly when the underlying VLA has been pretrained primarily on robot data. We introduce H2RB (Human-To-Robot Bridge), a human-robot co-training framework for adapting pretrained VLA policies from unpaired human and robot demonstrations. H2RB bridges the embodiment gap at both interfaces: geometry-anchored alignment grounds human and robot observations in a compatible representation, while a decoupled-decoder tokenizer shares action latents without forcing both domains through a single action mapping. This design allows human demonstrations to provide useful behavioral supervision while retaining the rich visual, semantic, and control priors of the pretrained VLA. Across real-world tasks, H2RB substantially improves object transfer performance from 8.0 to 51.8 and enables skill transfer to score 62.7, in settings where co-train baselines totally fail to transfer human-demonstrated skills. The benefit also persists under object-placement shifts, improving out-of-distribution transfer from 6.0 to 45.3. H2RB suggests a way for human demonstrations to serve as a scalable supervision source for adapting pretrained robotic policies, reducing the dependence on costly target-robot data collection.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Pretrained robotic policies, e.g., Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla , provide a strong starting point for adapting general robotic capabilities to a target deployment environment. However, a major bottleneck remains in the collection of target robot demonstrations, as collecting such data on physical robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. It requires access to the physical platform, a data collection pipeline (e.g., teleoperation), and repeated environment resets brohan2022rt,khazatsky2024droid . Human demonstrations, in contrast, can be collected quickly and naturally without relying on dedicated teleoperation systems~ chi2024universal,qiu2025humanoid,yang2025egovla, wang2023mimicplay , using only a lightweight camera setup. Yet, directly leveraging them to adapt robot policies remains challenging due to the substantial embodiment gap between humans and robots, particularly when the pretrained policy has been trained primarily on robot data. Prior works bridge human and robot demonstrations by placing them in a common action space, either through latent actions inferred from frame transitions~ ye2025latent,chen2026villa,dai2026conla,bu2025univla,chen2025moto or through reconstructed world-space hand motion~ li2025scalable,fu2026egograsp,hoque2026egodex . While these approaches reduce the action-space mismatch across embodiments, they leave the perceptual gap largely unresolved. As a result, VLAs must map distinct human and robot observations into a shared action space, making reliable robot action prediction difficult. However, a common action space alone does not make human demonstrations compatible with a robot-pretrained VLA. Embodiment-dependent observations remain perceptually misaligned, while human and robot motions can still require different action realization dynamics. Our approach.~ Based on this insight, we introduce , a training framework that incorporates human demonstrations into pretrained VLA policies without paired human-robot trajectories. First, a geometry-anchored alignment uses wrist-fingertip geometry to ground VLM output features across embodiments, without paired demonstrations or human-to-robot observation synthesis. Second, a decoupled-decoder latent tokenizer shares action latents across embodiments while using separate decoders to avoid collapsing human and robot motion dynamics into a single action mapping. Together, these components enable human-to-robot task transfer while facilitating learning from heterogeneous human-robot experience, as illustrated in~ . We evaluate on two complementary forms of human-to-robot adaptation: within-skill object transfer and skill-level transfer. On OpenArm, where target behaviors are provided only through human demonstrations, improves object transfer from 8.0 to 51.8 and achieves a skill-transfer score of 62.7, where shared-action co-training baselines fail. Heterogeneous human-robot training across multiple embodiments further improves these scores to 57.2 and 81.7, respectively. We additionally study robot-only downstream adaptation on RB-Y1, where cross-embodiment alignment improves success from 72 to 78 under matched heterogeneous training. Together, these results suggest that learning action-relevant representations from heterogeneous experience benefits both human-to-robot transfer and downstream robot adaptation. title: Cycle WAM: Coupling Action and Video through Cycle Consistency
summary: Recent advances in video modeling have driven substantial progress in world action models (WAMs). Existing approaches exploit pretrained video priors by decoding actions from latent representations or inferring them from generated videos. The underlying link is causal: robot actions produce changes in the scene, and video observations of these changes provide evidence for inferring the actions that produced them. However, existing training formulations do not by themselves ensure that actions and their predicted visual consequences are consistent, potentially limiting the use of pretrained capabilities. We treat video and action as paired modalities linked by this causal relationship and learn their correspondence through a unified training framework designed to better exploit pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM first augments video-action co-training with bidirectional conversion to reinforce cross-modal correspondence and recover forward and inverse dynamics. It then introduces a differentiable cycle-reconstruction objective to further couple the two mappings. The resulting model supports both forward and inverse dynamics, with the potential to improve performance through more effective use of pretrained video priors. Cycle WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance among comparable methods on LIBERO-Pro and substantially improves DreamZero on DROID. Comparisons with UWM characterize its inverse-dynamics performance and show sharper visual detail in the displayed forward-dynamics predictions.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We evaluate control, conditional dynamics, training-stage effects, and physical execution on LIBERO, DROID, and real-robot tasks. Bidirectional Conversion then updates all parameters for 5,000 steps with joint/inverse/forward probabilities . Cycle uses 3,000 steps, joint/Cycle probabilities , and shared LoRA adapters with rank and scaling 32; base weights, action/state interfaces, and query embeddings remain frozen. The 5,652 episodes contain 848,036 frame-indexed window starts. At start , we sample video at , actions at , and states at , repeating the final frame at episode boundaries. Official LIBERO-90-pretrained UWM zhu2025uwm , distinct from the policy checkpoint, uses two history and two endpoint frames with DDIM; Cycle WAM uses nine two-view frames, state, and FlowUniPC. Both receive observed future video. Table~ tab:inverse-dynamics shows lower rotation error and better motion-direction agreement for Cycle WAM, while UWM has lower aggregate action MSE. These component-specific strengths do not imply uniform superiority. The historical DreamZero row uses different windows and a longer horizon. Inverse prediction receives future video, so its ranking need not match autonomous control. Forward dynamics Cycle WAM improves reconstruction error, PSNR, SSIM, and Frame FID (Table~ tab:forward-dynamics ); its unrounded MSE is 9.65 lower despite the displayed tie. Sharper contours and textures in Fig.~ fig:qualitative agree with these metrics, although object placement and view composition differ from GT. This comparison does not measure temporal consistency or action-intervention sensitivity, or isolate Cycle's contribution. Training-Stage Ablations sec:matched-controls Training-stage variants Bidirectional Conversion improves the selected-condition control average (Table~ tab:ablation ). Cycle further improves it through Spatial-S and Goal-T gains, with declines on Spatial-T and Goal-S. Different budgets and update types prevent isolating each objective's contribution. Complete coverage limits these gains: Standard performance falls after Bidirectional Conversion and is not recovered by Cycle, while aggregate Pro performance changes little. Control improvements are therefore not uniform. Matched continuations From the same w/o Cycle checkpoint, we match 3,000-step rank-32 LoRA runs in data, noise, optimizer, and three-pass computation. The control replaces converted actions with recorded actions, changing both conditioning and gradient flow. Runs use 14 or 111 instructions, 10 demonstrations each, seeds 42--44, and a shared 20-task diagnostic whose separation from training is unverified. With the larger task set, paired intervals do not resolve differences in inverse prediction, reconstruction, joint-action consistency, or action-sensitivity margins. With the smaller set, video reconstruction and both forward-loss margins favor control under unadjusted intervals; the others are inconclusive. Matched training thus shows no consistent additional Cycle benefit and does not separately isolate gradient coupling. Real-Robot Experiments sec:real-robot Cycle WAM completes the task in three of five evaluated real-world scenes, whereas DreamZero completes none (Table~ tab:real-robot ). This provides initial comparative evidence of physical execution, while two scenes remain unsuccessful for Cycle WAM. These scene-level counts do not establish repeated-trial reliability. Fig.~ fig:real-robot illustrates coordinated arm and gripper motion: the remote control is placed inside the basket, and the lemon is transported in the opposite direction and released above it.

title: DreamX: Video Diffusion Model is a Universal Latent Action Learner
summary: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
full_text: sec:method sec:method_overview Given a video and instruction, uses learnable queries to extract compact latent actions from a pretrained video diffusion backbone's spatiotemporal features. Future-frame reconstruction conditioned on these latent actions and the initial frame provides generative supervision (Sec.~ sec:pretraining ). The learned representation enables video and action transfer with a target initial frame or robot state (Sec.~ sec:transfer ). For control, the policy predicts compact codes and low-level actions without generating future video (Sec.~ sec:latentwam ). Preliminaries: Video Diffusion Models sec:prelim We build on Cosmos-Predict2.5~ cosmos , a pretrained video diffusion transformer. A causal video autoencoder compresses a clip into latent frames, , where encodes only the initial frame. These frames are patchified into spatial tokens and jointly modeled through spatiotemporal attention. Through video pretraining, the model learns spatiotemporal priors that capture spatial context and temporal relationships across the clip. Conditioned on an initial frame and an additional signal such as text, collectively denoted by , the model learns future-video generation through flow matching. Given clean video latents and noise , we form , with , and minimize where predicts the flow velocity. By optimizing this objective over large-scale video data, the model acquires a generative prior over scene appearance and plausible dynamics. When the initial frame supplies the scene's appearance, additional conditioning steers how the scene evolves. We exploit this property by using latent actions to steer future-frame reconstruction, whose objective supervises what the latent actions encode. Learning Universal Latent Actions from Video Diffusion Priors sec:pretraining adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone for two complementary roles: encoding observed dynamics into latent actions and supervising them through future-frame reconstruction to encourage separation of motion from visual appearance. Building on Sec.~ sec:prelim , we introduce learnable queries that read out the video representations to summarize observed dynamics as latent actions, while the decoder reconstructs the future from these latent actions and the initial frame. Leveraging a video diffusion backbone for both the encoder and decoder allows its generative prior to account for visual appearance, encouraging the latent action tokens to focus on motion. uses pretrained video model itself to encode latent actions. As shown in Figure~ fig:pipeline (a), we append learnable query tokens to the video token sequence and process them jointly through the backbone's spatiotemporal attention. We assign a group of query tokens to each latent frame . Once contextualized by the video, their output features form the latent-action group . All groups are extracted in a single forward, where is the encoder and is the language instruction supplied through the backbone's original cross-attention. As shown in Figure~ fig:pipeline (b), query-to-video attention is frame-causal, so directly attends to , while query-to-query attention is unrestricted. This lets the queries encode temporally grounded motion from the pretrained dynamics, with query-layout settings in Appendix~ app:pretraining_details . Encoding from video alone may retain scene- and embodiment-specific visual cues. We therefore use the same pretrained video backbone as the encoder to supervise latent actions through future-frame reconstruction, conditioned on and without text. As provides scene appearance and the pretrained generative prior captures plausible evolution, is encouraged to encode the motion needed to explain the future, rather than visual cues already available to the decoder. As shown in Figure~ fig:pipeline (a), the decoder generates future frames conditioned on , concatenated with the video tokens along the temporal sequence. When action labels are available, it also takes the proprioceptive state and decodes action chunks as an auxiliary task: Under the decoder attention mask in Figure~ fig:pipeline (b), latent-action queries serve solely as conditioning signals and do not attend to any tokens. The video and action streams attend to these queries without attending to each other. Specifically, video frame attends to the query prefix , while action chunk attends to . We train both the encoder and the decoder end-to-end with the standard flow-matching objective applied to video and action generation as Eq.~ eq:stage-a-loss , with for video clips without action labels: Motion Transfer via Latent Actions sec:transfer Building upon the rich generative prior from the video diffusion backbone, learns latent actions that capture motion transferable across embodiments, even though cross-embodiment transfer is not an explicit training objective. This capability emerges from the pretraining described in the previous section and requires no additional training. The auxiliary robot action branch further encourages the latent actions to encode action-relevant cues and further enables motion extracted from a source video to be decoded into continuous actions executable by a target embodiment. Given a source video, we extract its latent actions using the frozen encoder, , which captures the motion to be transferred. As shown in Figure~ fig:downstream (a), we reuse the same in two complementary ways. For video transfer, we combine it with a target initial frame and use the frozen decoder to generate a target video that reproduces the source motion under the target scene and embodiment. For action transfer, we instead combine with the target robot state and decode the same motion into executable low-level actions, Thus, the shared latent action realizes the same underlying motion either as a generated video in a new domain or as executable actions on a target robot, without paired source--target datasets. Policy Learning with Compact Latent Actions sec:latentwam As a downstream application, we examine whether the latent actions learned by can serve as prediction targets for an observation-conditioned robot policy. Whereas motion transfer uses latent actions extracted from a source demonstration, the policy predicts them from the current observation and instruction. To this end, we repurpose the same pretrained video backbone used by to predict latent actions in place of future video~ kim2026compact . Although is compact in token count, each token retains the full backbone width, making direct diffusion high-dimensional~ dcae15 . We therefore compress into a low-dimensional code first, which serves as the policy's prediction target. Following~ fae , we learn a variational bottleneck that compresses each latent-action token from backbone width to while preserving the token layout, as shown in Figure~ fig:downstream (b). With the encoder frozen, we train the bottleneck using feature reconstruction and KL regularization. After training, we use its posterior mean to obtain deterministic compact codes for policy learning. The formulation and implementation details are provided in Appendix~ app:fae_details . With the learned bottleneck frozen, the compact codes serve as prediction targets for the policy . As shown in Figure~ fig:downstream (b), the policy generates these codes from the current frame and instruction , while a separate DiT action head predicts low-level actions conditioned on the generator's latent-action features, the same observation and instruction, and the state : Action tokens attend to latent-action features, but not vice versa. This separation allows human videos to supervise latent-code prediction without robot action labels, while robot demonstrations additionally supervise low-level action prediction. We train the policy with where both terms follow Eq.~ eq:fm-loss , applied to compact codes and low-level actions respectively, with for human videos without action labels. Further details are provided in Appendix~ app:policy_implementation .

title: 3DGS-VBench+ and 3DGSV-Assessor: A Multi-Dimensional Subjective Benchmark and a Reference-Flexible Objective Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting Video Quality Assessment
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis (NVS), but its heavy storage makes compression essential, and both training and compression introduce representation-specific distortions. Since generative compression in many methods treats geometric and color attributes via different parameters, it can induce dimension-specific distortions, motivating multi-dimensional assessment. Moreover, real-world captures generally lack an aligned ground-truth video for a synthesized, continuous camera trajectory, leaving only sparse captured views as references. To enable multi-dimensional quality assessment of 3DGS videos with scarce aligned references, we first present 3DGS-VBench+, a large-scale subjective video quality assessment (VQA) benchmark comprising 3{,}036 3DGS reconstructions, each paired with a rendered video, across 11 real-world and 22 synthetic scenes, generated by 6 representative compression algorithms at systematically designed levels and annotated with 9{,}108 MOSs covering overall, geometry, and color quality. Based on 3DGS-VBench+, we propose 3DGSV-Assessor, a reference-flexible, large multimodal framework that scores all three dimensions in one generation pass and fuses a ranking-based reference cue into the frozen regressor through a bounded gate, supporting both reduced-reference (RR) and no-reference (NR) assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art correlation with human perception on 3DGS-VBench+ and strong zero-shot generalization to other NVS benchmarks. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/YukeXing/3DGSV-Assessor.
full_text: 3DGS-VBench+ and 3DGSV-Assessor: A Multi-Dimensional Subjective Benchmark and a Reference-Flexible Objective Model for 3D Gaussian Splatting Video Quality Assessment Yuke Xing, William Gordon, Jiarui Wang, Yujie Zhang, Guangtao Zhai,~ and Yiling Xu,~ Yuke Xing, Jiarui Wang, Guangtao Zhai and Yiling Xu are with the School of Information Science and Electronic Engineering, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai 200240, China (e-mail: xingyuke-v, wangjiarui, zhaiguangtao, yl.xu @sjtu.edu.cn). 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis (NVS), but its heavy storage makes compression essential, and both training and compression introduce representation-specific distortions. Since generative compression in many methods treats geometric and color attributes via different parameters, it can induce dimension-specific distortions, motivating multi-dimensional assessment. Moreover, real-world captures generally lack an aligned ground-truth video for a synthesized, continuous camera trajectory, leaving only sparse captured views as references. To enable multi-dimensional quality assessment of 3DGS videos with scarce aligned references, we first present 3DGS-VBench+, a large-scale subjective video quality assessment (VQA) benchmark comprising 3 , 036 3DGS reconstructions, each paired with a rendered video, across 11 real-world and 22 synthetic scenes, generated by 6 representative compression algorithms at systematically designed levels and annotated with 9 , 108 MOSs covering overall, geometry, and color quality. Based on 3DGS-VBench+, we propose 3DGSV-Assessor, a reference-flexible, large multimodal framework that scores all three dimensions in one generation pass and fuses a ranking-based reference cue into the frozen regressor through a bounded gate, supporting both reduced-reference (RR) and no-reference (NR) assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art correlation with human perception on 3DGS-VBench+ and strong zero-shot generalization to other NVS benchmarks. The dataset and code will be released at . 3D Gaussian Splatting, video quality assessment, benchmark, compression, large language model Introduction ovel View Synthesis (NVS) seeks to reconstruct complete scenes from a limited set of captured viewpoints and render images from arbitrary novel perspectives. The field has progressed rapidly from neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ nerf to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3DGS , which replaces implicit volume rendering with an explicit set of anisotropic Gaussians, thereby achieving real-time, high-fidelity rendering~ 3DGSsurvey . However, this explicit form comes at the price of heavy storage footprints that limit practical use, motivating a wave of state-of-the-art (SOTA) 3DGS variants~ Scaffold-GS,HAC,LightGaussian,CompGS,C3dgs,Compact-3DGS that embed compression directly into the reconstruction pipeline. Despite this significant progress, 3DGS is still far from visually flawless: its training and compression introduce characteristic distortions~ NVS-SQA,ENeRF-QA,3DGS-IEval-15K . Since human evaluation is expensive and inefficient, it is important to develop reliable 3DGS video quality assessment (VQA) metrics that align well with human perception, both to judge the perceptual quality of a reconstructed scene and to guide downstream applications. Traditional metrics such as PSNR and SSIM~ PSNR remain widely used for NVS evaluation, despite their limited correlation with perceived 3DGS quality~ NVS-SQA,GSC-QA,ENeRF-QA,3DGS-IEval-15K . Developing a VQA metric tailored to 3DGS requires addressing three key challenges. First, the unique representation of 3DGS introduces characteristic artifacts, such as structural omissions, floating and fogging~ 3DGS-IEval-15K,ENeRF-QA . Some of these, such as flickering caused by uneven fitting across training and novel views, further manifest as temporal instability that only a continuous viewing path can expose~ NVS-SQA,ENeRF-QA,sparse-view-3dgs . Second, 3DGS compression can affect geometric and color fidelity differently, making an overall quality score alone insufficient. Many 3DGS compression methods separately control the compression of geometric attributes (e.g., scale and rotation) and color attributes (e.g., spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients), resulting in different degrees of geometric and color degradation. These differences motivate separate geometry and color assessments alongside an overall quality judgment, as illustrated in Fig.~ figure:teasor1 . Third, reference information for 3DGS VQA is often limited and varies across practical scenarios. Scenes are reconstructed from discrete captured views but may be rendered along arbitrary, user-chosen trajectories, for which aligned ground-truth videos are generally unavailable. Full-reference (FR) assessment is therefore often impractical, whereas no-reference (NR) assessment is the common case, and reduced-reference (RR) assessment is feasible because a captured training view can accompany the model as a weak reference at marginal cost. Together, these challenges call for a single, multi-dimensional, reference-flexible VQA model that captures 3DGS-specific distortions, exploits the weak reference when available, and remains robust in its absence. Developing and validating such a model requires a suitable subjective quality benchmark. However, current NVS VQA benchmarks exhibit three key limitations, as summarized in Table~ tab:relate : (1) Insufficient scale. Most existing datasets contain fewer than 500 videos, largely due to high reconstruction training costs, limiting their support for learning perceptually robust and generalizable models. (2) Limited distortion coverage. Few benchmarks systematically cover different compression strategies and parameter levels, resulting in limited diversity of compression-induced distortions. (3) Coarse annotation granularity. Existing benchmarks provide only overall quality scores, leaving geometric and color quality assessment without dedicated subjective supervision. To address these gaps, we first present 3DGS-VBench+, a large-scale, multi-dimensional subjective VQA benchmark for compressed 3DGS. It contains 3 , 036 3DGS models reconstructed from 11 real-world and 22 synthetic scenes taken from mainstream multi-view datasets~ Mip-NeRF-360,Tanks-Temples,Deep-Blending,ENeRF-QA . Six representative compression algorithms~ Scaffold-GS,HAC,LightGaussian,CompGS,C3dgs,Compact-3DGS are applied at systematically designed levels, spanning a broad and controlled range of distortion types and strengths. Each model is rendered into a video along an orbital camera trajectory around the scene. Through a subjective study, we collect mean opinion scores (MOSs) for the overall, geometry, and color dimensions, giving 9 , 108 MOSs in total, and we verify the reliability of the dataset and the diversity of its content. Building on 3DGS-VBench+, we propose 3DGSV-Assessor, a large multimodal model (LMM)-based framework for all-in-one, multi-dimensional 3DGS VQA that supports both NR and RR assessment through three stages. Stage~1 builds the foundation: an NR regressor that adapts a vision-language backbone to score all three quality dimensions jointly in a single generation pass, and stands alone as a complete NR assessor whenever no reference is available. Stage~2 brings the reference in: it treats a captured training view used for reconstruction as a weak reference. Supervised by human scores, it learns a cue that encourages higher-rated renderings of each scene to have greater embedding similarity to the reference, without requiring pixel-level alignment. Stage~3 makes the reference optional rather than required: a bounded gate folds the cue into the frozen regressor to refine its calibrated scores when a reference is available and reverts to the Stage-1 prediction otherwise, so a single model supports both the RR and NR assessment. On 3DGS-VBench+, 3DGSV-Assessor surpasses traditional metrics, deep VQA models, and recent LMM-based assessors on all three dimensions, and it transfers zero-shot to other NVS quality assessment benchmarks. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We construct 3DGS-VBench+, a large-scale, multi-dimensional subjective VQA benchmark for compressed 3DGS, comprising 3 , 036 rendered videos across 33 scenes and 6 compression algorithms, annotated with MOSs for overall, geometry, and color dimensions. Extending the preliminary conference version 3DGS-VBench~ 3DGS-VBench , this work adds 22 synthetic scenes to the original 11 real-world scenes, refines the distortion-level design for each algorithm, and expands the single overall dimension into three fine-grained dimensions. These extensions grow the benchmark from 660 to 3,036 models and their rendered videos. The annotation volume grows correspondingly, from 660 to 9,108 MOSs. We propose 3DGSV-Assessor, the first multi-dimensional, reference-flexible VQA metric tailored to 3DGS. This LMM-based framework jointly scores the overall, geometry, and color dimensions, and exploits a captured view of the scene as a weak reference through a bounded gating mechanism, supporting both RR and NR assessment in a single model. Extensive experiments show that 3DGSV-Assessor achieves SOTA correlation with human perception on 3DGS-VBench+ under both RR and NR settings, and generalizes well to other NVS quality assessment benchmarks. Related Work Quality Assessment Databases for NVS Quality assessment research for NVS spans both image-level and video-level evaluation, as summarized in Table~ tab:relate . On the IQA side, NVS-QA NVS-QA introduces a benchmark covering NeRF and 3DGS pipelines with 65 image samples. 3DGS-IEval-15K+ 3DGSI-Assessor,3DGS-IEval-15K establishes the first large-scale 3DGS IQA dataset comprising 15,200 images rendered from 10 real-world scenes across 6 representative compression algorithms with multi-dimensional MOS annotations. In parallel, the VQA branch of NVS evaluation shifts from NeRF studies toward 3DGS-centered benchmarks. NeRF-QA NeRF-QA and NeRF-VSQA NeRF-VSQA provide subjective quality assessment datasets containing 48 and 88 videos, respectively. FFV FFV adopts a pairwise comparison protocol over 220 samples. ENeRF-QA ENeRF-QA contributes systematic distortion modeling by leveraging NeRF compression pipelines across 440 sequences and characterizing nine NeRF-specific distortion categories. For 3DGS content, GSC-QA GSC-QA examines a single 3DGS compression scheme with 120 samples, GS-QA GS-QA offers comparative evaluation between 3DGS and NeRF over 64 samples, and NVS-QA NVS-QA contributes an additional 65 video samples alongside its image counterpart. However, existing 3DGS VQA datasets exhibit three key limitations: few systematically design compression parameters to cover diverse distortion types and severity levels; most contain fewer than 500 samples; and all provide only overall MOS, lacking the multi-dimensional annotations necessary for fine-grained video screening and downstream 3DGS optimization. To address these gaps, we present 3DGS-VBench+, which contains 3 , 036 compressed 3DGS video sequences with three-dimensional MOS annotations covering overall, geometry, and color quality, constituting the largest 3DGS VQA dataset to date and the first to provide multi-dimensional subjective labels for 3DGS video content. Quality Assessment Metrics for NVS Many video quality assessment models have been proposed in the literature. Learning-based VQA models (e.g., VSFA~ VSFA , SimpleVQA~ simpleVQA , FAST-VQA~ FAST-VQA ) learn quality-aware representations to predict overall video quality but do not explicitly provide separate geometry and color scores in their original formulations, which is crucial for 3DGS quality monitoring. LMM-based models~ Qwen2.5-VL,GLM-4.1V,InternVL3 offer strong visual understanding and the flexibility to report multiple dimensions, yet they remain limited in their sensitivity to lo

title: Predicting Void Points in Self-Occluding Forest Volumes
summary:
Synthetic Aperture Imaging (SAI) enables drones to observe forest canopies by warping and averaging multiple displaced views at a common depth. However, occlusion is suppressed rather than eliminated, causing poorly observed regions to appear occupied and leading to systematic biomass overestimation. The Deep Forest project cannot distinguish reconstruction artifacts from real vegetation because its training data relies on measured reflectance points, excluding empty space and preventing the network from learning explicit occupancy boundaries.
  This thesis addresses the problem by modifying training labels rather than the imaging process. Each simulated scene is rendered twice: as a 9x9 grid of top-down captures for focal-stack generation and as 550 depth-clipped slabs derived from scene geometry to provide occupancy labels, explicitly representing void space as a negative class. A Gazebo pipeline generates procedural forest stands containing 80-200 trees across three species. A pretrained Pix2Pix model translates rendered RGB images into a synthetic near-infrared band, and Light Field Rendering produces aligned focal stacks of 550 planes across three channels.
  Four architectures were evaluated on a held-out scene. The plain 2D U-Net achieved an IoU of 0.6290, outperforming the volumetric 3D U-Net (0.5707). Established reconstruction methods performed substantially worse: COLMAP achieved 0.3446 and DepthAnything3 0.2959, both after their respective optimal dilation sweeps. An RGB-input variant of the volumetric architecture achieved the highest IoU of 0.6514 without dilation or per-scene calibration. These results highlight the limitations of conventional reconstruction methods, which recover visible surfaces but struggle to infer occupancy within closed canopies.
full_text: 28 Predicting Void Points in Self-Occluding Forest Volumes Improving the DeepForest approach with Void Point Volumes ccc Benjamin Bachmayr & Mohamed Youssef & Oliver Bimber Institute of Computer Graphics\\ Johannes Kepler University Linz, Austria October 2026 sec:abstract-en Synthetic Aperture Imaging (SAI) lets a camera drone see into a forest canopy by warping many displaced views onto a common depth and averaging them. Occlusion is suppressed this way, but it is not removed. A position deep inside a canopy that only few camera rays ever reached still receives a value during reconstruction, and that value looks like real matter to any filter working on intensity alone. Aggregating occupied voxels over a stand therefore overestimates biomass in one direction only. The learning-based pipeline of the Deep Forest project cannot tell the two apart, because its training pairs are anchored on points that carry a measured reflectance. Empty air produces no such anchor and is dropped from the training set, so the network is never asked the question it is later expected to answer. This thesis changes the labels rather than the imaging. Each simulated scene is rendered twice: once as the grid of top-down captures that becomes the focal stack the network sees, and once as 550 depth-clipped slabs that read occupancy straight off the scene geometry. Void space becomes an explicit negative class instead of a gap. A Gazebo pipeline generates procedural stands of 80 to 200 trees across three species, a pre-trained Pix2Pix generator translates the rendered RGB into a synthetic near-infrared band, and all three channels are pushed through Light Field Rendering into aligned focal stacks of 550 planes. Four architectures were compared on a held-out scene, and the ordering does not follow the architectural progression. The plain 2D U-Net scores highest at an IoU of 0.6290, ahead of the volumetric 3D U-Net at 0.5707. Against established reconstruction methods the gap is wide. COLMAP peaks at 0.3446 and DepthAnything3 at 0.2959, each after its own best dilation sweep, while an RGB-input variant of the volumetric architecture reaches 0.6514 with neither dilation nor any per-scene calibration. Both baselines fail for structural reasons rather than through poor tuning: they reconstruct visible surfaces, and the interior of a closed canopy offers none. No per-voxel reference exists for any real capture, so the transfer to real drone data is described qualitatively and its accuracy remains unmeasured. sec:acknowledgements sec:toc figures/ resources/images/ 1 chap:intro This chapter introduces the motivation behind the thesis, identifies the specific research gap in current literature, and outlines the core objectives and contributions. Background and Motivation sec:intro_bg Remote sensing enables quantitative ecological monitoring. Estimating forest attributes like canopy structure (the spatial arrangement of the uppermost branches and leaves) and biomass (the total mass of living plant material) dictates the accuracy of global carbon cycle models asner2010highres . Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) and Structure-from-Motion (SfM) photogrammetry schoenberger2016sfm routinely capture forest topologies. They fail, however, in heavily self-occluded environments. The layered arrangement of dense foliage blocks line-of-sight for both optical and active sensors. This physical occlusion leaves lower canopy layers and underlying terrain entirely unsampled. The result is shadowing. Critical biomass estimates are skewed by these incomplete data representations. The problem is geometric, not one of sensor quality. In a closed broadleaf canopy only a small part of the sky is visible from the forest floor. A camera ray that enters such a canopy stops at the first leaf it meets. A better sensor does not help here, because the missing information was never carried by any ray that reached it. The only way out is to combine many rays that entered the canopy through different gaps. Synthetic Aperture Imaging (SAI) does exactly that kurmi2019statistical . By aggregating multiple observations from displaced aerial viewpoints, SAI synthetically expands the imaging aperture. This achieves high-resolution capture with a narrow depth of field youssef2025deepforest . The system computationally refocuses on specific depth planes. Partial occlusions in the foreground are blurred out, allowing the sensor to effectively look through gaps in the canopy. Multi-perspective reflectance data is merged into a dense volumetric representation. This makes SAI highly effective for structurally complex forests where standard single-view approaches yield only surface measurements. The idea behind it is simple. A leaf that hides a target from one camera position does not hide it from a position two meters to the side. Averaging multiple views keeps the target sharp and smears the leaf across the image. With the 81 views used here the leaf only adds a weak haze while the target stays in place. Occlusion is therefore not removed but suppressed, and the suppression gets better as the number of views and the width of the aperture grow kurmi2019statistical . Hardware flexibility is another distinct advantage. While LiDAR relies on single-wavelength laser pulses, SAI processes image streams from passive sensors. Low-cost RGB sensors (regular cameras) or off-the-shelf multispectral cameras are sufficient. Capturing broad spectral ranges allows differentiation between vegetation types. Shifts in near-infrared reflectance indicate plant physiology and stress levels---metrics hard to capture with standard LiDAR. A drone with one machine-vision camera flying a grid pattern is enough to produce the input data, which keeps a survey cheap compared to airborne LiDAR. Despite this capacity for penetration, SAI does not eliminate self-occlusion. Overlapping leaves, twigs, and branches create deep void spaces that no camera angle can observe. During volumetric reconstruction, these void regions can manifest as structured artifacts. The DeepForest framework predicts noisy values at those areas youssef2025deepforest . A reconstructed canopy might appear physically continuous where empty space exists. This corrupts downstream pipelines. Vegetation detection, instance segmentation, and subsequent biomass calculations become highly error-prone. Filtering out these void areas would make it possible to utilize SAI data in forestry. Void regions are not random noise, which makes them a problem. Structures can appear where the integration of many views gives a consistent but wrong reflectance value, so they can look like real matter to any filter that works on intensity alone. A voxel deep inside the canopy that no camera ever saw still gets a value, because the integration averages whatever the contributing rays happened to hit. That value usually sits in the middle of the intensity range, and it changes slowly from voxel to voxel. Both properties are the ones a classical filter uses to decide that something is a real surface. The DeepForest Context and Identified Gap sec:intro_gap The DeepForest framework youssef2025deepforest established a learning-based baseline for processing dense forest environments from SAI preprocessed aerial imagery. It applies 3D Convolutional Neural Networks generated focal stacks after passing it through the Point-Spread-Function as a transformation. This demonstrated that data-driven interpretation of heavily occluded canopies outperforms deterministic geometric rendering. Natural vegetative scenes are highly irregular. Learned feature extractors handle this self-occluding complexity more robustly than classical filtering techniques. The goal of the DeepForest network determines the training data. The task is reflectance estimation, and a reflectance target has to be anchored on a voxel that carries a measured value. Empty air carries none, and neither does the inside of a tree trunk. Both are therefore outside the training distribution. This follows from the task. A regression target needs a measured value to regress toward, so dropping the unsampled positions is necessary for a reflectance estimator. The consequence is that the network is never asked the question this thesis asks, which is whether a given position contains matter at all. At inference time it still returns a reflectance value everywhere, including at the positions it saw no example of, and nothing in the training says what that value should be there. The DeepForest paper pairs the network output with data from SfM techniques partly for this reason, to make the resulting renders easier to read. For a downstream consumer that matters, because empty canopy gaps still carry values that read as weak returns. Anything that aggregates over the volume then counts them. Estimates for carbon sequestration (the biological process of capturing and long-term storing atmospheric carbon dioxide within plant matter) grow with the number of voxels counted as vegetation, so an error of this kind does not cancel out over a large area. NDVI is more sensitive still, since it is a ratio of the red and near-infrared bands and gets unstable wherever both bands are small. Separating matter from empty air therefore has to happen before any product built on top of the volume can be trusted. That separation is a classification task and not a regression task. Void labels are not a new idea in this setting. A dual-head variant that predicted reflectance and void points from one network was tried by the DeepForest authors and did not reach a usable result ( ). The published framework does estimate void points, but only the ones above the top vegetation layer, and it does so through photogrammetric depth reconstruction rather than through the network youssef2025deepforest . Void regions below the canopy are named there as an open problem. No accuracy is reported for that filtering step, so there is no learned void result to measure against. What this work proposes is to separate the two. Void estimation becomes a task of its own, with its own labels and its own loss, and no reflectance objective shares the network or influences the architecture. Two properties of the problem suggest that a supervised formulation should work. First, void space usually has a distinct lack the sharp intensity change that a real structures would produces when the focal plane crosses them. Second, that signature is spread across neighboring depth planes, so it is easier to identify if a system has access to many layers. A convolutional neural network with a receptive field that covers the depth axis can use both. This is the observation the present work builds on. Thesis Objectives and Contributions sec:intro_obj This thesis, titled Predicting Void Points in Self-Occluding Forest Volumes, introduces a 3D Convolutional Neural Network formulation trained explicitly on data containing zero-reflectance voxels. A semi-realistic synthetic data pipeline leverages Gazebo physics simulations derived from the DeepForest framework youssef2025deepforest coupled with NIR-GAN donike2025nir to generate paired training data (detailed in ). title: Phase-DGS: Phase-guided Dynamic Gaussian Splatting from Unsynchronized Multi-view Video
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://oc-dev74.github.io/Phase-DGS/
summary: Spatiotemporal scene reconstruction with Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS) fundamentally depends on perfect temporal synchronization across all cameras, an assumption rarely achievable in practice. Industry-standard synchronization requires expensive specialized hardware and complex setup, while data-driven alternatives including audio-based alignment, geometry matching, and pose tracking remain limited by restrictive environmental or scene-specific assumptions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Phase-DGS, a framework that replaces conventional timestamps with a semantic phase representing each frame's inherent state within the underlying motion cycle. Frames capturing the same motion state share the same phase regardless of which camera records them or when, naturally establishing spatiotemporal correspondence across unsynchronized cameras. We validate Phase-DGS under temporal offsets, frame drops, and camera freezes, achieving up to +8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines while enabling seamless integration with existing DGS backbones including RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS.
full_text: Spatiotemporal scene reconstruction with Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS) fundamentally depends on perfect temporal synchronization across all cameras, an assumption rarely achievable in practice. Industry-standard synchronization requires expensive specialized hardware and complex setup, while data-driven alternatives including audio-based alignment, geometry matching, and pose tracking remain limited by restrictive environmental or scene-specific assumptions. To overcome these limitations, we propose Phase-DGS, a framework that replaces conventional timestamps with a semantic phase representing each frame's inherent state within the underlying motion cycle. Frames capturing the same motion state share the same phase regardless of which camera records them or when, naturally establishing spatiotemporal correspondence across unsynchronized cameras. We validate Phase-DGS under temporal offsets, frame drops, and camera freezes, achieving up to +8.5 dB PSNR improvement over baselines while enabling seamless integration with existing DGS backbones including RealTime-4DGS and FreeTimeGS. Introduction In recent years, radiance field representations such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ nerf2,nerf1,nerf3 and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs1,3dgs3,3dgs2 have been extended to dynamic scenes, leading to Dynamic NeRF (DNeRF) and Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS), which have emerged as a leading paradigm for spatiotemporal scene reconstruction. The latest of these methods~ dnerf2,dnerf1,ftgs,4dgs reconstruct complex real-world scenes with striking realism, enabling applications spanning from autonomous navigation to immersive content creation. However, such results come with a prerequisite: perfect temporal synchronization across all cameras, with each camera capturing the scene at exactly the same instant, frame-by-frame~ syncnerf,synctrack,sync_learning2 . Without such synchronization, observations from different viewpoints no longer correspond to the same scene instant, making it ill-posed to learn a consistent radiance field under a shared timestamp. This spatiotemporal incoherence inevitably produces floaters, severe ghosting, and geometric distortion in rendered views. A straightforward approach is to enforce camera synchronization during the capture stage through standardized solutions, providing the radiance field with already-aligned frames that guarantee spatiotemporal coherence. Trigger-based methods such as Genlock~ genlock3, genlock2, genlock1 synchronize all camera shutters via a master sync signal, achieving high precision. However, depending on the capture environment, trigger signals can be degraded by attenuation and noise, and maintaining high-quality synchronization requires expensive specialized hardware and complex wiring. Protocol-based methods such as the Precision Time Protocol (PTP)~ PTP and Network Time Protocol (NTP)~ NTP avoid dedicated wiring and offer synchronization at reasonable cost, but rely heavily on network bandwidth and stability. When transmission delays or packet losses occur, frames can be dropped, or cameras may suffer temporal drift in which their time axes gradually diverge from one another. Beyond capture-stage synchronization, recent works have explored training radiance fields with improved spatiotemporal coherence by using cues extracted from the captured data itself. Audio-based alignment methods~ sync_audio5, sync_audio3, sync_audio2, sync_audio1, sync_audio4 synchronize cameras by matching audio signals across microphones. However, they rely on a carefully controlled acoustic environment, a condition that rarely holds in open-capture settings. Geometry- and feature-matching methods~ sync_feature1, sync_feature3, sync_feature2b, sync_feature2c estimate the degree of unsynchrony by finding spatiotemporal correspondences across views, but they struggle with weak scene texture or large viewpoint differences. Human- and pose-tracking approaches~ sync_human3, sync_human5, sync_human1, sync_human2, sync_human4 align frames by tracking human body poses across cameras, but such reliance restricts their use to human-centric scenarios where a person remains visible across all frames. Reconstruction-coupled methods~ syncnerf, synctrack, sync_learning2 jointly optimize sub-frame-level temporal misalignment together with the radiance field while most assign only a single offset per camera. Furthermore, these methods require camera pose information, which is typically obtained from synchronized data or provided as known calibration in the dataset. In unsynchronized recordings, however, temporal misalignment makes accurate camera pose estimation difficult. Instead of estimating absolute temporal offsets to synchronize videos, we infer an inherent semantic phase for each image that represents its position within the dynamic instance. Based on this idea, we propose Phase-DGS, a framework that integrates a phase extraction module into 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) to learn a radiance field with high spatiotemporal coherence, where images sharing the same phase naturally establish spatiotemporal correspondence regardless of which camera captures them or when. As shown in Fig.~ fig:sample1 , even when cameras are unsynchronized and their frame indices no longer correspond to the same instant, our phase extraction module assigns the same inherent semantic phase to images capturing the same motion state, such as the "jumping" pose, across different cameras. The estimated phases then replace absolute timestamps as input to 4DGS, allowing it to reconstruct spatiotemporally coherent rendered images. Its modular design further enables plug-and-play integration with state-of-the-art 4DGS backbones, as validated on RealTime-4DGS~ 4dgs and FreeTimeGS~ ftgs . Experimentally, we validate that the proposed method optimizes 4DGS with enhanced spatiotemporal coherence under various frame-level errors, including temporal offsets, frame drops, and camera freezes. Our method achieves up to +8.5 dB improvement in PSNR over baseline methods under unsynchronized conditions. Related Works Existing synchronization approaches fall into several categories, each with its own limitations. Hardware- and software-based methods such as Genlock, Timecode, and PTP offer high precision but provide no post-hoc correction for timing errors induced by signal drift, and their cost remains a barrier to practical deployment. Audio-based methods~ sync_audio5, sync_audio3, sync_audio1,sync_audio2,sync_audio4 align videos through shared acoustic events but rely on a controlled acoustic environment and suffer from non-negligible audio-visual latency in large-scale setups, where the finite speed of sound introduces meaningful error. Geometry and feature matching methods~ sync_feature1, sync_feature3, visualsync, rocsync estimate the amount of unsynchrony by finding spatiotemporal correspondences across views, and they are highly dependent on the quality of feature extraction and degrade considerably under the occlusion of tracked features. Approaches based on human or pose tracking~ sync_human3, sync_human5, sync_human1, sync_human2, sync_human4 align frames by tracking human body poses across cameras, and strictly require the presence of humans in the scene. It substantially limits their applicability to common real-world environments. Learning-based methods such as Sync-NeRF~ syncnerf, synctrack, sync_learning2 jointly optimize temporal offsets as learnable parameters by using rendering quality as a supervisory signal, yet they assume continuous frame availability across all views and fundamentally cannot recover from per-camera frame drops and freezes that arise independently across cameras. Method Overview Phase-DGS replaces the absolute timestamp used in conventional 4DGS with a per-frame phase derived from the image content. We observe that each frame possesses an inherent semantic phase within video sequences, independent of its absolute timestamp. For instance, in a sit-to-stand motion, the "fully seated" pose corresponds to the same phase regardless of which camera captures it or at what moment. Based on this observation, Phase-DGS extracts a phase from each camera image and uses it instead of the timestamp to supervise 4DGS training. Note that and represent the frame and camera indices, respectively. Since the phase is derived from the image content, it naturally accommodates unsynchronized capture conditions such as frame drops, frame freezes, and temporal offsets between cameras. Phase Extraction Module sec:PEM We introduce the phase projector module, which extracts a phase from each camera image using a pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder~ transformer, dinov2 followed by a lightweight MLP. Feature Generation. The input image of the -th frame of the -th camera is coarsely cropped to a motion-intensive region of interest (ROI) and resized to match the input resolution of the ViT encoder. Then, the cropped image is passed through a pretrained ViT encoder, which partitions it into patches and generates a token for each patch. We spatially aggregate all patch tokens by averaging to obtain a -dimensional global feature vector that summarizes the visual content of the image: Phase Projector. The global feature vector is subsequently passed through a lightweight MLP that consists of three fully connected layers, which produces a normalized phase value , Notably, the phase projector is trained without any explicit phase supervision; instead, it is optimized through the rendering loss together with the phase consistency and monotonic losses (see Sections~ sec:loss and~ sec:training ), enabling unsupervised phase extraction directly from visual observations. Feature Bank sec:feature bank The feature bank serves as a learnable reference repository that enforces cross-camera phase coherence, ensuring that identical motion states share the same phase across all views by enabling the phase projector to map each input feature to a phase through comparison against stored references. The feature bank is defined as , where is the number of cameras, is the video length, is an upsampling factor, and is the dimension of the feature. is designed to handle videos with varying frame rates or staggered frame timestamps on some cameras, providing finer temporal resolution in the feature bank. Since the DINOv2 features are extracted independently from each image and do not contain temporal information, we make the feature bank learnable rather than fine-tuning the entire ViT encoder for every scene. Inspired by temporal prototype learning~ prototype , which aligns multiple videos through learned prototypes, the feature bank is optimized jointly with the phase projector to adapt to the scene, so that frames capturing the same motion state are assigned the same phase across all views. When the feature bank is fixed, which corresponds to a fixed-memory alternative, the accuracy of phase estimation drops substantially (see Section~ sec:ablation ). title: HTCE: Homeomorphism-inspired Topological Cross-Scene Experience Canonicalization and Reuse for Object Navigation
summary: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in https://github.com/startracker0/htce.git
full_text: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable.
